PREFACE

This work emerges from a deep and abiding fascination with the convergence of two supreme intellectual traditions of ancient India — the performing arts as codified in Bharata Muni’s Natya Shastra, and the non-dual philosophy articulated by Adi Shankaracharya. At first glance, these may appear to inhabit separate domains: one the world of embodied movement, rhythm, and theatrical expression; the other, the rarefied realm of Advaita Vedanta where the physical world dissolves into the luminous awareness of Brahman. Yet, as this study endeavours to demonstrate, the two traditions are not merely tangential — they are profoundly, almost inevitably, intertwined.

The 108 Karanas of the Natya Shastra — those exquisite units of coordinated bodily movement first described in the fourth chapter of Bharata’s monumental treatise — have long been celebrated as the technical foundation of Indian classical dance. Carved in stone on the gopurams of Chidambaram and the corridors of Thanjavur, they stand as testimony to a civilisation that understood the dancing body as a sacred instrument. But beyond their technical brilliance lies a deeper metaphysical claim:

3
Preface

that the 108 Karanas embody the very movement of consciousness, the pulse of the cosmos, the dance of Shiva himself.

It is precisely here that Shankaracharya’s voice enters — not as a dance theorist, but as a philosopher-poet who saw in the imagery of cosmic dance the most perfect metaphor for his Advaitic vision. In Soundarya Lahari, Vivekachudamani, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, and his numerous hymns, Shankara employs the language of movement, mudra, and performance to illuminate the deepest truths about consciousness, Maya, and liberation. This book systematically traces those metaphorical threads and weaves them into a contemporary scholarly framework.

The work is organised into fifteen chapters, moving from historical and philosophical foundations through technical analysis of the Karanas, the aesthetic theory of Rasa, temple iconography, and finally toward contemporary applications in neuroscience, psychology, and global performance studies. It is simultaneously a work of Indology, performance theory, philosophy, and cultural studies — reflecting the inherently interdisciplinary nature of its subject.

I am deeply grateful to the teachers, scholars, and performers whose insights have informed this work over many years of study. I am particularly indebted to the classical tradition itself — its texts, its temples, and its living practitioners — without whom none of this intellectual exploration would be possible.

“Nritta, Nritya, Natya — in these three syllables lies the entire universe of human expression.”

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This monograph presents the first comprehensive contemporary study of the intersection between Bharata Muni’s Natya Shastra — specifically its doctrine of the 108 Karanas — and the metaphysical philosophy of Adi Shankaracharya (788–820 CE). It argues that Shankaracharya’s frequent recourse to the imagery of cosmic dance, theatrical performance, and bodily movement in his works is not merely decorative but constitutes a sustained philosophical strategy: the elevation of embodied art to the status of spiritual epistemology. The 108 Karanas, far from being merely technical prescriptions for classical dance, function as a cosmological map — a physical encoding of Advaita Vedanta’s core insights about the nature of consciousness, energy, and liberation.

Central Thesis

The 108 Karanas of the Natya Shastra constitute a cosmological map encoded in embodied movement. Shankaracharya’s metaphors — particularly in Soundarya Lahari and Vivekachudamani — constitute a philosophical commentary on this map, reading the body in motion as a text of spiritual truth.

6
The Cosmic Choreography

The Rasa theory of Abhinavagupta provides the bridge between both traditions, establishing that the highest aesthetic experience and the highest philosophical recognition converge on the same non-dual awareness.

Scope and Methodology

The study employs a multi-disciplinary methodology drawing on: textual scholarship (philological analysis of Sanskrit primary sources including Natya Shastra, Soundarya Lahari, Vivekachudamani, Abhinavabharati, and related texts); performance theory (structural and phenomenological analysis of the Karana system and its embodied practice); art history (systematic study of temple sculptures at Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Darasuram, and related sites); philosophy (comprehensive analysis of Advaita Vedanta and its aesthetic dimensions); and contemporary frameworks from cognitive science, somatic studies, and global performance theory.

Key Findings

  • The Natya Shastra’s concept of Karana — coordinated hand-foot unit — corresponds structurally to Shankaracharya’s philosophical concept of Spanda: the primordial vibration or pulsation of consciousness that underlies all manifestation.
  • The 108 Karanas collectively encode the full spectrum of consciousness-states described in Advaita Vedanta, from gross physical engagement (Bhumi Karanas) to pure transcendent awareness (Urdhva/Akasha Karanas).
7
Executive Summary
  • Shankaracharya’s Soundarya Lahari contains at least seventeen verses whose imagery directly parallels specific Karanas described in Natya Shastra Chapter IV, demonstrating the deliberate, philosophically precise nature of his movement imagery.
  • The Shanta Rasa advocated by Abhinavagupta as the meta-rasa finds its philosophical grounding in Shankaracharya’s concept of Ananda — the bliss-consciousness that is Brahman’s deepest nature.
  • Temple sculptures of the 108 Karanas at Chidambaram, Thanjavur, and Darasuram function as three-dimensional philosophical texts, translating Shankaracharya’s metaphysics into a permanent iconographic programme.
  • Cognitive neuroscience — particularly research on mirror neurons, the Default Mode Network, and embodied cognition — provides indirect empirical support for the tradition’s deepest claims about the transformative potential of sustained Karana practice.

Structure

The book is organised into fifteen chapters spanning approximately 250 pages. Chapters One through Four establish foundations — the meeting of two traditions, the Natya Shastra’s cosmological framework, the 108 Karanas’ technical architecture, and Shankaracharya’s philosophical and aesthetic vision. Chapters Five through Eight develop the philosophical synthesis — Soundarya Lahari and the dance of consciousness,

8
The Cosmic Choreography

Advaita and movement aesthetics, Rasa theory, and Tandava cosmology. Chapters Nine through Eleven explore material and technical dimensions — temple iconography, mudra and gesture, sound and rhythm. Chapters Twelve through Fourteen examine contemporary dimensions — living transmission, global perspectives, and cognitive science. Chapter Fifteen synthesises and concludes. The work includes a comprehensive Glossary of Sanskrit Terms, two Appendices (complete Karana descriptions and Shankaracharya’s dance metaphor concordance), and a full Bibliography.

CHAPTER I

The Two Traditions

An Introduction

“Where the dance of Shiva ceases, there creation ends; where it resumes, life begins anew.”

— Ananda Coomaraswamy, The Dance of Shiva, 1918

1.1The Meeting of Two Worlds

India’s intellectual heritage presents a paradox that has fascinated scholars for centuries: a civilisation that simultaneously cultivated the most rigorous forms of philosophical abstraction and the most sensuous, embodied forms of artistic expression, regarding these not as opposites but as complementary pathways toward the same ultimate truth. Nowhere is this paradox more strikingly embodied than in the relationship between the Natya Shastra of Bharata Muni and the philosophical corpus of Adi Shankaracharya. These two extraordinary bodies of knowledge, separated by nearly a millennium in their final crystallisation, share a common root in India’s oldest intellectual soil and converge, with remarkable

12
The Cosmic Choreography

precision, on a single insight: that the human being is most completely alive, most transparently conscious, when the body moves in full awareness of the spirit it houses.

The Natya Shastra, composed somewhere between 200 BCE and 200 CE — with the scholarly consensus placing its core strata around the second century BCE and its later accretions extending well into the early centuries of the Common Era — represents the most comprehensive treatise on performing arts ever produced in the ancient world. Its thirty-six chapters cover every conceivable aspect of theatrical production, from the measurement and consecration of the stage to the psychology of aesthetic experience and the metaphysics of artistic creation. The text moves with equal confidence through the technicalities of hand-gesture vocabulary and the philosophical depths of aesthetic theory, treating with identical seriousness the angle of a dancer’s wrist and the nature of consciousness itself. This breadth is not encyclopaedic sprawl but deliberate philosophical vision: Bharata understood Natya as a total art form in the deepest sense, one that encompassed every dimension of human experience and therefore demanded a theory of every dimension of reality.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical corpus, composed roughly nine to ten centuries after the Natya Shastra’s core was laid down, represents an equally comprehensive intellectual achievement of a very different kind. Where Bharata built outward — from the divine origin of Natya through the detailed specification of its techniques to the heights of aesthetic theory — Shankara built inward: from the apparent complexity of the experienced world through progressive layers of philosophical analysis to the simple,

13
The Two Traditions

luminous ground of pure consciousness that he identified as the only ultimately real thing. Yet at their respective summits, both thinkers arrive at the same place: a recognition of reality as non-dual, as a unity that manifests as diversity without ever ceasing to be one, as consciousness that dances in and as the world without ever being bound by it.

This study traces the pathways by which these two great traditions meet, illuminate, and enrich each other. It argues that Shankaracharya’s frequent recourse to the imagery of dance, movement, and theatrical performance in his philosophical and devotional writings is not decorative or incidental but constitutes a sustained, philosophically serious engagement with the very tradition codified in the Natya Shastra. And conversely, it argues that the Natya Shastra’s doctrines — especially its teaching on the 108 Karanas — contain, encoded in the language of embodied movement, the same metaphysical insights that Shankaracharya articulated in the language of philosophy.

The convergence of these two traditions has practical as well as theoretical significance. For the contemporary student of classical Indian dance, understanding the Advaitic philosophical dimensions of the Karana system transforms the entire enterprise: what might otherwise appear as demanding technical training becomes a form of philosophical inquiry conducted through the medium of the body. For the student of Advaita Vedanta, understanding that Shankaracharya’s dance imagery is not merely metaphorical but points toward a genuine embodied path opens new dimensions of practice that purely discursive philosophy cannot access. And for the scholar of Indian civilisation more

14
The Cosmic Choreography

broadly, the convergence of Natya Shastra and Advaita Vedanta in the figure of Shankaracharya represents one of the clearest examples of what makes Indian intellectual culture uniquely capable of holding philosophy and art, theory and practice, transcendence and embodiment, in a single, integrated vision.

1.2Bharata Muni and the Divine Origin of Dance

According to the Natya Shastra’s own account — presented in a frame narrative that is at once mythological, philosophical, and pedagogically precise — the art of Natya was created by Brahma himself at the request of the gods, who desired an entertainment and instruction that would be accessible to all four castes and capable of addressing the full range of human experience, including joy, sorrow, laughter, terror, and spiritual liberation. This narrative of divine origin is significant not merely as mythology but as philosophical statement: Natya partakes of all four domains of Vedic knowledge and transcends the social restrictions that limited access to the Vedas, offering the possibility of liberation through the medium of aesthetic experience to every human being regardless of birth or station.

Brahma’s method of creation is itself philosophically instructive. He is said to have extracted Pathya (recitation/speech) from the Rigveda, Gita (song and music) from the Samaveda, Abhinaya (gesture and expression) from the Yajurveda, and Rasa (aesthetic emotion and flavour) from the Atharvaveda. This fourfold structure — word, music, gesture, emotion —

15
The Two Traditions

constitutes what we might today call the total semiotics of performance: the complete range of sign systems through which human beings communicate and create meaning. By deriving Natya from all four Vedas rather than any single one, Bharata’s mythological narrative establishes dance-drama as a synthetic, integrative art form that cannot be reduced to any single dimension of human expression.

The sage Bharata himself — whether a single historical figure or, as some scholars argue, a collective name for a lineage of performance theorists — received this art from Brahma and transmitted it to his hundred sons, who became the first actors and dancers. This lineage of transmission is not merely a genealogical claim but a philosophical one: it establishes Natya as a tradition in the precise Sanskrit sense of sampradaya — a living current of knowledge that flows from teacher to student across generations, maintaining its essential quality precisely through the intimacy of this personal transmission. The same model of transmission, it is worth noting at the outset, is central to Shankaracharya’s understanding of the transmission of Brahma-vidya, the knowledge of Brahman.

Shiva himself enters this origin narrative in the subsequent tradition as the supreme dancer — Nataraja, Lord of Dance — who performs the Ananda Tandava in the cosmic hall of Chidambaram. This Tandava is not merely a metaphor but an ontological description: the universe exists as a dance of Shiva’s consciousness, maintained by the rhythm of divine will. The 108 Karanas that Shiva is said to have performed at Chidambaram and which were subsequently codified by Bharata Muni represent

16
The Cosmic Choreography

the complete vocabulary of this cosmic dance. When the Natya Shastra specifies 108 Karanas — not 100, not 112, but precisely 108 — it is making a cosmological claim: these 108 movement-units constitute the complete vocabulary of cosmic self-expression, the full range of positions that consciousness can take in the dance of manifestation.

The significance of the mythological origin narrative should not be underestimated by the modern reader inclined to dismiss it as pre-scientific religious thinking. In the Indian intellectual tradition, a narrative of divine origin is a way of asserting the absolute, trans-historical validity of the knowledge being transmitted. To say that Natya was created by Brahma is to say that the principles of great performance are not cultural conventions but cosmic laws — that the relationship between a beautifully executed Karana and the consciousness that perceives it is as necessary and universal as the relationship between the sun and light. Shankaracharya, working in the same intellectual tradition, makes a precisely analogous claim for Brahma-vidya: the knowledge of non-duality is not a human invention but a recognition of what has always been the case.

1.3Shankaracharya and the Non-Dual Vision

Adi Shankaracharya — traditionally dated 788-820 CE, though some scholars propose alternative chronologies — represents one of the most extraordinary intellectual achievements in the history of world philosophy. Born in Kaladi, a small village in what is now

17
The Two Traditions

Kerala, he is said to have achieved the rare status of a bal-sanyasi, renouncing the world in childhood with his mother’s reluctant blessing after demonstrating the philosophical precocity that would characterise his entire brief life. He became a disciple of the great sage Govinda Bhagavatpada, who himself was a disciple of Gaudapada — the author of the Mandukya Karika, the first systematic exposition of the Advaitic interpretation of the Upanishads.

Within a lifespan that tradition limits to thirty-two years, Shankaracharya accomplished a philosophical renovation of Indian thought whose scope and depth remain astonishing. He traversed the entire subcontinent on foot, engaging in philosophical debate with representatives of every major school — the Mimamsakas who insisted on the ultimate authority of Vedic ritual, the Buddhists in their various forms, the Jains, the Samkhyas, the Vaisheshikas, the devotional Shaivites and Vaishnavites. In every case, his aim was not merely to defeat his opponents in argument but to locate the grain of truth in their positions and show how it was more completely and coherently expressed within the Advaitic framework.

His philosophical system — Advaita Vedanta, non-dual Vedanta — holds that reality is fundamentally one: pure, self-luminous consciousness that he calls Brahman, which is identical with the innermost self of every being, the Atman. The apparent multiplicity of the world — its diversity of objects, beings, experiences, and relationships — is the result of Maya, a cosmic power of illusion or creative appearance that superimposes apparent difference upon the undivided ground of being. Maya is

18
The Cosmic Choreography

neither fully real (because it depends on Brahman for its existence) nor fully unreal (because it is the experienced world, not mere nothing). It is mithya — apparently real at the conventional level, ultimately non-existent at the absolute level, like the apparent silver seen in a shell or the apparent snake perceived in a rope.

Liberation, in Shankara’s system, consists not in any kind of physical or spiritual achievement but in a shift of understanding: the direct recognition, through Viveka (discrimination) and Vichara (philosophical inquiry), that one has always been Brahman, that the separate self was always an appearance and never a reality, that consciousness is the only substance and the world is its dance. This recognition — Aparoksha Anubhuti, direct non-mediate awareness — does not require any particular practice, austerity, or achievement. It requires only the removal of the ignorance (Avidya) that concealed what was always already the case.

This philosophical framework has the most profound implications for the arts. If Brahman is the only reality, and if Maya — the world of apparent diversity — is Brahman’s own creative power of self-expression, then the highest art is that which makes Brahman’s own nature most transparently visible through the medium of Maya. The great dancer who performs the 108 Karanas with complete technical mastery and inward illumination is not merely executing a skillful physical performance but manifesting Brahman through the medium of embodied movement — making the cosmic dance visible in human form. Shankaracharya understood

19
The Two Traditions

this with extraordinary clarity, as his devotional poetry demonstrates on virtually every page.

1.4The Historical Relationship Between the Two Traditions

The historical relationship between the Natya Shastra tradition and the Advaita Vedanta tradition is complex and has been insufficiently studied. The Natya Shastra’s philosophical framework draws primarily from the Samkhya system — the ancient dualistic philosophy that posits an eternal, conscious Purusha (spirit) and an eternal, dynamic Prakriti (matter/nature) as the twin foundations of existence. Prakriti’s three fundamental qualities — Sattva (luminosity/clarity), Rajas (energy/activity), and Tamas (inertia/darkness) — are understood to underlie all phenomena, including the various Rasas of aesthetic experience.

Shankaracharya, as is well known, was deeply critical of the Samkhya system, regarding its dualism as philosophically incoherent: he could not accept the postulation of an eternal Prakriti independent of Purusha, since in his view consciousness alone is ultimately real and all apparent matter is its projection through Maya. Yet his criticisms of Samkhya are directed at its metaphysical framework, not at the insights it contains about the structure of experience — insights that Shankaracharya largely accepts and reinterprets within an Advaitic framework. The Samkhyan analysis of the three Gunas, for instance, appears in Shankara’s own exposition of the three states of consciousness

20
The Cosmic Choreography

(waking, dream, deep sleep), reinterpreted in terms of the relative predominance of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas in the veiling activity of Maya.

The temple culture of South India, which developed the most elaborate and beautiful expressions of both the Natya Shastra’s performing arts traditions and the Advaita Vedanta philosophy, provides the most concrete historical context for understanding how these two great traditions interacted. The Agamic tradition — the body of scripture and practice governing temple worship throughout South India — draws from both sources: it employs the Natya Shastra’s gesture vocabulary in ritual contexts and simultaneously draws from Advaitic and Shaiva philosophical frameworks to interpret the meaning of these gestures. The temple itself, in the Agamic understanding, is both a performance space (where the ritual drama of creation, sustenance, and dissolution is continuously enacted) and a philosophical text (where every architectural element encodes a philosophical principle).

Shankaracharya’s relationship to the temple tradition is fascinating and somewhat paradoxical. As a proponent of Nirguna Brahman — the formless, attributeless absolute — he might be expected to be indifferent or even hostile to the elaborate iconographic programmes of South Indian temples. Yet his compositions include some of the most beautiful hymns to the temple deities in the Sanskrit canon, and his philosophical interpretations of these deities consistently find in their imagery — including their dance imagery — expressions of the deepest Advaitic truths. The Nataraja icon, in particular, seems to have held a special place in Shankaracharya’s philosophical

21
The Two Traditions

imagination: the cosmic dancer who is simultaneously pure consciousness (Shiva) and dynamic energy (Shakti), simultaneously the ground of all being and the most beautiful of all forms, embodies with perfect visual precision the Advaitic vision of Brahman as simultaneously Nirguna (formless) and Saguna (with form).

The Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE), which occurred roughly two to four centuries after Shankaracharya, witnessed the most systematic integration of the two traditions in physical form: the great Chola temples with their sculptural programmes of the 108 Karanas represent the materialisation of the philosophical synthesis that this book traces. The Chola kings and their priestly scholars appear to have understood precisely the relationship between the Advaitic philosophy that Shankaracharya had systematised and the dance tradition that the Natya Shastra had codified, and they gave that understanding monumental expression in stone. The Chidambaram gopuram panels — where all 108 Karanas are carved in sequence, presided over by the Nataraja image in the innermost shrine — are not merely art historical documents but philosophical statements of extraordinary precision.

1.5The Number 108: Cosmological Significance

Before proceeding to the detailed analysis that forms the body of this study, it is worth pausing to consider the number 108 itself, which is far from arbitrary and which, properly understood,

22
The Cosmic Choreography

already encodes much of the philosophical programme that this book will explore. The number 108 carries enormous symbolic weight throughout Indian intellectual and religious culture, appearing in contexts ranging from astronomy to music theory to the organisation of canonical texts.

In Vedic cosmological mathematics, 108 is understood as the product of 12 zodiacal signs and 9 celestial bodies — a formula that maps the complete range of cosmic influences governing earthly existence. The ancient astronomers observed, with remarkable accuracy, that the distance from the Earth to the Sun is approximately 108 times the diameter of the Sun, and that the distance from the Earth to the Moon is approximately 108 times the diameter of the Moon. These observations, whether or not they were made before the composition of the Natya Shastra, reflect the same cosmological intuition that the number 108 represents a kind of cosmic completeness — a set of relationships that constitutes the full expression of a given order of reality.

In the textual tradition, there are 108 Upanishads, representing the complete range of Vedantic wisdom. Each of the major deities has 108 names, arranged in Ashtottara Shatanamavali (108-name hymns) that enumerate the complete range of the deity’s attributes and manifestations. The standard mala (rosary) used in meditation and japa practice contains 108 beads, the full circuit of which represents a complete traversal of the range of consciousness. In music, the Sangita Ratnakara — the thirteenth-century compendium of Indian musical theory — identifies 108 talas (rhythmic cycles), just as the Natya Shastra identifies 108 Karanas.

23
The Two Traditions

Shankaracharya was deeply attentive to this symbolism. His own compositions include numerous Ashtottara Shatanamavali — 108-name hymns to Shiva, to the Goddess, to Vishnu — and these hymns are understood not as arbitrary lists but as systematic enumerations of the complete range of divine attributes, each name capturing a different facet of the deity’s infinite nature. To compose a 108-name hymn is to claim that the 108 names constitute a complete description of the deity — not exhaustive in the sense of leaving nothing out, but complete in the sense that every subsequent expansion would merely elaborate what these 108 names already contain.

When Bharata Muni specifies exactly 108 Karanas, he is making the same kind of claim: these 108 movement-units constitute the complete vocabulary of sacred movement, not arbitrary in their selection but cosmologically necessary in their totality. The 108 Karanas are not 108 of the possible movements that a human body can make but rather 108 fundamental movement-types that collectively cover the entire range of the body’s expressive possibilities — from the most grounded and earthbound to the most elevated and transcendent, from the most inward and still to the most dynamic and expansive. Like the 108 names of Shiva, the 108 Karanas together constitute a complete portrait of the divine in the medium of embodied movement.

This cosmological understanding of the number 108 should inform the reader’s approach to this entire study. The 108 Karanas are not a curriculum that happens to contain 108 items; they are a mandala, a sacred diagram, a map of consciousness expressed in the language of the body. When Shankaracharya

24
The Cosmic Choreography

employs the imagery of cosmic dance in his philosophical works, he is not reaching for a convenient metaphor; he is invoking a system of symbols — the 108 Karanas, the Nataraja icon, the Ananda Tandava — whose philosophical content is as precise and rigorous as anything in the Upanishads themselves.

1.6Methodology and Organisation of This Study

This study employs a multi-disciplinary methodology that reflects the inherently interdisciplinary nature of its subject. No single academic discipline — Sanskrit philology, performance studies, art history, philosophy, cognitive science — is individually adequate to the full dimensions of the question being addressed. The relationship between Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy is simultaneously a textual question (what do the primary sources actually say?), a philosophical question (what do these claims mean and how do they relate?), an art historical question (how are these relationships materialised in sculpture, temple architecture, and iconographic tradition?), a performance studies question (how do these relationships manifest in the living practice of classical Indian dance?), and an anthropological question (what does this convergence reveal about Indian civilisation’s distinctive ways of organising and transmitting knowledge?).

The primary texts examined in this study include, on the Natya Shastra side: the complete Natya Shastra in the edition of M.M. Ghosh, with particular attention to Chapters 1-9 (covering

25
The Two Traditions

philosophical foundations, theatrical space, the Karana and Angahara systems, and the theory of Rasa) and Chapter 36 (the concluding philosophical synthesis); the Abhinavabharati of Abhinavagupta, the most important commentary on the Natya Shastra and itself a work of major philosophical significance; and the Sangita Ratnakara of Sarngadeva for its thirteenth-century synthesis of the performance arts traditions.

On the Shankaracharya side, the primary texts include: Soundarya Lahari (complete, with particular attention to verses 1-41 of the Ananda Lahari section and verses 42-100 of the Soundarya Lahari section); Vivekachudamani; Upadesha Sahasri; Dakshinamurti Stotra and its commentary by Sureshvara; Shiva Tandava Stotram; Bhaja Govindam; Nirvana Shatakam; Aparoksha Anubhuti; and the major Upanishad commentaries (Mandukya with Gaudapada’s Karika, Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya) insofar as they contain relevant aesthetic or movement imagery.

Secondary scholarship has been consulted across multiple languages and disciplines. Foundational works include Ananda Coomaraswamy’s The Dance of Shiva (1918), still unsurpassed as a philosophical interpretation of the Nataraja iconography; Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts (1968) and Bharata: The Natyashastra (1996); V. Raghavan’s The Number of Rasas (1940) and his Sanskrit studies; Padma Subrahmanyam’s Karanas: Common Dance Codes of India and Indonesia (1997); Stella Kramrisch’s The Hindu Temple (1946); and more recent work by scholars including

26
The Cosmic Choreography

Mandakranta Bose, Anne-Marie Gaston, David Shulman, and Srinivasa Ayya Srinivasan.

The organisation of the study proceeds from general foundations to specific analyses and back to synthetic conclusions. Chapters Two and Three establish the historical, textual, and technical foundations of the Natya Shastra and the 108 Karanas. Chapters Four and Five do the same for Shankaracharya and the Soundarya Lahari. Chapters Six through Eight examine the philosophical dimensions of the relationship: the aesthetics of movement in Advaita Vedanta, the theory of Rasa and its Advaitic dimensions, and the cosmological significance of the Tandava. Chapters Nine through Eleven examine the material and technical dimensions: temple iconography, mudra and gesture, sound and rhythm. Chapters Twelve through Fourteen examine contemporary dimensions: living transmission, global perspectives, and cognitive science. Chapter Fifteen synthesises the entire argument and draws conclusions for contemporary practice and scholarship. The Epilogue, Glossary, Appendices, and Bibliography provide supplementary resources for the reader wishing to pursue specific dimensions of the argument in greater depth.

1.7The Intellectual Climate of Bharata’s India

To appreciate the full significance of the Natya Shastra’s emergence, one must situate it within the extraordinary intellectual ferment of the centuries around the turn of the

27
The Two Traditions

Common Era in India — a period that produced not only the Natya Shastra but also the Mahabharata in its final redaction, the major Upanishads' synthesis, the foundational texts of the Samkhya, Yoga, Nyaya, and Vaisheshika schools, and the earliest systematic treatments of grammar, medicine, mathematics, and statecraft. This was an age of systematic intellectual synthesis unprecedented in world history, in which the remarkable diversity of India’s earlier intellectual traditions was being organised, codified, and brought into coherent relationship with each other.

The Natya Shastra participates directly in this project of synthesis. Its claim that Natya is a fifth Veda, encompassing the knowledge of all four earlier Vedas, is not a modest suggestion but a bold intellectual manifesto: performing arts are not a subsidiary cultural activity but a complete system of knowledge capable of encompassing and transmitting the entire range of human wisdom. This claim demanded, and received, an elaborate philosophical justification in the text’s opening chapters — a justification that draws simultaneously from Vedic authority, Samkhya philosophical analysis, and the direct authority of divine revelation to establish Natya’s credentials.

The intellectual climate of this period was also shaped by the presence of Buddhism and Jainism as major intellectual and spiritual forces, and the Natya Shastra cannot be fully understood without acknowledging the implicit dialogue it conducts with these traditions. Buddhism’s emphasis on the cessation of suffering through the transcendence of desire, Jainism’s insistence on the complete independence of the conscious soul from material entanglement — both of these positions present

28
The Cosmic Choreography

challenges to any tradition that valorises sensory experience and embodied expression as paths to liberation. The Natya Shastra’s response to these challenges is sophisticated: it agrees that attachment and desire are obstacles to liberation, but argues that the aesthetic experience generated by great performance is precisely not attachment or desire but their purification and transcendence — the Rasa experience that transforms personal emotion into universal awareness.

The role of royal patronage in shaping the intellectual environment of the Natya Shastra cannot be overlooked. The great royal courts of the Gupta and Kushana periods maintained elaborate performance traditions and competed with each other in the brilliance of their artistic productions. This patronage context gave performing arts both social prestige and philosophical aspiration: the great ruler who patronised fine performance was understood to be not merely providing entertainment for his court but enacting the cosmic order, demonstrating through the beauty and excellence of the arts under his patronage that his kingdom participated in the divine order of things. The philosophical dimensions of the Natya Shastra must be understood against this backdrop of royal patronage and its associated ideological commitments.

The relationship between the Natya Shastra and the Sanskrit grammatical tradition — particularly Panini’s Ashtadhyayi and its commentarial tradition — is another dimension of the intellectual context that deserves acknowledgment. Panini’s grammar, which reduced the entire structure of Sanskrit to a set of compact, elegant rules, represented the paradigmatic

29
The Two Traditions

achievement of systematic analysis in ancient India, and later intellectual traditions consistently modelled their own systematic analyses on the Paninian achievement. The Natya Shastra’s systematic enumeration of movement types, gesture categories, emotional states, and dramatic forms reflects this same impulse toward complete, systematic analysis — the ambition to reduce the infinite variety of performance to a finite set of fundamental elements whose combinations can generate the complete range of theatrical possibility.

Understanding the Natya Shastra in this intellectual climate allows us to appreciate more fully what Shankaracharya is doing when he draws on its traditions in his own philosophical work several centuries later. He is not reaching across a vast cultural divide to borrow a few picturesque metaphors; he is engaging with a living intellectual tradition of the highest sophistication, one that had developed, in the centuries between Bharata and Shankara, an elaborate philosophical commentary tradition (culminating in Abhinavagupta’s Abhinavabharati) and had permeated every dimension of Indian cultural life from the village festival to the royal court to the temple ritual.

1.8The Question of Shankara’s Direct Engagement with Performance Traditions

A question that must be addressed directly in any study of the relationship between Shankaracharya and the Natya Shastra tradition is the extent to which Shankara had direct, personal

30
The Cosmic Choreography

engagement with performing arts practice, as distinct from theoretical or literary familiarity with the tradition. The traditional biographies provide some evidence on this point, though it must be evaluated with appropriate critical caution. The Madhaviya Shankaravijaya, the most comprehensive of the traditional biographies, describes Shankara as having participated directly in temple ritual performance in Kerala, having studied Sanskrit drama and poetics as part of his comprehensive education, and having composed not merely devotional poetry but elaborate dramatic compositions including at least one Bhana (monologue play).

The Kerala cultural context of Shankara’s birth and early formation is crucial here. Kerala in the eighth century CE was a culture of extraordinarily rich performance traditions. The Kutiyattam tradition — the oldest surviving form of Sanskrit theatre in continuous performance — was already well established in the Kerala temple complex system, performed in the special theatre halls (Kuttambalams) attached to major temples. The Koothu and Krishnanattam traditions were developing the forms of dance-drama that would eventually evolve into Kathakali. The tradition of Thullal — a form of expressive solo performance combining poetry, music, and expressive gesture — was probably already present in some form. And the martial arts tradition of Kalaripayattu, which shares fundamental movement principles with the Karana system of the Natya Shastra, was deeply embedded in Kerala cultural life.

For a precocious, intellectually omnivorous child of the Brahmin class in this environment, exposure to all these

31
The Two Traditions

performance traditions would have been not merely possible but virtually inevitable. The distinction between philosophical study and performance culture that seems natural to a modern Western reader was far less pronounced in eighth-century Kerala: the Brahmin intellectual was expected to be conversant with the full range of cultural forms, including performance, and the philosophical and ritual dimensions of performance were inseparable from its artistic dimensions in the temple culture of the time.

This suggests that when Shankaracharya employs the imagery of the Natya Shastra in his philosophical and devotional compositions, he is drawing not merely on book knowledge but on embodied cultural knowledge — knowledge that includes the kinaesthetic experience of having witnessed, and possibly participated in, the performance forms he references. The specificity and precision of his dance imagery, which we will trace in detail in Chapter Five, points toward this kind of embodied familiarity rather than purely textual acquaintance.

The philosophical implications of this biographical speculation are significant. If Shankara’s engagement with performance traditions was genuinely embodied and not merely literary, then his use of performance imagery in his philosophy represents something more than analogy or illustration. It represents the bringing into philosophical articulation of an insight that had been formed, at least in part, through direct aesthetic experience — the kind of experience that the Natya Shastra itself identifies as the highest vehicle of truth, the experience of genuine Rasa that provides a direct, if transient and

32
The Cosmic Choreography

mediated, taste of the non-dual awareness that Advaita Vedanta identifies as liberation.

1.9Overview of the Arguments in Each Chapter

The argument of this book proceeds through a carefully structured sequence of analytical moves, each chapter building on the foundations laid by the preceding ones while contributing something new to the overall case. A brief overview of each chapter’s specific contribution will help the reader navigate the complexity of the argument.

Chapter Two, 'Natya Shastra — Text, Context, and Cosmology,' establishes the textual and philosophical foundations of the Natya Shastra tradition, with particular attention to the philosophical framework within which the 108 Karanas are situated. It argues that the Natya Shastra’s claim that Natya is a fifth Veda is not merely rhetorical but reflects a genuine philosophical position about the relationship between aesthetic experience and spiritual liberation that will be central to every subsequent chapter.

Chapter Three, 'The 108 Karanas — Technical Architecture and Spiritual Geometry,' provides the technical foundation necessary for understanding the philosophical arguments of later chapters. It analyses the internal structure of the Karana system, its relationship to the Angahara system, and the philosophical significance of the number 108. Detailed analyses of selected Karanas demonstrate the kind of philosophical reading that the

33
The Two Traditions

tradition encourages and that Shankaracharya’s writings implicitly perform.

Chapter Four, 'Shankaracharya — Philosopher, Poet, and Visionary,' presents the philosophical and biographical context of Shankaracharya’s work, with particular attention to the dimensions of his thought most relevant to the aesthetic and performance traditions. It argues that the coexistence of rigorous philosophical analysis and intensely sensuous devotional poetry in Shankara’s work reflects not an internal contradiction but a deliberate pedagogical strategy — a strategy that culminates in the use of the cosmic dance as the supreme metaphor for the non-dual truth.

Chapters Five through Eight constitute the philosophical heart of the book, examining the relationship between the two traditions at the level of their most fundamental philosophical claims. Chapter Five analyses the Soundarya Lahari in detail, mapping its movement imagery onto specific Karanas and demonstrating the systematic character of Shankara’s engagement with the Natya Shastra vocabulary. Chapter Six examines the broader question of the body in Advaita philosophy, arguing that Shankara’s treatment of embodiment is more nuanced and more sympathetic to embodied practice than is usually recognised. Chapter Seven analyses Rasa theory and its Advaitic dimensions, with particular attention to Abhinavagupta’s identification of Shanta Rasa with the experience of Brahman. Chapter Eight examines the cosmological dimensions of the Tandava, showing how the five-function theology of the Nataraja icon

34
The Cosmic Choreography

maps onto Shankara’s account of the relationship between Brahman and Maya.

Chapters Nine through Eleven examine the material and institutional dimensions of the synthesis: the temple iconographic programmes that materialise it in stone, the mudra vocabulary that expresses it in gesture, and the sound and rhythm systems that embed it in time. These chapters demonstrate that the philosophical synthesis traced in the earlier chapters is not merely a theoretical possibility but had actual historical expression in the art, architecture, and practice of South Indian temple culture.

Chapters Twelve through Fourteen bring the argument into the present: the living transmission of the traditions through the guru-shishya parampara, the global dimensions of the insight encoded in the Karana system, and the contemporary scientific frameworks that provide new ways of understanding the tradition’s deepest claims. Chapter Fifteen synthesises the entire argument and draws out its implications for contemporary theory and practice.

Throughout, the reader should bear in mind that this book is simultaneously a work of scholarly analysis and an act of philosophical engagement. Its argument is not merely that these two great traditions happen to be related but that their relationship illuminates something fundamental about the nature of consciousness, embodiment, and liberation — something that remains as relevant and as challenging to contemporary human understanding as it was when Bharata Muni first described the 108 movements of Shiva’s cosmic dance.

35
The Two Traditions

1.10The Vedic Background: Sound, Sacrifice, and the Body of the Cosmos

The deepest roots of both the Natya Shastra’s performance theory and Shankaracharya’s philosophical vision lie in the Vedic tradition’s understanding of the universe as constituted by sacrificial action — specifically the primordial sacrifice of the cosmic Person (Purusha), described in the Rigveda’s Purusha Sukta, from whose dismembered body all of creation arose. This mythological narrative is not merely a cosmogonic story but a philosophical statement about the relationship between consciousness, sacrifice, and the structure of existence: the universe is the self-offering of the divine consciousness, a sacrifice in which the one gives itself to become the many without ceasing to be one.

The Natya Shastra’s positioning of itself as a fifth Veda must be understood against this Vedic background. If the four Vedas represent the complete vocabulary of the Vedic sacrificial tradition — the sacred sounds through which the divine order is maintained through ritual enactment — then a fifth Veda would need to represent a complete expansion of that vocabulary into a new domain. Bharata’s claim is that Natya constitutes this expansion: where the four Vedas maintain the divine order through sound-based ritual, Natya maintains it through movement-based performance. The dancer’s body, in the Natya Shastra’s understanding, is a sacrificial body — a body given over completely to the service of the divine, in which every movement is

36
The Cosmic Choreography

an offering and every gesture a form of the primordial sacrifice through which the cosmos is continuously renewed.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical commentary on the Purusha Sukta provides the most systematic Advaitic interpretation of the Vedic sacrifice mythology. For Shankara, the sacrifice of the cosmic Person is not a historical event but an ongoing metaphysical truth: the one consciousness continuously gives itself, through the medium of Maya, to become the apparent multiplicity of the world, without ever actually being divided or diminished. This is the philosophical meaning of the term Yajna (sacrifice) in the Advaitic context: not a ritual action but the eternal self-giving of consciousness in its creative self-expression as the world.

The 108 Karanas, understood within this framework of Vedic sacrifice, are the complete vocabulary of the cosmic body’s self-offering — the complete set of the ways in which divine consciousness gives itself in the medium of embodied movement. Each Karana is a moment of sacrifice in the philosophical sense: a moment in which the infinite gives itself to the finite, in which the formless takes on form, in which the one appears as many. And the complete performance of all 108 Karanas is the complete enactment of the cosmic sacrifice — the complete offering of the divine body in the full range of its creative self-expression, from the most grounded earthward gesture to the most elevated transcendent pose.

This Vedic dimension of the Karana tradition helps explain why the performance of the Karanas in the temple context has always been understood as a form of worship (Puja) rather than

37
The Two Traditions

merely entertainment or artistry. The dancer who performs the 108 Karanas in the sanctified space of the temple is not merely executing skillful movements for an appreciative audience; she is enacting the cosmic sacrifice, offering the divine body’s complete vocabulary of self-expression as an act of worship to the divine consciousness whose self-expression it is. This is the deepest meaning of the Devadasi tradition’s understanding of performance as divine service: not service rendered by the human to the divine, but the divine serving itself through the medium of a consecrated human instrument.

The connection between the Vedic sacrifice tradition and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta is explicit in Shankara’s own writings. His commentary on the Bhagavad Gita’s analysis of Yajna (sacrifice) in Chapter Four consistently reads the term in its Advaitic register: the highest sacrifice is not the external ritual offering of materials to a fire but the internal offering of the ego-self to the fire of knowledge — the dissolution of the false identification with the limited self in the recognition of identity with the infinite consciousness. The 108 Karanas, performed with this understanding, constitute precisely this highest sacrifice: the complete offering of the performer’s ego-consciousness in the service of the divine consciousness whose complete vocabulary of embodied self-expression they constitute.

38
The Cosmic Choreography

1.11The Aesthetics of Cosmic Play: Lila and the Philosophical Significance of Performance

The Sanskrit concept of Lila — divine play or cosmic sport — provides another essential framework for understanding the relationship between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. Lila designates the spontaneous, purposeless, joyful creative activity of the divine — the creation and maintenance of the universe not as a serious project with external goals but as an expression of the divine’s own blissful, free, self-sufficient nature. The universe, in the Lila framework, is not a problem to be solved or a task to be accomplished but a dance to be danced — a play of consciousness that is its own justification and its own reward.

Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta integrates the concept of Lila as the most philosophically adequate description of the relationship between Brahman and Maya. The world-appearance is not Brahman’s mistake or Brahman’s bondage but Brahman’s Lila — the spontaneous, free, purposeless, blissful creative play of consciousness expressing itself through the medium of apparent diversity. This understanding immediately dissolves the apparent problem of the world’s existence: if the world is Brahman’s Lila, then its existence requires no external justification and its complexity requires no explanation beyond the simple fact that this is what blissful consciousness does — it plays, creating infinite variety from its own inexhaustible creative abundance.

The Natya Shastra’s performance tradition is the human analogue of this cosmic Lila. The classical performance —

39
The Two Traditions

especially when it achieves the highest level of artistic quality — is not merely an activity with external goals (entertaining an audience, expressing specific meanings, demonstrating technical skill) but a form of Lila: purposeless play that is its own justification, joyful expression that needs no external validation, creative abundance that flows from the performer’s own nature when technique has been fully internalised and all obstacles to spontaneous expression have been dissolved.

The 108 Karanas, in this framework, are not merely the technical vocabulary of a professional craft but the vocabulary of divine Lila — the specific forms in which the cosmic play of consciousness expresses itself in the medium of the human body. A complete performance of the 108 Karanas is a complete performance of cosmic Lila in human miniature: the full range of consciousness’s playful self-expression, from the most grounded to the most elevated, from the most simple to the most complex, from the most earthward to the most skyward.

The philosophical implications of the Lila framework for understanding the Karana tradition are significant. If the performance is Lila, then the performer’s motivation is not achievement but expression — not the desire to accomplish something but the spontaneous overflow of the consciousness that has been fully developed through training. This is the quality that experienced performers consistently describe as the hallmark of their greatest performances: not the feeling of having 'done well' but the feeling of having been 'used' by something larger than the individual ego — of having been, for the duration of the performance, a transparent vehicle for a creativity that flowed

40
The Cosmic Choreography

through them rather than from them. This is the quality that Shankaracharya attributes to the Jivanmukta in all their activities: not the purposeful striving of the ego-self but the spontaneous, purposeless, blissful expression of the infinite consciousness that has recognised itself as the ground of all activity.

The Lila framework also helps resolve a potential tension in the relationship between the tradition’s demanding technical training and its ultimate goal of spontaneous, free expression. The years of rigorous technical training required to master the 108 Karanas might seem to be at odds with the spontaneous, effortless quality of genuine Lila. But the tradition’s answer is clear: the technical training is not an end in itself but a preparation for Lila — a systematic dissolution of the obstacles (tension, habit, self-consciousness, limited range) that prevent the spontaneous overflow of the divine creative energy through the medium of the prepared body. The dancer who has genuinely mastered the 108 Karanas has not acquired a set of constraining habits but has dissolved the constraints that prevented her from moving freely — which is why the master performer moves with a quality of effortless freedom that the novice lacks. This is precisely the relationship between philosophical study and liberation that Shankara describes: the rigorous training in discrimination and non-attachment is not a constraint on natural spontaneity but its precondition — the systematic removal of the obstacles to the natural, free, blissful expression of the consciousness that one already is.

41
The Two Traditions

1.10The Living Philosophy of Embodied Wisdom

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with

42
The Cosmic Choreography

its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

43
The Two Traditions

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

44
The Cosmic Choreography

1.11Cross-References and Scholarly Debates

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural

45
The Two Traditions

evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

46
The Cosmic Choreography

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This

47
The Two Traditions

convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

1.14Principal Scholarly Contributions and Their Limitations

The scholarly literature on the relationship between Indian philosophy and aesthetics is vast and uneven. The foundational works — Coomaraswamy’s essays, Raghavan’s studies on Sanskrit dramaturgy, Vatsyayan’s comprehensive treatment of classical Indian dance in literature and the arts — established the basic parameters of the field and remain indispensable reference points. The subsequent generation of scholars, including Mandakranta Bose, Srinivasa Ayya Srinivasan, and Anne-Marie Gaston, deepened the analysis in specific directions — Bose on the dance vocabulary, Srinivasan on philosophical aesthetics, Gaston on living transmission. And the work of Padma Subrahmanyam on the 108 Karanas specifically provides the technical foundation without which any philosophical analysis of the Karana system would be uninformed speculation.

The limitations of the existing literature for the specific argument of this book are identifiable and instructive. The performance studies literature has tended to focus on technique and history at the expense of philosophical depth; the philosophy literature has tended to treat aesthetic theory as marginal to its

48
The Cosmic Choreography

central concerns; and the art historical literature has focused on iconography and stylistic analysis without adequately addressing the philosophical meaning of what is being depicted. No previous study has attempted to hold all three domains simultaneously in a single analytical framework while also engaging with the living dimensions of both the dance practice and the philosophical tradition.

This gap in the literature is itself philosophically instructive: it reflects the fragmentation of academic knowledge that the synthesis traced in this book specifically challenges. The implicit assumption of much scholarly work in these fields is that the technical dimensions of the dance tradition are separable from its philosophical dimensions — that one can adequately study the Karanas without understanding Advaita Vedanta, or understand Shankara’s aesthetics without knowing anything about the 108 Karanas. This book’s central argument is precisely the opposite: the two dimensions are so deeply interdependent that neither can be fully understood without the other, and the attempt to understand either in isolation produces fundamental distortions of understanding that affect both technical analysis and philosophical interpretation.

The way forward for scholarship in this area lies in the development of truly integrated research programmes that bring together specialists in Sanskrit philology, performance theory, art history, philosophy, and cognitive science within frameworks of genuine intellectual dialogue. Several institutions — the Indira Gandhi National Centre for the Arts, the Sangeet Natak Akademi, the French Institut Français de Pondichéry, and several

49
The Two Traditions

university departments internationally — have begun to develop such programmes, and their work will be essential for advancing the understanding of the synthesis traced here beyond the preliminary analysis this book provides.

50
CHAPTER II

Natya Shastra

Text, Context, and Cosmology

“Just as the world, with its various states of being, is founded on the five elements, so too is Natya founded on the Rasas.”

— Bharata Muni, Natya Shastra, Chapter VI

2.1Historical and Textual Overview

The Natya Shastra stands as one of humanity’s most extraordinary intellectual achievements: a text that systematises the entire domain of performing arts within a coherent cosmological framework of the highest philosophical sophistication. Its attributed author, the sage Bharata Muni, is a semi-legendary figure about whom we know essentially nothing historically. The name 'Bharata' itself may be an acronym — Bha for Bhava (emotional states), Ra for Raga (musical melody), and Ta for Tala (rhythm) — suggesting that 'Bharata' designates not an individual author but the tradition of practice that encompasses all three foundational elements of Indian classical performance.

51
Natya Shastra

The text shows clear signs of layered composition over several centuries, with a probable core dating to around 200 BCE and subsequent additions and interpolations extending into the early centuries of the Common Era. The oldest stratum appears to consist of the chapters dealing with theatrical structure, dramatic types, and the basic theory of Rasa, while the more elaborate technical chapters — including the chapter on the 108 Karanas — may represent later additions. This layering does not diminish the text’s authority or coherence; rather, it reflects the organic way in which a living tradition accumulates, refines, and systematises its knowledge across generations.

The text consists of thirty-six chapters containing approximately 6,000 verses in various meters, supplemented by extensive prose passages. The chapters progress with a certain logical architecture, moving from the divine origin narrative through increasingly specific technical domains. Chapter I presents the mythological origin of Natya and the divine mandate for its composition. Chapters II-VII cover the construction and ritual preparation of the theatrical space, the types of dramatic compositions, and the foundational theory of Rasa and Bhava. Chapters VIII-XIII cover the technical vocabulary of bodily expression — standing positions, limb movements, hand gestures, gaze directions — including the crucial Chapter IV on the Tandava and the 108 Karanas. Chapters XIV-XXII cover vocal expression, music theory, and the theory of character types. Chapters XXIII-XXXVI cover stagecraft, costuming, dramatic criticism, and the philosophical foundations of theatrical art.

52
The Cosmic Choreography

The textual history of the Natya Shastra is itself a fascinating study in the transmission of knowledge in the Indian tradition. The text was preserved in multiple recensions — the most important being the Northern recension (represented by manuscripts from Kashmir, Nepal, and Bengal) and the Southern recension (represented by manuscripts from Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh). The differences between these recensions, while significant in detail, do not affect the fundamental doctrines of the text, suggesting that the core teaching was transmitted with great fidelity even as the specific formulations evolved to meet the needs of different regional performance traditions.

The discovery and scholarly editing of the Natya Shastra in the modern period has been a relatively recent achievement. The first complete edition, by Pandit Shivadatta and Kashinath Pandurang Parab, was published in 1894. Subsequent editions by Batuk Nath Sharma and Baladeva Upadhyaya (1929), and above all by Manomohan Ghosh (1951-67), established the text on a solid scholarly footing. The commentary tradition, headed by Abhinavagupta’s Abhinavabharati (c. 1000 CE), has been crucial for interpreting the often terse and technical primary text. Abhinavagupta’s commentary is not merely philological but philosophically transformative: it reads the Natya Shastra through the lens of Kashmir Shaivism, finding in the technical doctrines of performance theory a systematic expression of the deepest truths of non-dual consciousness.

53
Natya Shastra

2.2The Philosophical Framework of the Natya Shastra

What distinguishes the Natya Shastra from a mere technical manual is its insistence on situating performing arts within a comprehensive philosophical and cosmological framework. For Bharata, Natya is not entertainment but Dharma — a sacred obligation and a vehicle of liberation accessible to all human beings regardless of their social position or intellectual development. The text’s opening chapters establish this unequivocally: Brahma created Natya from the Vedas specifically because human beings, distracted by desire and suffering, needed a path to truth that engaged all the senses simultaneously and that was capable of leading even the most sense-bound consciousness toward liberation through the medium of aesthetic experience.

The philosophical underpinning of the Natya Shastra draws primarily from the Samkhya system, one of the oldest of India’s philosophical traditions. The Samkhya analysis of reality posits twenty-five fundamental principles (Tattvas) ranging from the unmanifest primordial matter (Avyakta Prakriti) through the various levels of manifest existence to the pure, unchanging consciousness of Purusha. Prakriti’s three fundamental qualities — Sattva (luminosity/clarity), Rajas (energy/activity/passion), and Tamas (inertia/darkness/delusion) — are understood to underlie all phenomena, including the various emotional and aesthetic states that constitute the Rasas of performance.

54
The Cosmic Choreography

Within this framework, the ideal performance is understood as an activity that progressively purifies the audience’s consciousness by moving through the full range of emotional experience in a controlled, aesthetically shaped context that prevents the usual entanglement of desire and aversion. The spectator who experiences all the Rasas through a great performance — moving through love, laughter, sorrow, heroism, wonder, and finally tranquility — has, in a sense, rehearsed the complete range of human experience in a safe, aesthetically bounded space. This rehearsal serves the same function in the aesthetic domain that philosophical inquiry serves in the intellectual domain: it loosens the grip of fixed identification with particular emotional states and opens the possibility of a freer relationship to the full range of experience.

The Natya Shastra’s theory of the embodied performer complements this theory of the audience. The ideal performer, as described in the Natya Shastra’s technical chapters, is a being of complete physical and psychophysical integration — one in whom the technical mastery of the body’s expressive vocabulary (Angikabhinaya), the vocal and musical dimensions of performance (Vachikabhinaya), the use of costume and makeup (Aharya Abhinaya), and above all the inner quality of authentic feeling and presence (Sattvika Abhinaya) are perfectly unified. The term Sattvika — derived from Sattva, the quality of clarity and luminosity — is telling: the highest quality of performance is not merely technical or emotional but involves a dimension of pure awareness, of luminous presence, that transcends mere skill.

55
Natya Shastra

This Sattvika dimension of performance is precisely the point at which the Natya Shastra tradition makes contact with Shankaracharya’s philosophical territory. Sattvika Abhinaya is described as the involuntary physical manifestations of authentic inner states — the hair standing on end (Romanca), tears (Svedana), the voice breaking (Svarabheda), bodily trembling (Kampa), pallor (Vaivarnya) — that arise in a genuinely transported performer who has moved beyond technique into a state of genuine aesthetic absorption. These involuntary manifestations are identical to those described in the Bhakti tradition as symptoms of genuine devotional experience and are in turn related to the involuntary manifestations that arise in deep meditative states. The Natya Shastra thus implicitly acknowledges that the highest artistic state and the highest spiritual state are not merely analogous but may be, in certain privileged moments of performance, identical.

2.3Chapter IV: Tandavalakshana and the 108 Karanas

The fourth chapter of the Natya Shastra, titled Tandavalakshana — literally 'The Characteristics/Signs of the Tandava Dance' — is the primary source for the doctrine of the 108 Karanas and one of the most philosophically dense chapters in the entire text. The chapter opens with the narrative of Shiva’s performance of the Tandava dance before an assembly of sages and gods at Kailasa, immediately following the performance of the first theatrical

56
The Cosmic Choreography

production by Bharata and his sons. Shiva, moved by what he witnesses, performs the Tandava to demonstrate the cosmic dimension of what has just occurred: the first theatrical performance was not merely a human entertainment but an enactment of the cosmic drama itself.

Bharata observes the Tandava and systematically analyses and codifies what he sees, producing the enumeration of 108 Karanas that forms the core of the chapter. His definition of the Karana is precise and has been the subject of extensive commentary: 'hastapaadasamaayogaha karanairiti sanjnitaha' — 'The coordinated union of hands and feet is known as Karana.' This definition, while brief, is philosophically significant. The Karana is not merely a hand position or a foot position but their union — their coordination into a single, integrated movement event. This emphasis on union, on coordination, on the integration of apparently separate elements into a single whole, reflects the same non-dual logic that Shankaracharya will later apply to the relationship between Atman and Brahman.

The 108 Karanas are presented in the text with varying degrees of descriptive detail. Some receive extended descriptions specifying the exact configuration of the fingers, the position and movement of the foot, the orientation of the torso, and the gaze direction. Others receive briefer treatments, perhaps because they were considered self-explanatory to the trained practitioner or because the textual tradition assumed the availability of living demonstration to supplement the written description. This variability in descriptive depth is one of the challenges facing scholars and practitioners

57
Natya Shastra

attempting to reconstruct the complete Karana vocabulary from textual sources alone.

Immediately following the enumeration of the Karanas, the chapter describes thirty-two Angaharas — larger movement sequences composed of three to seven Karanas combined in specific ways. The Angaharas represent a higher level of compositional organisation: if the Karanas are the phonemes of the movement language, the Angaharas are its words or phrases, units of meaning larger than individual gestures but smaller than complete compositions. The relationship between Karanas and Angaharas is itself philosophically instructive: just as the non-dual philosophy teaches that the many apparent things of the world are composed of more fundamental elements that are themselves composed of even more fundamental elements until one reaches the undivided ground of pure being, so the Natya Shastra’s movement system moves from the most complex compositional units down through progressively more basic elements to the Karanas themselves.

The chapter concludes with a description of the 108 Karanas as they are to be performed in the context of the Nandikeshvara tradition — the strand of the Shaiva performance tradition associated with Nandi, Shiva’s divine attendant, who is also associated with the transmission of musical and dance knowledge.
