This Nandikeshvara connection is important because it situates the Karana doctrine within the specifically Shaiva philosophical framework that will be relevant throughout this study: the 108 Karanas are not generic dance techniques but Shaiva

58
The Cosmic Choreography

sacred technology, tools for the materialisation of Shiva’s cosmic dance in the human body.

2.4Rasa Theory: The Philosophical Foundation of Aesthetic Experience

Bharata Muni’s theory of Rasa — the foundational theory of Indian aesthetics — is inseparable from the Karana doctrine and must be understood alongside it for the relationship between Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy to be fully appreciable. The word Rasa means literally 'juice', 'sap', or 'essence'; in aesthetic contexts it designates the fundamental quality of flavour or tone that characterises a particular type of aesthetic experience. Bharata enumerates eight primary Rasas — Shringara (erotic/romantic), Hasya (comic), Karuna (pathetic/sorrowful), Raudra (furious), Vira (heroic), Bhayanaka (terrifying), Bibhatsa (disgusting), and Adbhuta (wondrous) — and his sutra for the generation of Rasa has become one of the most discussed sentences in Indian intellectual history.

The Rasa Sutra — 'Vibhava Anubhava Vyabhichari Samyogad Rasa Nishpattih' — states that Rasa arises from the combination of Vibhavas (the determinants: the persons, situations, and objects that evoke an emotion), Anubhavas (the consequents: the physical expressions and behaviours that manifest the emotion), and Vyabhichari Bhavas (the transitory states: the subsidiary emotions that accompany and vary the primary emotion). The master term in this sutra is 'Nishpattih',

59
Natya Shastra

which can be translated as 'arising', 'production', or 'realisation'. The choice of this term is philosophically significant: it suggests not merely that Rasa is produced as an effect of its causes but that it is somehow realised — made real — through the interaction of these elements. Rasa is not merely a psychological effect in the spectator’s mind but a genuine aesthetic reality, an actually existing quality of the performance event.

The question of how Rasa arises in the spectator — how the audience member comes to experience genuine aesthetic emotion in response to the representation of fictional events by actors — generated one of the richest philosophical debates in the Indian tradition. The most sophisticated answer was provided by Abhinavagupta, who argued that Rasa arises through a process of Sadharanikarana — universalisation or generalisation — in which the spectator’s personal emotional responses are purified of their individual, private, ego-bound quality and transformed into a universal, impersonal, disinterested aesthetic experience. The spectator’s personal fear becomes the universal Rasa of Bhayanaka; their personal love becomes the universal Rasa of Shringara. This transformation from the personal to the universal is precisely the movement that Shankaracharya describes as the core of the spiritual path: the dissolution of individual identification in the recognition of universal consciousness.

The connection between Rasa theory and Advaita Vedanta goes even deeper through the concept of the Sahridaya — the ideal spectator, the 'person of similar heart' whose aesthetic sensitivity is so refined that they are capable of experiencing pure

60
The Cosmic Choreography

Rasa rather than merely personal emotional reactions to the performance. The Sahridaya is described by Abhinavagupta in terms that closely parallel Shankaracharya’s description of the Jnani — the person of wisdom. Both are defined by a quality of openness, sensitivity, and non-attachment that allows them to experience the full intensity of aesthetic or philosophical experience without being bound or disturbed by it. The Sahridaya who experiences Shringara Rasa is as fully moved by the beauty and tenderness of the performance as any ordinary lover would be by actual romantic encounter, yet remains perfectly free and undisturbed — not because they are cold or unresponsive but because their experience is not contaminated by personal desire or aversion.

The theory of the Sahridaya thus provides a bridge between the Natya Shastra’s aesthetics and Shankaracharya’s soteriology. Liberation, in Shankara’s understanding, is not the absence of experience but its transformation: the liberated sage does not cease to see, hear, taste, and feel but does so without the distortion of ego-identification, without the filter of personal desire and aversion, in a condition of pure, clear, unobstructed awareness. This is exactly the condition of the Sahridaya in the theatre: full experience without distorting identification, pure aesthetic sensation without personal entanglement. The theatre, for the tradition of Bharata and Abhinavagupta, is a space in which the ordinary person can momentarily inhabit the condition of the liberated sage — and can thereby get a taste, however temporary and mediated, of what liberation actually means.

61
Natya Shastra

2.5The Natya Shastra’s Theory of the Body

The Natya Shastra’s technical vocabulary for the human body is extraordinarily precise and philosophically sophisticated. The text divides the body into Major Limbs (Anga: head, hands, chest, sides, waist, and feet) and Minor Limbs (Pratyanga: shoulders, arms, back, abdomen, thighs, shins), and then further into very small limbs (Upanga: eyes, eyebrows, nose, cheeks, lower lip, chin), and specifies precise vocabularies of movement for each. This systematic dismemberment and then reassembly of the body in performance theory is itself philosophically significant: it teaches the performer to understand their body as a complex of coordinated parts, each capable of independent expressive action, rather than as a unitary, undifferentiated mass.

The education of the classical dancer, as prescribed by the Natya Shastra, involves a progressive training of awareness: beginning with the grossest, most easily observable movements of the major limbs and progressing through increasingly fine and subtle control of the minor limbs, the upangas, and finally the most subtle dimensions of expression — the quality of the gaze, the modulation of the voice, the inner state from which all external expression flows. This training in progressive refinement of awareness is structurally identical to the process described in Shankaracharya’s Vivekachudamani: the Adhikari (qualified student of Vedanta) must develop, through practice and discernment, an increasingly refined capacity to distinguish between the Self and the non-Self, beginning with the grossest

62
The Cosmic Choreography

misidentifications (I am this body) and progressing through increasingly subtle levels until the subtlest and most persistent illusion — the identification of the Self with the individual ego — is finally dissolved.

The Natya Shastra’s concept of Sthana — the standing position or foundational configuration of the body — is of particular philosophical relevance for our study. The word Sthana shares a root with the Sanskrit stha, 'to stand, to be established', and the related noun Pratishtha, 'establishment, foundation, grounding'. In the performance context, Sthana refers to the complete configuration of the lower body that establishes the weight distribution, energy grounding, and directional orientation of the entire movement. In the philosophical context, Sthana evokes the idea of the stable, unchanging ground of being from which all dynamic activity arises — precisely the role that Shankara assigns to Brahman in relation to the dynamic play of Maya.

The six primary Sthanas described in the Natya Shastra — Vaisnava, Samapada, Vaisakha, Mandala, Alidha, and Pratyalidha — represent a complete range of foundational orientations, from the most balanced and centred (Samapada, the equal-foot standing position) to the most dynamically asymmetrical (Alidha and Pratyalidha, the forward- and back-weighted warrior stances). These six Sthanas can be read as a map of the fundamental ways in which consciousness relates to its ground: equally balanced in the full recognition of non-duality, dynamically engaged in the various modes of active engagement with the world of experience. The Karana system builds on these

63
Natya Shastra

Sthanas as its foundation, so that every one of the 108 Karanas is ultimately an elaboration of one of these six fundamental ways of being grounded.

This analysis suggests that the technical vocabulary of the Natya Shastra is not merely a practical code for dancers and choreographers but a phenomenological map of the ways in which consciousness inhabits and expresses itself through a human body. The Karana system, read through this philosophical lens, becomes a complete atlas of embodied consciousness: a catalogue of the 108 fundamental ways in which awareness can take physical form, corresponding to the 108 fundamental configurations of consciousness in its dance of manifestation and liberation. It is this understanding — fully available to a philosophically trained reader of the Natya Shastra and made explicit by Abhinavagupta in his commentary — that Shankaracharya invokes when he employs the imagery of cosmic dance in his philosophical and devotional writings.

2.6The Natya Shastra’s Theory of the Theatrical Space

The Natya Shastra’s treatment of the theatrical space — the physical and ritual environment within which the Karanas are performed — reveals another dimension of the text’s philosophical depth that is directly relevant to our study. Chapters Two and Three of the Natya Shastra, which deal with the measurement, construction, and consecration of the

64
The Cosmic Choreography

theatrical hall (Natya Mandapa), establish that the performance space is not merely a neutral container for artistic activity but an actively constituted sacred space that participates in the philosophical meaning of what occurs within it.

The Natya Shastra describes three types of theatrical hall — the Vikrista (oblong), the Caturasra (square), and the Tryasra (triangular) — each with precise measurements specified in terms of the standard unit of measure called the Hasta (literally 'hand', the cubit). The choice of the Hasta as the unit of theatrical measurement is itself philosophically significant: the hand, in Indian philosophical tradition, is the organ most intimately connected with intentional, creative action, and using it as the unit of theatrical measurement establishes the performance space as a domain of intentional, creative consciousness rather than merely physical geometry.

The ritual consecration of the theatrical space, described in elaborate detail in the third chapter, involves the invocation of numerous deities who are understood to preside over different parts of the hall: the four walls, the central pillar, the orchestra pit, the stage proper, and the backstage area. This ritual mapping transforms the architectural space into a cosmic diagram — a three-dimensional yantra in which every physical element corresponds to a metaphysical principle. The performance that occurs within this consecrated space is therefore not merely an artistic event but a ritual enactment: a participation in the cosmic order that the spatial geometry embodies.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical vocabulary for understanding sacred space — particularly his analysis of the

65
Natya Shastra

relationship between the individual consciousness (Jiva) and the infinite consciousness (Brahman) in terms of spatial metaphors (the pot-space and the cosmic space, Ghata-Akasha and Maha-Akasha) — finds a direct analogue in this Natya Shastra architecture of sacred performance space. The theatrical hall, like the individual human body, is a bounded, finite space; but the consciousness that fills it, like the Atman that fills the body, is not bounded by that space but identical in nature with the infinite consciousness that fills the cosmos. The performance event is therefore an occasion for the recognition of this identity: the finite, bounded performance space becomes transparent to the infinite, unbounded space of pure consciousness.

The centrality of the pillar (Sthambha) in the Natya Shastra’s theatrical architecture also deserves philosophical attention. The central pillar of the theatrical hall is understood as the axis mundi — the cosmic axis around which the drama of existence turns. In the Shaiva philosophical tradition that culminates in Shankaracharya’s work, the Sthambha is identified with the Stambha of the Lingadhyaya — the pillar of light without beginning or end that Shiva is said to have manifested to humble Brahma and Vishnu. The theatrical hall’s central pillar is thus not merely an architectural element but a symbol of the cosmic consciousness that grounds all activity, including the activity of performance. And the Karanas performed around this central axis trace, in their variety and completeness, the full range of consciousness’s self-expression in the world.

This analysis of theatrical space has practical as well as theoretical significance for understanding the relationship

66
The Cosmic Choreography

between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya. The temple — which is simultaneously the architectural embodiment of Shankara’s Advaitic philosophy (its spatial hierarchy from gross exterior to subtle interior reflecting the hierarchy of consciousness from gross body to pure Atman) and the primary site of performance in the temple dance tradition — is the synthesis of these two traditions in built form. The temple is simultaneously Natya Shastra’s sacred theatre and Advaita Vedanta’s sacred diagram: a space in which the performance of the Karanas and the contemplation of the non-dual truth are not separate activities but aspects of a single, integrated practice.

2.7Abhinava Gupta’s Philosophical Transformation of the Natya Shastra

No account of the Natya Shastra’s philosophical tradition would be complete without a substantial engagement with Abhinavagupta (c. 950-1020 CE), whose Abhinavabharati stands as the most philosophically ambitious and influential commentary on Bharata’s text ever composed. Abhinavagupta was not merely a commentator but a philosophical innovator of the first rank — the greatest synthesiser of Kashmir Shaivism, the author of the monumental Tantraloka that systematised the entire tradition of Shaiva Tantra, and a thinker whose influence on every subsequent development in Indian aesthetics, philosophy of consciousness, and performance theory is difficult to overstate.

67
Natya Shastra

The Abhinavabharati does not merely explain Bharata’s text; it transforms it. Where Bharata had situated Natya within a Samkhya philosophical framework, Abhinavagupta re-reads the entire text through the lens of Pratyabhijna (Recognition) philosophy — the Kashmir Shaivite epistemology that holds that liberation consists in the direct recognition (Pratyabhijna) of one’s identity with the supreme consciousness (Paramashiva). This re-reading is not a distortion but a philosophical deepening: it reveals dimensions of meaning in Bharata’s text that are genuinely present but not fully articulated in the original.

Abhinavagupta’s most celebrated contribution to aesthetics is his theory of Rasa as Brahmananda-Sahodarah — 'born of the same family as the bliss of Brahman.' This famous phrase encapsulates his argument that the aesthetic experience of Rasa is not merely analogous to but genuinely continuous with the philosophical experience of Brahman-recognition. The spectator who experiences genuine Shanta Rasa in the theatre is not having an experience that merely resembles liberation; they are having a genuine, if transient and impure, form of the same experience. The difference between Rasa and Brahmananda is not qualitative but quantitative: Rasa is bounded in time and dependent on the external conditions of the performance, while Brahmananda is unlimited and self-sustaining; but both involve the same dissolution of ego-identification into universal awareness, the same experience of pure, blissful, undistorted consciousness.

This argument has crucial implications for the relationship between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s work. Abhinavagupta was writing roughly two centuries after

68
The Cosmic Choreography

Shankara, and his aesthetic philosophy represents, among other things, a conscious engagement with and development of Shankara’s Advaitic insights in the domain of aesthetics. The identification of Shanta Rasa with Brahmananda in the Abhinavabharati is a response to and elaboration of the aesthetic implications of Shankara’s Advaita — an attempt to articulate what the non-dual philosophy means for the theory and practice of performing arts. In this sense, Abhinavagupta’s work represents the most systematic historical attempt to build the bridge between the two traditions whose relationship this book traces.

The specific Abhinavaguptan concept most relevant for understanding the 108 Karanas is Camatkara — literally 'astonishment' or 'wonder', but in Abhinavagupta’s technical philosophical vocabulary, the quality of aesthetic delight that arises when the spectator’s consciousness recognises itself in the mirror of the performance. Camatkara is the moment when Rasa is experienced, and it corresponds precisely to the Pratyabhijna moment in Kashmir Shaivite epistemology: the moment of self-recognition in which consciousness recognises its own nature as the ground of all experience. The 108 Karanas, performed with full mastery and genuine inward awareness, are instruments of Camatkara: each Karana, at the peak of its execution, creates a moment of pure aesthetic recognition that is simultaneously a moment of philosophical self-recognition.

Abhinavagupta’s commentary on the Natya Shastra’s treatment of the 108 Karanas is unfortunately lost — the Abhinavabharati commentary has survived only up to the

69
Natya Shastra

twenty-seventh chapter of the text, stopping short of the chapters on Tala and falling well short of a full commentary on the Tandava chapter. This lacuna is a genuine loss for scholarship, but it also invites the kind of philosophical reconstruction that this book undertakes: drawing on Abhinavagupta’s general philosophical principles and applying them to the Karana system whose detailed commentary he unfortunately did not complete. The result, while necessarily speculative, is philosophically coherent with everything else Abhinavagupta wrote and represents the most plausible account of what his commentary on the Karanas might have looked like had it survived.

2.8Regional Traditions and Textual Variants

The Natya Shastra as we have it today is a synthesis of multiple regional traditions and textual strata, and understanding the 108 Karanas in their full depth requires some engagement with this complexity. The Northern and Southern recensions of the text differ in their accounts of certain Karanas, and the regional performance traditions of North India, Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, and Kerala have each developed their own interpretations of the Karana vocabulary based on their specific cultural contexts, artistic aesthetics, and philosophical frameworks.

The Tamil tradition is particularly important for our study because it provides the most continuous historical link between the Natya Shastra’s codification of the Karanas and their

70
The Cosmic Choreography

sculptural representation in the great Chola temples. The classical Tamil literary tradition — including the Sangam poetry (c. 300 BCE to 300 CE), the Silappatikaram (c. 2nd century CE), and the Tevaram devotional hymns (c. 6th-9th centuries CE) — contains abundant evidence for a rich performance culture in Tamil Nadu that was in continuous dialogue with the Sanskrit Natya Shastra tradition. The Silappatikaram’s extraordinary description of the classical dancer Madhavi and her performance, which draws directly on Natya Shastra vocabulary while embedding it in a distinctively Tamil cultural context, demonstrates that the synthesis between Sanskrit theoretical tradition and regional performance practice was already well advanced by the early centuries of the Common Era.

The Telugu-Andhra tradition, which produced the most elaborate sculptural programmes of the 108 Karanas at sites including Darasuram, Tiruvannamalai, and Kanchipuram, represents another important regional inflection of the Natya Shastra tradition. The Andhra tradition’s emphasis on the devotional dimensions of performance — its integration of classical dance with the Bhakti traditions of the Alvar and Nayanar saints — anticipates in cultural practice the philosophical synthesis that Shankaracharya would later articulate in philosophical language. The Andhra choreographic tradition’s development of the Padam (devotional song form) as the primary vehicle for combining classical technique with devotional expression represents a practical realisation of the same insight that Shankaracharya articulates theoretically: that

71
Natya Shastra

the highest embodied art is inseparable from the highest spiritual aspiration.

The Kerala tradition holds special significance because of its direct relationship to Shankaracharya’s biographical context. The Natya Shastra’s prescriptions for theatrical performance are most completely preserved in the Kerala Kutiyattam tradition, which has maintained an unbroken performance lineage from at least the ninth century CE to the present day. UNESCO’s recognition of Kutiyattam as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2001 acknowledged what scholars of Indian performance have long understood: that this tradition preserves dimensions of the Natya Shastra’s theatrical practice that have been lost or transformed beyond recognition everywhere else. For the study of the relationship between Shankara and the Natya Shastra, the Kerala context provides not only biographical background but a living laboratory: the performance tradition that Shankara would have encountered in his formative years is, in its broad outlines, still accessible through the Kutiyattam performance that continues in Kerala temples today.

The Karnataka tradition, centred on the great Shaiva pilgrimage sites of Hampi-Vijayanagara and the Shiva temples of Mysore district, represents yet another important dimension of the Natya Shastra’s regional reception. The Yakshagana tradition of Karnataka, while it developed primarily in the post-medieval period, preserves elements of a performance culture that reaches back to the Karana tradition through multiple intermediary forms. The Karnataka tradition’s philosophical engagement is perhaps most visible in the Vachana literature of the Lingayat

72
The Cosmic Choreography

tradition — the intensely philosophical devotional poetry of figures like Basavanna and Allama Prabhu — which, while not a performance tradition in the strict sense, employs movement and dance imagery in ways that closely parallel Shankaracharya’s own usage in the Soundarya Lahari.

Understanding this regional diversity is important for the argument of this book because it demonstrates that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra’s performance theory and the Advaitic philosophical tradition was not a single, once-for-all event but an ongoing, distributed process of cultural elaboration occurring simultaneously in multiple regional contexts. Shankaracharya’s philosophical articulation of this synthesis represents its most systematic and philosophically rigorous expression, but it does not stand alone: it is embedded in and supported by a rich texture of regional performance cultures that had been exploring similar insights through the medium of artistic practice for centuries before Shankara and would continue to do so for centuries after him.

2.9The Natya Shastra and the Concept of Rasasvadana: Tasting the Essence

The word Rasa, as we have noted, means literally 'juice', 'sap', or 'essence' — the concentrated vital fluid that gives life to plants and, by extension, the concentrated essential quality that gives life to aesthetic experience. The verb form Rasasvadana — 'tasting the essence' — describes the activity of the ideal spectator or

73
Natya Shastra

Sahridaya: not merely watching the performance but tasting it, allowing its essential quality to penetrate and nourish the consciousness in the same way that the juice of a fruit nourishes the body.

This culinary metaphor for aesthetic experience is philosophically significant because it situates aesthetic understanding in the domain of direct, immediate, embodied experience rather than in the domain of detached, intellectual observation. To taste something is to allow it to enter one into the most intimate possible relationship with the tasting consciousness: the boundaries between the tasted object and the tasting subject temporarily dissolve, and the essential quality of the tasted thing is directly experienced rather than merely perceived. This is precisely the quality of genuine Rasa experience that Abhinavagupta describes: not the observation of a performance from a safe distance but a genuine encounter in which the spectator’s consciousness is penetrated, nourished, and transformed by the performance’s essential quality.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical vocabulary includes several terms that parallel the Rasasvadana concept. The most important is Anubhava — literally 'after-cognition' but in the philosophical context, 'direct experience' or 'immediate cognition', the quality of knowing that goes beyond intellectual observation to direct, non-mediated apprehension. The Brahmanubhava — the direct experience of Brahman — is the ultimate form of Anubhava, the quality of knowing that dissolves the distinction between the knower and the known in the recognition that they are the same single consciousness. This Brahmanubhava is structurally

74
The Cosmic Choreography

identical to the Rasasvadana of the ideal spectator: both involve the temporary dissolution of the subject-object distinction in a direct, immediate, transformative experience that the ordinary analytical mind cannot achieve.

The connection between Rasasvadana and Brahmanubhava has practical implications for the training of both performers and philosophers. For the performer, it suggests that the goal of technical training is not the production of a perfectly executed external form but the cultivation of the inner quality of direct, immediate embodied experience — the capacity to inhabit each Karana from the inside, to 'taste' it rather than merely execute it. For the philosopher, it suggests that the goal of philosophical inquiry is not the acquisition of correct intellectual positions about Brahman but the cultivation of the capacity for direct, immediate, non-mediated experience of the non-dual truth — the Brahmanubhava that Shankara consistently identifies as the ultimate goal of all Vedantic study.

The implication of this parallel for the synthesis this book traces is that the classical dancer who achieves genuine Rasasvadana in her performance and the Advaita Vedanta student who achieves genuine Brahmanubhava in their inquiry are having experiences that are not merely analogous but continuous with each other — experiences that differ in their medium and context but share the same fundamental quality of direct, non-mediated, transformative encounter with the deepest reality. This continuity is what gives the relationship between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy its deepest philosophical significance: they are not two separate paths that

75
Natya Shastra

happen to run parallel but two approaches to the same destination, two vocabularies for the same direct experience of the non-dual reality that is the ultimate truth of consciousness.

2.11Textual Depth and Performance Practice

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not

76
The Cosmic Choreography

separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by

77
Natya Shastra

reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human

78
The Cosmic Choreography

consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

2.12Philological Notes on Key Terms

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical

79
Natya Shastra

relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the

80
The Cosmic Choreography

two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple

81
Natya Shastra

sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

2.11The Natya Shastra’s Theory of the Ideal Spectator

The Natya Shastra’s theory of the ideal spectator — the Sahridaya — is one of the most philosophically sophisticated elements of the text and deserves extended treatment beyond what the earlier analysis provided. The concept of the Sahridaya ('person of similar heart') operates simultaneously at multiple levels: aesthetic (the spectator who is capable of genuine Rasa experience), social (the cultivated courtly audience for whom the finest performances were designed), philosophical (the person whose consciousness has been sufficiently refined through practice and study to respond to the deepest dimensions of the performance), and spiritual (the person who is, potentially, capable of the direct recognition of the non-dual truth through the medium of aesthetic experience).

The word Sahridaya itself is philosophically rich: Sa-hridaya means 'one who has heart', but in the context of Indian philosophical psychology, the Hridaya (heart) is not merely the seat of emotion but the centre of consciousness — the innermost

82
The Cosmic Choreography

awareness that underlies both thinking and feeling. The Sahridaya is therefore not merely a person of refined feeling but a person of refined consciousness: one in whom the quality of awareness has been developed sufficiently to respond to the subtle dimensions of a great performance. This is precisely the quality that Shankaracharya identifies as the prerequisite for genuine philosophical understanding: not mere intellectual cleverness but the Adhikara (qualification) of a consciousness that has been prepared through Viveka (discrimination), Vairagya (dispassion), Shat-Sampat (the six virtues of Sama, Dama, Uparama, Titiksha, Shraddha, and Samadhana), and Mumukshutva (desire for liberation).

The parallel between the Natya Shastra’s Sahridaya and Shankaracharya’s Adhikari (qualified student) is direct and structurally precise. Both are defined by a quality of prepared receptivity — a consciousness that has been refined through sustained practice to the point where it can receive and be genuinely transformed by the highest forms of its respective tradition. And both traditions insist that this preparation is not merely intellectual but involves the whole person: the Sahridaya must have cultivated aesthetic sensitivity through sustained engagement with the arts, not merely theoretical knowledge about them; the Adhikari must have cultivated philosophical sensitivity through sustained practice of discrimination and dispassion, not merely intellectual familiarity with philosophical arguments.

The implication for contemporary engagement with both traditions is significant. The person who wants to experience genuine Rasa from a performance of the 108 Karanas, or genuine

83
Natya Shastra

philosophical insight from studying Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, must be willing to undertake the preparatory cultivation that each tradition describes as necessary. There are no shortcuts: the Sahridaya quality must be genuinely cultivated, not merely claimed, and the cultivation requires the sustained, patient engagement with the tradition’s full dimensions that the guru-shishya transmission provides. This is not elitism but realism: the deepest truths of any tradition are accessible only to those who have prepared themselves for the encounter.
