CHAPTER III

The 108 Karanas

Technical Architecture and Spiritual Geometry

“The body is the temple of the Divine. In its movements, the cosmic scripture is written afresh in each moment.”

— Kapila Vatsyayan, Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts, 1968

3.1Structural Analysis of the Karana System

To appreciate fully the philosophical dimensions of the 108 Karanas, one must first understand their technical architecture with precision sufficient to recognise what is actually happening when a body executes a Karana. The Karana is not a simple gesture or a static pose but a complex, dynamic, three-dimensional event involving the simultaneous coordination of multiple bodily systems. Each Karana integrates five components that must operate as a unified whole: Sthana (the standing position/ground contact establishing foundation), Chari (the single leg movement defining spatial trajectory), Nritta Hasta (the hand gesture in pure dance expressing communicative

85
The 108 Karanas

content), Angahara (the full body posture and its sequential development), and Drishti (the gaze direction coordinating the visual and spatial dimensions of the movement). The integration of these five elements into a single seamless unit is what transforms individual technical elements into an embodied philosophical statement.

The Sthana, as we have noted, establishes the architectural foundation of the Karana — the fundamental relationship between the body and the ground, the configuration of weight, balance, and directional orientation that will determine the character of everything that follows. The six primary Sthanas are not merely physical positions but psychophysical orientations: the Samapada standing position, with feet together and weight perfectly balanced, creates a quality of centered equanimity that is entirely different from the expansive, laterally open quality of the Vaisakha position with feet wide apart, or the forward-driving energy of the Alidha warrior stance. A performer who has truly internalised these distinctions does not merely stand differently in each Sthana — they inhabit different qualities of consciousness.

The Chari — the single-leg movement — introduces the dimension of temporal development into the Karana. While the Sthana establishes spatial foundation, the Chari creates movement, trajectory, and change. The thirty-two basic Charis described in the Natya Shastra range from simple, grounded stepping patterns to complex aerial trajectories involving jumps, turns, and elaborate foot articulations. Each Chari has its own quality of energy: some are soft and flowing, others sharp and decisive, others spiraling and centripetal. The relationship

86
The Cosmic Choreography

between Sthana and Chari in any given Karana can be understood as a relationship between ground and movement, being and becoming, the stable and the dynamic — precisely the relationship that Shankaracharya describes between Brahman (the unchanging ground) and Maya (the dynamic play of manifestation).

The Nritta Hasta — the hand gesture specific to pure dance — adds the communicative and expressive dimension to the movement. Where the Sthana and Chari establish the spatial and temporal architecture, the Nritta Hasta shapes the quality of awareness and intention that flows through that architecture. The thirty Nritta Hastas described in the Natya Shastra range from gestures of offering and protection to gestures of aspiration and surrender, from gestures of cosmic expansiveness to gestures of intimate inwardness. The specific Nritta Hasta chosen for a Karana determines what the movement is expressing: the same spatial trajectory and foundational stance, combined with different hand gestures, can communicate entirely different qualities of consciousness.

The Drishti — the gaze direction — is perhaps the most philosophically significant of the five Karana components, and the one most directly relevant to Shankaracharya’s philosophical concerns. The Natya Shastra describes thirty-six Drishtis, ranging from direct forward gaze to upward, downward, and lateral gaze, and including specific gazes associated with particular emotional states and devotional orientations. In Indian philosophical tradition more broadly, the gaze is understood as the most direct expression of the quality of consciousness inhabiting a person: the

87
The 108 Karanas

gaze of the enlightened sage differs fundamentally from the gaze of the ordinary person not merely in its direction but in its quality — what the tradition calls the Brahmadrishti, the divine gaze that sees Brahman in everything it encounters. The Drishti component of the Karana thus encodes, in each of the 108 movement-units, a specific quality of conscious attention — making the Karana system as a whole a complete typology of the ways in which consciousness attends to the world.

3.2The 108 Karanas: A Philosophical Taxonomy

While the Natya Shastra presents the 108 Karanas in a sequence that reflects the progression of Shiva’s actual Tandava performance, it is possible and illuminating to organise them according to their philosophical significance. Several different taxonomic principles suggest themselves, each revealing a different dimension of the system’s philosophical architecture. The taxonomy presented here is not definitive but heuristic: a way of reading the system that makes its philosophical structure visible without claiming to exhaust its complexity.

A primary division can be made between Bhumi Karanas (Earth Karanas) and Akasha Karanas (Sky Karanas), reflecting the two poles of the Karana system’s cosmological range. The Bhumi Karanas are characterised by strong ground contact, low centre of gravity, and earthward energy; they embody the principle of manifestation, of consciousness taking on material form and density. The Akasha Karanas are characterised by airborne

88
The Cosmic Choreography

moments, elevated postures, and upward energy; they embody the principle of transcendence, of consciousness releasing the density of material form and moving toward its own unbound nature. Between these two poles lies the vast middle territory of the Karana system: movements that negotiate the tension between earth and sky, between grounded embodiment and transcendent freedom, between the specific and the universal.

A second taxonomic principle organises the Karanas according to their Rasa quality — the specific aesthetic flavour they embody. Some Karanas are unmistakably Shringara in quality: soft, flowing, intimate, beautiful, evoking the quality of love and aesthetic delight in its most refined form. Others are powerfully Vira: expansive, strong, heroic, evoking the quality of courage and noble action. Others embody Adbhuta (wonder) — the quality of profound aesthetic amazement before something that exceeds ordinary understanding. And a significant subset of the later Karanas — particularly those involving Urdhva (elevated) configurations — embody Shanta: the aesthetic quality of perfect peace, of consciousness resting in its own nature, undisturbed by any desire or aversion. This Shanta quality is, as we shall argue in detail in Chapter Seven, the aesthetic dimension of what Shankaracharya calls the state of Brahman-recognition.

A third taxonomic principle, perhaps the most philosophically revealing, organises the Karanas according to the dimension of the five-element (Pancha-Bhuta) cosmology they embody. Indian cosmology understands all of manifest existence as constituted by five fundamental elements: Earth (Prithvi), Water (Jala), Fire (Agni), Air (Vayu), and Space (Akasha), each

89
The 108 Karanas

with its characteristic quality of energy and consciousness. The Karanas can be broadly mapped onto these five elements: the stable, grounded Karanas correspond to the Earth element; the fluid, flowing Karanas to the Water element; the sharp, dynamic, transformative Karanas to the Fire element; the light, expansive Karanas to the Air element; and the most elevated, spacious Karanas — those embodying Shanta and Adbhuta — to the Space element. This elemental mapping is not arbitrary: the Pancha-Bhuta cosmology is explicitly integrated into Shankaracharya’s analysis of the Kosha system (the five sheaths of consciousness), and the connection between the Karana system and this cosmological framework suggests that the 108 Karanas were understood by the tradition as a complete map of consciousness in its embodied, elemental form.

The number 108 itself, as we noted in Chapter One, encodes this sense of cosmological completeness. The 108 Karanas are not a random selection from the infinite number of possible body configurations but a systematic, complete enumeration of the fundamental types of movement possible for a consciousness inhabiting a human body. This completeness is not merely mathematical but experiential: a practitioner who has genuinely mastered all 108 Karanas — not merely as physical forms but in their full psychophysical depth, understanding each one from the inside as a specific quality of consciousness-in-movement — has traversed the complete range of possible embodied experience. She or he has, in the language of the Karana tradition, performed the complete Ananda Tandava: the full self-expression of divine consciousness through every mode of embodied existence.

90
The Cosmic Choreography

3.3Selected Karanas: Detailed Analysis

To ground the abstract philosophical analysis in the specific texture of the tradition, this section offers detailed examinations of five Karanas that are particularly significant for understanding their relationship to Shankaracharya’s philosophical metaphors. These five are selected not as representative of the entire system but as especially illuminating focal points for the philosophical analysis that will follow.

Talapushpaputa — 'The Handful of Flowers': In this Karana, both hands are brought together in the Anjali position (joined palms facing upward, as if offering flowers) while the feet execute a soft, even stepping pattern in the Samapada Sthana. The name itself is poetically precise: Tala refers to the palm of the hand (and also to Tala as in the rhythm cycle, suggesting the temporal dimension of the offering gesture), Pushpa to flowers, and Puta to a container or receptacle. The image is of two cupped palms holding flowers to be offered — the quintessential gesture of devotion, of the self making an offering to the divine. The philosophical significance of this Karana for Shankaracharya’s tradition is immediate: the Dakshinamurti Stotra’s central image is of the sage who teaches through silence, whose whole being is an offering, whose very presence is a Talapushpaputa — a constant act of spontaneous, effortless devotion. The technical precision of the hand gesture (exact configuration of fingers, angle of wrists, softness of palms) corresponds to the philosophical

91
The 108 Karanas

precision of Shankara’s doctrine of Sharanagati (complete surrender to the divine).

Urdhva-Janu — 'The Raised Knee': This Karana, one of the most important among the Urdhva (elevated) group, involves raising one knee to hip level or above while the standing leg maintains perfect balance, the torso remains erect, and the arms extend in a specific configuration that counterbalances the raised leg. The movement quality is one of effortless elevation — not the straining effort of physical exertion but the natural buoyancy of a consciousness that has loosened its attachment to the weight of material existence. This Karana directly embodies the Urdhva Tandava pose of Nataraja — the raised-leg form of Shiva’s cosmic dance that is perhaps the most iconic image in all of Indian sacred art. Shankaracharya’s Nirvana Shatakam can be read as a progressive Urdhva-Janu: each verse lifts another weight from the dancer’s foot, releasing another identification with limitation, until the final verse — 'Chidananda Rupa Shivoham Shivoham' — achieves the fully elevated position, the foot of identification with the body finally raised free of the ground of ignorance.

Nikuttaka — 'The Trembling or Vibrating Movement': This Karana involves a fine, rapid vibration that begins in the feet and travels upward through the body, reaching eventually to the fingertips. It is one of the most technically demanding Karanas to execute well because the vibration must be genuinely whole-body — not a mechanical shaking but an organic pulsation that arises from the body’s own energy. The philosophical connection to the concept of Spanda — the primordial vibration of consciousness that underlies all manifestation — is unmistakable. In Kashmir

92
The Cosmic Choreography

Shaivite philosophy, Spanda is the self-movement of consciousness, its inherent dynamism, the pulse of its own being. Shankaracharya’s description in Soundarya Lahari of the Divine Mother’s movements as waves (Lahari — wave) of bliss corresponds precisely to this vibratory quality: the Divine Mother’s whole being is a Nikuttaka, a ceaseless pulsation of bliss-consciousness that manifests as the universe.

Gajahasta — 'The Elephant’s Trunk': This widely known Karana involves extending one arm forward in a gesture that mimics the sweeping, graceful motion of an elephant’s trunk — supple, strong, purposeful, and beautiful simultaneously. The elephant imagery is significant in the Indian tradition: Ganesha, the elephant-headed deity who is the remover of obstacles and the lord of beginnings, embodies precisely the quality of graceful, powerful, purposeful movement that this Karana expresses. Shankaracharya’s Ganesha Pancharatnam — his five-verse hymn to Ganesha — opens with an invocation of Ganesha’s graceful movement, using imagery that closely parallels the Gajahasta Karana. The philosophical quality this Karana embodies is Sattva in its most refined form: the graceful, powerful, unobstructed movement of a consciousness that has cleared the obstacles of ego-identification and moves with the natural grace of its own unbound nature.

Lina — 'The Absorbed or Dissolved': This Karana involves a movement of progressive dissolution — the body gradually releases its held tension, the arms lower, the gaze softens, the breath deepens, until the entire figure embodies a quality of profound absorption, of consciousness returning to its source.

93
The 108 Karanas

The word Lina shares a root with the Sanskrit li, 'to dissolve, to merge, to be absorbed', which is precisely the root of the term Laya — dissolution — used in the context of the dissolution of individual consciousness into Brahman at liberation. The Lina Karana is not a movement of collapse or defeat but of blissful return: consciousness not suppressed but fulfilled, not extinguished but recognising its own source. Shankaracharya’s Bhaja Govindam — the famous composition urging the abandonment of intellectual cleverness in favour of direct devotion — culminates in precisely this quality of Lina: the dissolution of the separate self in the ocean of divine awareness.

3.4The Angaharas: Movement Phrases and Larger Structures

The thirty-two Angaharas described in the Natya Shastra represent a higher organisational level of the Karana system, combining groups of three to seven Karanas into coherent movement phrases with their own names, qualities, and philosophical significances. The word Angahara combines Anga (body/limb) with Hara (that which takes away/that which adorns), suggesting a movement that takes the body somewhere — that carries consciousness from one state to another through the medium of physical movement. The Angahara is thus a miniature journey: a complete arc of movement that begins in one state, passes through intermediate transformations, and arrives at a resolution.

94
The Cosmic Choreography

The philosophical significance of the Angahara system lies in its demonstration of how individual Karanas, placed in sequence with each other, create meanings larger than any single Karana can contain. Just as words in a sentence create meanings that transcend any individual word, and as musical phrases create meanings that transcend any individual note, so Angaharas create philosophical statements through the sequencing of Karanas that the individual Karanas cannot make alone. A Angahara might begin with a grounded, earthward Karana, pass through a middle Karana of dynamic transformation, and conclude with an elevated, skyward Karana — tracing in three movement-units the complete philosophical arc of manifestation, sustenance, and liberation.

The thirty-two Angaharas can be understood as the Natya Shastra’s equivalent of philosophical aphorisms or slokas: compact, precisely formulated statements that contain, in highly concentrated form, philosophical insights requiring elaborate commentary to fully unpack. Just as Shankaracharya’s Brahma Sutras — the terse, aphoristic statements of Vedantic philosophy to which his Brahma Sutra Bhasya provides the extended commentary — are not merely preliminary sketches for the full exposition but contain in compact form the complete philosophical insight, so the Angaharas are not merely sequences of Karanas but complete philosophical statements requiring the fullness of living practice to fully express.

The relationship between Karanas and Angaharas also illuminates the Natya Shastra’s implicit theory of knowledge. Knowledge, in this tradition, is not merely propositional — a

95
The 108 Karanas

matter of correct statements about the world — but embodied and progressive. One comes to understand an Angahara not by learning its definition but by moving through it, by inhabiting each Karana in sequence and feeling the way in which each transition takes consciousness from one state to another and delivers it, finally, to the resolution that the Angahara’s name and quality describe. This embodied, experiential, progressive mode of knowing is precisely what Shankaracharya calls Aparoksha Anubhuti — direct, non-mediate experience — as distinguished from the merely intellectual understanding that knows about liberation without directly experiencing it.

The tradition of teaching Angaharas in the classical dance context provides a concrete example of this embodied epistemology. The guru does not explain an Angahara with words and then ask the student to execute it; rather, the guru demonstrates it with her own body, and the student’s body responds to and learns from that demonstration at a level that precedes and exceeds verbal explanation. Over many repetitions, the student’s body comes to know the Angahara from inside — to understand it not as an external sequence to be reproduced but as a quality of movement-consciousness that can be inhabited. When this understanding is reached, the student has not merely learned the Angahara but has been changed by it: their body-consciousness has been expanded to include a new way of being in movement, a new configuration of the relationship between awareness and action.

96
The Cosmic Choreography

3.5The Karana as Psychophysical Event

The most philosophically significant feature of the Karana, as we have noted, is the integration it requires between the practitioner’s physical, cognitive, and intentional dimensions. But this integration goes deeper than mere simultaneous coordination of different body parts. The ideal Karana execution — as described in the Natya Shastra and as elaborated in the commentary tradition — involves a specific quality of unified awareness in which the distinction between the body that is moving and the consciousness that is aware of the movement temporarily dissolves. This dissolution is not unconsciousness or trance but the opposite: a heightened, unified awareness in which the quality of attention is simultaneously more precise (every detail of the movement is clearly apprehended) and more spacious (the entire movement is apprehended as a single whole rather than as a sequence of parts).

The Sanskrit tradition has developed several technical terms for this quality of unified psychophysical awareness in the performance context. The most important is Tanmayata — literally 'that-ness' or 'completeness', the quality of being completely absorbed in and identified with what one is doing. Tanmayata is not the loss of awareness but its full deployment: when a dancer executes the Talapushpaputa Karana with genuine Tanmayata, her awareness is not fragmented across the multiple technical demands of the movement but unified in a single, complete act

97
The 108 Karanas

of attention that simultaneously comprehends hand, foot, body, gaze, and breath as aspects of a single whole.

The philosophical connection between this Tanmayata quality of the ideal Karana execution and Shankaracharya’s analysis of consciousness is profound. In the Vivekachudamani and the Upadeshasahasri, Shankara describes the ideal state of philosophical inquiry as a condition of complete, undivided attention to the question at hand — a quality of Nididhyasana (deep meditation on the truth) that, at its highest, dissolves into Aparoksha Anubhuti, the direct, non-mediated experience of the non-dual truth. This dissolution is structurally identical to the dissolution of the subject-object distinction that the ideal Karana execution involves: in both cases, the distinction between the knowing subject and the known object dissolves in an experience that is simultaneously more fully knowing and more fully present than ordinary, divided attention.

The Natya Shastra’s description of the Sattvika Bhavas — the eight involuntary physical manifestations that arise in the performer who has entered this state of Tanmayata — provides the most concrete evidence for the tradition’s understanding of the Karana as a psychophysical event rather than merely a physical one. The Sattvika Bhavas include: Stambha (paralysis or extreme stillness), Sveda (perspiration), Romanca (horripilation or goosebumps), Svarabheda (breaking of the voice), Vepathu (trembling), Vaivarnya (change of colour), Ashru (tears), and Pralaya (fainting). These involuntary responses, arising spontaneously in the performer who has moved beyond technical execution into genuine aesthetic and spiritual absorption,

98
The Cosmic Choreography

correspond in the Indian philosophical tradition to the signs of authentic devotional experience described in the Bhakti literature and to the symptoms of genuine meditative absorption described in the Yoga tradition.

The appearance of the Sattvika Bhavas in a performer is, in the Natya Shastra tradition, the gold standard of genuine artistic quality: not technical perfection in the execution of the Karanas (though this is necessary), not emotional authenticity in the expression of the Bhavas (though this too is necessary), but the involuntary, uncontrolled manifestation of genuine inner states that indicates the performer has moved beyond the domain of voluntary control into the domain of genuine Tanmayata. Shankaracharya describes precisely analogous involuntary manifestations in the Jivanmukta — the liberated sage — whose recognition of the non-dual truth sometimes produces the same physical symptoms, not as artifice or display but as the unavoidable overflow of an inner experience too intense to be contained within ordinary physical composure.

This parallel between the Natya Shastra’s Sattvika Bhavas and the Advaita Vedanta’s symptoms of genuine liberation is not coincidental. Both are descriptions of the same underlying phenomenon: the breakthrough of the deeper dimension of consciousness through the surface of ordinary ego-bound awareness. Whether this breakthrough occurs in the context of intense philosophical inquiry (as in Shankara’s own account of liberation) or in the context of complete absorption in artistic performance (as in the Natya Shastra’s account of the highest level of the performer’s craft), it manifests the same physical signs

99
The 108 Karanas

because it involves the same fundamental transformation of consciousness.

3.6Temporal Structure and the Karana’s Relationship to Tala

The Karanas are not static poses but dynamic movement events with a specific temporal structure — a beginning, a development, and a resolution — and this temporal structure is inseparable from their philosophical significance. The Natya Shastra’s treatment of the relationship between the Karanas and the Tala (rhythmic cycle) makes this explicit: each Karana has a prescribed relationship to the rhythmic cycle within which it is performed, and the quality of the Karana’s execution is partly constituted by the precision and sensitivity of this rhythmic relationship.

The Sanskrit term that most precisely describes the ideal temporal quality of a Karana execution is Laya — literally 'dissolution' or 'absorption', but in the music and dance context, the precise coordination with the rhythmic cycle. Laya operates on three levels: Druta (fast), Madhya (medium), and Vilambita (slow). A great dancer is capable of performing any Karana in any Laya without losing its essential quality, and the ability to do so demonstrates a fundamental understanding of the Karana that transcends any particular tempo. This capacity corresponds, at the level of embodied practice, to what Shankaracharya describes as the Atman’s freedom from temporal limitation: just as the Atman is the same pure consciousness whether the mind is

100
The Cosmic Choreography

moving quickly or slowly, whether life is proceeding at a frenetic or a leisurely pace, so the essential quality of a Karana is the same whether it is executed in Druta, Madhya, or Vilambita Laya.

The concept of Sama — the beat where the melodic and rhythmic cycles coincide, the 'one' of the Tala cycle — is of particular philosophical significance for understanding the temporal structure of the Karanas. In Indian classical performance, the Sama is the point of absolute temporal reference: everything in the performance is understood in relation to it, and the performance event as a whole has the quality of a continuous movement away from and back toward the Sama. The peak moment of a Karana’s execution — the point of maximum expression, what the tradition calls the Abhiniaya-Kala or 'expressive moment' — is ideally coincident with the Sama: the body arrives at its most complete, most fully expressed configuration precisely as the rhythmic cycle arrives at its point of return.

This coincidence of the Karana’s peak moment with the Sama of the Tala cycle is the temporal equivalent of the spatial coincidence of the Karana’s configuration with the ideal form described in the Natya Shastra. Just as the spatial form must be precise and complete, the temporal placement must be precise and complete: both are dimensions of the same fundamental quality of rightness, of perfect fit between the form and its context. Shankaracharya’s philosophical vocabulary for this quality of perfect fit is Yukta — literally 'yoked' or 'appropriate', the quality of a thing or action that is perfectly suited to its purpose and context. The Yukta action is the action that has the

101
The 108 Karanas

quality of Dharma — rightness, cosmic appropriateness — and in the context of performance, the Karana executed with perfect temporal precision achieves this quality of Yukta-ness in its temporal dimension.

The deeper philosophical implication of the Karana’s temporal structure is the insight it encodes about the nature of time itself. In the Indian philosophical tradition, time is understood as the medium in which the eternal non-dual truth appears as sequence, differentiation, and change. The Tala cycle — which recurs endlessly, always returning to the same Sama from which it departed — is a form of time that makes visible the eternal dimension of the present moment: each Sama is both a new beginning and a perfect return, a point at which the linear flow of time is momentarily suspended in the recognition of the eternal ground that underlies it. A Karana executed at the Sama embodies this recognition in physical form: the body arrives at its most complete expression precisely at the moment when time acknowledges its own eternal ground.

This analysis is consistent with Shankaracharya’s treatment of time in the context of liberation. Liberation, in Advaita Vedanta, is not an event in time but the recognition that the true Self has never been bound by time — that the Atman is eternally free, and that the apparent bondage of time is a feature of the Maya-world of appearance, not of the ultimate reality. The dancer who performs the Karanas with genuine understanding is not merely coordinating physical movement with rhythmic time; she is embodying, in each perfectly timed Karana execution, the recognition that her own deepest nature

102
The Cosmic Choreography

is the eternal ground of which the Tala’s recurring Sama is a temporal symbol.

3.7The Karana System and the Nataraja Icon: A Deep Correspondence

The most direct and powerful correspondence between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition lies in the relationship between the Karana system as a whole and the Nataraja icon that is the supreme visual expression of Shankara’s philosophical vision. The Nataraja is not merely one icon among many in the Indian artistic tradition but the most complete, most philosophically sophisticated, and most aesthetically accomplished visual statement of the Advaitic truth ever produced. Its relationship to the 108 Karanas is not merely thematic — that both deal with the cosmic dance of Shiva — but structural: the Nataraja icon encodes, in a single visual statement, the same philosophical insights that the 108 Karanas encode, collectively, in the complete vocabulary of sacred movement.

The Nataraja icon, as developed to its canonical perfection during the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE), depicts Shiva in the Ananda Tandava — the Dance of Bliss. His upper right hand holds the Damaru drum, symbolising Srishti (creation). His upper left hand holds Agni (fire), symbolising Samhara (dissolution). His lower right hand is raised in Abhaya Mudra, symbolising Sthiti (preservation). His left leg is raised in the Urdhva Tandava position, symbolising Tirobhava (concealment).

103
The 108 Karanas

And his lower left hand, extended in the Gajahasta gesture toward the raised foot, symbolises Anugraha (grace/liberation). Beneath both feet lies the figure of Apasmara — the dwarf of ignorance — upon whom Shiva’s right foot firmly treads.

Each of these five elements of the Nataraja icon corresponds to a specific set of Karanas in the 108-Karana vocabulary. The Damaru gesture corresponds to the Karanas of the creative dimension — those opening Karanas that embody the quality of emergence, of form arising from formlessness. The fire-holding gesture corresponds to the Karanas of dissolution — those dynamic, powerful movements that embody the energy of transformation and release. The Abhaya gesture corresponds to the Karanas of preservation — the balanced, grounded movements that embody the quality of sustained presence and protective awareness. The raised leg corresponds to the Karanas of transcendence — the Urdhva Karanas whose elevated configurations embody the quality of liberation from earthly limitation. And the Gajahasta gesture toward the raised foot corresponds to the Karanas of grace — those movements in which the very gesture of transcendence is simultaneously a gesture of compassionate indication, pointing the way for those who follow.

The figure of Apasmara beneath Shiva’s foot — the dwarf of ignorance being trampled in the cosmic dance — corresponds to what the 108 Karanas collectively overcome through their complete execution. Apasmara is not merely ignorance in the abstract but specifically the false identification of the Self with the non-Self — the same Avidya that Shankaracharya identifies as the root of all suffering and the obstacle to liberation. When the

104
The Cosmic Choreography

dancer performs the complete sequence of 108 Karanas with full awareness and philosophical understanding, she is symbolically performing the same act that the Nataraja performs eternally: dancing on the head of ignorance, liberating consciousness from its false identification with limitation.

The Prabhamandala — the circle of flames that surrounds the Nataraja figure — corresponds to the boundary of the complete Karana performance space: the sacred circle within which the cosmic dance occurs. In the Natya Shastra’s architecture of the theatrical space, this boundary is physically realised in the walls of the consecrated theatre hall; in the Nataraja icon, it is symbolised by the ring of fire. Both are the boundary between the ordinary world of appearance and the sacred space within which the cosmic truth is revealed. The dancer who enters this space and performs the 108 Karanas is not merely doing exercises in a practice room; she is entering the Nataraja’s ring of fire and participating in the cosmic dance that the icon depicts.

The Chola sculptors who created the canonical Nataraja image appear to have understood this correspondence with complete clarity. Their placement of the Nataraja in the innermost shrine of the Chidambaram temple, surrounded by the sculptural panels of the 108 Karanas in the adjacent hall, is not accidental but constitutes a philosophical statement of extraordinary precision: the 108 Karanas are the complete vocabulary of the dance whose supreme expression and eternal embodiment is the Nataraja. To understand any single Karana in depth is to understand one aspect of the Nataraja icon; to understand all 108 Karanas in their full philosophical depth is to

105
The 108 Karanas

understand the Nataraja icon completely — which is, in Shankaracharya’s tradition, to understand the non-dual truth itself.

3.8Learning the Karanas: A Philosophical Education Through the Body

The process of learning the 108 Karanas, as transmitted in the classical tradition through the guru-shishya relationship, is itself a philosophical education — a systematic development of the practitioner’s capacity for the kind of integrated, unified body-mind awareness that Shankaracharya identifies as the precondition for genuine philosophical understanding. This education does not proceed through intellectual instruction followed by physical practice but through a process of embodied inquiry in which the understanding and the practice are inseparable from the beginning.

The traditional learning sequence for the Karanas, while it varies somewhat across different lineages, typically begins with the Adavus (basic movement units) that constitute the foundational building blocks of the Karana vocabulary, before proceeding to the Karanas themselves. This progression from simpler to more complex is not merely a pedagogical convenience but a philosophical statement: the practitioner must first learn to inhabit the most basic qualities of embodied consciousness — weight, balance, direction, rhythm, breath — before attempting the more complex integrations that the full Karanas require. This

106
The Cosmic Choreography

corresponds precisely to the pedagogical sequence in Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition: the student must first develop the basic qualities of Viveka (discrimination) and Vairagya (dispassion) before they can profitably engage with the more complex philosophical inquiries that lead to Brahman-recognition.

The experience of learning a new Karana for the first time has a characteristic phenomenological structure that experienced practitioners recognise and that reflects the tradition’s philosophical framework. The first encounters with an unfamiliar Karana are typically characterised by cognitive effortfulness: the practitioner must consciously attend to each of the multiple components simultaneously, and the result is typically a jerky, uneven, effortful attempt that lacks the fluidity and integration of the master’s execution. This corresponds to what Shankara describes as the state of Savikalpa Samadhi — the meditative absorption that still retains traces of effort and deliberateness.

As the practice deepens and the Karana begins to be genuinely internalised — as the form begins to inhabit the practitioner’s body rather than being imposed upon it — the quality of the execution changes. The effortfulness gives way to a flowing, natural quality in which the components coordinate themselves without deliberate attention. This corresponds to the state of Nirvikalpa Samadhi — the meditative absorption in which the effort and deliberateness have dissolved into a natural, spontaneous clarity. And the final stage — in which the practitioner can execute the Karana under any conditions, in any

107
The 108 Karanas

Tala, in any emotional context, with perfect freedom and authenticity — corresponds to Sahaja Samadhi, the 'natural' or 'spontaneous' liberation that is the Advaita tradition’s description of the fully realised sage’s engagement with the world: completely free, completely natural, neither practising nor not practising, simply being what one has always been.

This phenomenological parallel between the stages of Karana internalisation and the stages of Samadhi described in Shankara’s philosophical tradition is not a coincidence but a reflection of the fundamental truth that both traditions are investigating: the nature of consciousness in its relationship to skill, knowledge, and freedom. The question that both traditions are addressing is the same: how does consciousness move from the effortful, divided, self-conscious condition of the beginner to the effortless, unified, self-transparent condition of the master? The answer that both traditions give is also the same: not through the acquisition of more and more, but through the progressive dissolution of the obstacles — the tensions, habits, fears, and limited self-concepts — that prevent the natural flow of the consciousness that one already is.

The teacher’s role in this learning process is, in both the Karana tradition and the Advaita Vedanta tradition, primarily that of a mirror and a catalyst rather than a transmitter of external information. The guru does not give the student the Karana or the knowledge of Brahman; she or he removes the obstacles that prevent the student from discovering what was always already present. In the Karana context, this means the patient, attentive observation of the student’s execution —

108
The Cosmic Choreography

identifying the specific tensions, habits, and limited self-concepts that are preventing the natural flow of the movement — and finding the precise intervention (a subtle postural adjustment, a specific verbal description, a demonstration that the student’s mirror neurons will respond to) that will dissolve that particular obstacle. In the Advaita Vedanta context, the guru’s role is described in identical terms: patient observation of the student’s understanding, precise identification of the specific form of Avidya (ignorance) that is obscuring the recognition, and the skillful deployment of the precise teaching that will dissolve that particular form of ignorance and allow the recognition to dawn.

3.12Sacred Movement and Cosmic Order

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated

109
The 108 Karanas

experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

110
The Cosmic Choreography

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

111
The 108 Karanas

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

3.13Archaeological Evidence and Material Culture

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S.

112
The Cosmic Choreography

Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in

113
The 108 Karanas

increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily

114
The Cosmic Choreography

selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

3.9The Karana Notation Systems: Ancient and Contemporary

The challenge of notating the 108 Karanas — capturing in a stable, transmissible written form the complex, three-dimensional, temporally extended movement events that the Karanas represent — has engaged Indian and international scholars for several generations. The Natya Shastra’s own descriptions, as noted earlier, range from the detailed to the terse, and the temple sculptures provide important visual supplements. But a complete notation system — one capable of fully specifying

115
The 108 Karanas

every relevant dimension of a Karana execution — has proven elusive.

The most systematic modern attempt to develop such a notation system is that of Padma Subrahmanyam, who developed a modified version of Laban Movement Analysis adapted to the specific vocabulary of the classical Indian tradition. Subrahmanyam’s notation system has been applied to the complete reconstruction of the 108 Karanas and provides the most rigorous and comprehensive codification of the Karana system currently available. However, like all notation systems for embodied practice, it captures the external form while necessarily leaving unnotated the internal qualities — the breath, the inner attention, the quality of awareness — that are, in the tradition’s understanding, as important as the external form.

Other scholars have proposed alternative notation approaches based on the Sanskrit grammatical tradition (treating the Karana forms as words in a movement grammar), the cognitive science of action representation (treating the Karanas as motor programs with specific kinaesthetic signatures), and the iconometric analysis of temple sculptures (using the proportional relationships and configurations of the sculptural forms as a primary basis for reconstruction). Each of these approaches illuminates different dimensions of the Karana system while leaving others in shadow.

The philosophical implications of the notation challenge are significant. The difficulty of fully notating the Karanas reflects the fundamental insight that embodied knowledge cannot be completely captured in any representational system — that the

116
The Cosmic Choreography

living quality of a genuine Karana execution exceeds any description, notation, or recording of it. This is the tradition’s wisdom about the limits of text: the Natya Shastra’s prescriptions are necessary but not sufficient for understanding the Karanas; the temple sculptures are illuminating but not complete; even the best video documentation is partial. The complete transmission of the Karana knowledge requires the living encounter between teacher and student through which the qualities that cannot be notated — the quality of attention, the quality of breath, the quality of inward awareness — are transmitted directly, body to body, consciousness to consciousness.

CHAPTER IV

Shankaracharya

Philosopher, Poet, and Visionary

“In a span of thirty-two years, this one man achieved more than most traditions achieve in centuries — and all of it was saturated with the joy of awareness.”

— Swami Vivekananda, on Adi Shankaracharya

4.1Biographical and Historical Context

Adi Shankaracharya’s life, as recounted in the various traditional biographies (Shankaravijaya) composed by his followers across several centuries, reads almost like myth — yet even the most sceptical historian cannot deny that this extraordinary figure transformed Indian philosophical culture in ways whose effects are still felt today. Born in the village of Kaladi in present-day Kerala, Shankara displayed precocious intellectual gifts from earliest childhood. Traditional accounts speak of his mastery of all the Vedas before the age of eight, his renunciation of worldly life while still a young child, his discipleship under the great sage Govinda Bhagavatpada on the

118
The Cosmic Choreography

banks of the Narmada, and his eventual consecration as a Sannyasin despite the initial reluctance of his widowed mother.

The historical context of Shankara’s work is important for understanding both its intellectual content and its cultural significance. He lived during a period of extraordinary philosophical pluralism in India — a period when the subcontinent was simultaneously home to numerous competing schools of thought, each with its own sophisticated philosophical framework, its own body of scripture and commentary, and its own institutional expressions in the form of monasteries, temples, and traditions of teaching. The major Buddhist schools — Madhyamaka, Vijnanavada or Yogacara, Sautrantika, and Vaibhashika — were still vital forces in the philosophical landscape, particularly in the monastic universities of Nalanda and Vikramashila. The Mimamsa school, which insisted on the absolute authority of Vedic ritual and denied the reality of any consciousness beyond the everyday empirical self, represented the most powerful orthodox challenge to the Vedantic project. The various devotional traditions — Vaishnavism in its many forms, Shaivism, Shaktism — were gaining popular and royal patronage across the subcontinent.

Shankara’s intellectual project in this context was simultaneously critical and constructive. He needed to establish the Advaitic interpretation of the Upanishads as the supreme and final philosophical truth — superior to the various Buddhist positions (which he regarded as ultimately nihilistic or solipsistic, despite their genuine philosophical insights), superior to the dualistic Samkhya and Vaisheshika systems, and superior to the

119
Shankaracharya

literalist Mimamsa interpretation of the Vedas. At the same time, he needed to demonstrate that his non-dual philosophy was not an abstract, world-negating teaching for the spiritually elite few but a practical wisdom relevant to every human being in every condition of life — the farmer as well as the philosopher, the devotee as well as the jnani, the dancer as well as the monk.

It is this second, constructive dimension of Shankara’s work that is most relevant to our study. His decision to compose, alongside his rigorous philosophical commentaries and treatises, a body of devotional poetry of extraordinary beauty and emotional depth was not a concession to popular taste but a deliberate philosophical strategy. The Soundarya Lahari, the Shiva Tandava Stotram, the Bhaja Govindam, the Dakshinamurti Stotra — these are not peripheral to Shankara’s philosophical achievement but central to it. They demonstrate that the non-dual philosophy, far from impoverishing human experience by reducing it to abstract monism, actually enriches and deepens it: the world seen through the eyes of Advaita is more beautiful, not less; more vibrant and alive, not more remote and lifeless; more worthy of wonder and love, not less.

The geographical dimension of Shankara’s life also deserves attention. His famous Digvijaya — his conquest of the philosophical world through a journey to every corner of the Indian subcontinent — took him from Kerala in the far south to Kashmir in the far north, from the temples of Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh to the banks of the Ganga at Varanasi and the high Himalayas. This comprehensive traversal of the subcontinent’s intellectual and spiritual landscape is not merely

120
The Cosmic Choreography

biography but philosophical methodology: Shankara was not content to establish the truth of Advaita in the abstract but insisted on establishing it concretely, in engagement with every significant philosophical tradition, in every cultural and geographical context, demonstrating that the non-dual insight is not the property of any particular region, tradition, or school but the universal ground of all genuine philosophical inquiry.

4.2The System of Advaita Vedanta

The central claim of Shankara’s Advaita Vedanta can be stated simply — Brahman alone is real; the world is appearance; the individual self is identical with Brahman — but the philosophical elaboration of this claim into a complete, coherent, rigorous system of thought is extraordinarily complex and subtle. The simplicity of the central claim is deceptive: each of its three elements requires extensive philosophical analysis to understand precisely what is being claimed, and the relationships among the three elements are not immediately obvious.

Brahman, in Shankara’s exposition, is to be understood as Nirguna — without qualities or attributes — in the ultimate sense. This is not to say that Brahman is a blank emptiness or a philosophical placeholder for the unknown; rather, Brahman is understood as the reality that underlies all qualities and attributes, the pure consciousness that is presupposed by every experience, the awareness in which all objects of knowledge appear without being itself an object of knowledge. Shankara’s great contribution

121
Shankaracharya

to the understanding of Brahman is his insistence on its identity with pure consciousness — Chit — as the most fundamental characterisation. Brahman is not a material substance, not a cosmic person, not a ground of being in any sense that implies a substrate beneath consciousness; Brahman is consciousness itself, self-luminous, self-knowing, without beginning, without end, without limit.

Maya, in Shankara’s system, is the power by which Brahman appears as the world — the mechanism of apparent differentiation that transforms the simple unity of pure consciousness into the apparent multiplicity of experienced reality. Shankara is careful to distinguish his concept of Maya from various forms of nihilism or idealism: Maya does not mean that the world is unreal in the sense of not existing at all (that would be nihilism), nor does it mean that the world is merely a mental projection with no objective correlate (that would be the Vijnanavada position that Shankara explicitly criticises). Maya means, rather, that the world has a paradoxical status: it is real enough at the conventional level of experience, real enough to require philosophical analysis and practical engagement, but ultimately real only as an appearance of Brahman — as Brahman seen through the distorting filter of ignorance (Avidya).

The concept of Avidya — ignorance — is central to Shankara’s soteriology. Liberation requires the removal of Avidya, not the performance of any ritual action or the achievement of any spiritual state. Avidya is the primordial confusion between the real and the apparent, the self and the non-self, consciousness and its objects. It is beginningless — one cannot ask when it began,

122
The Cosmic Choreography

because the very asking of such a question already presupposes a subject of inquiry who is already caught in the web of Avidya — but it is not endless: it can be and is removed by the dawn of Viveka, the discriminative wisdom that distinguishes the real from the apparent, the self from the non-self, Brahman from Maya.

The relationship between Maya and artistic creation is one of the most productive dimensions of Shankaracharya’s philosophy for understanding his relationship to the Natya Shastra. If Maya is understood as Brahman’s creative power — the power by which the one appears as many, by which the formless takes on form, by which the utterly simple gives rise to apparent complexity — then the greatest art is that which consciously enacts this creative power in miniature. The artist who creates a great work is, in this sense, Brahman creating through the medium of a human instrument. And the 108 Karanas, as the complete vocabulary of Shiva’s cosmic creation, are the ultimate artistic vocabulary: the complete set of creative gestures through which the divine artist enacts his creation. Understanding the Karanas philosophically requires understanding Maya philosophically — understanding Brahman’s own creative play as the most fundamental art form, of which all human art is both an imitation and a genuine participation.

123
Shankaracharya

4.3Shankara as Artist and Aesthetician

The aesthetic dimensions of Shankaracharya’s work have been insufficiently appreciated in the scholarly literature, which has tended to treat his devotional poetry as secondary to his philosophical commentaries. This is a serious distortion of the tradition. Shankara’s devotional compositions are not merely popular simplifications of philosophical doctrines that find their real expression in the more demanding technical texts; they are autonomous philosophical achievements in a different medium, using the resources of poetic language, aesthetic imagery, and emotional resonance to communicate truths that the discursive philosophical medium cannot fully capture.

The Soundarya Lahari is the clearest evidence for this claim. Written in the sophisticated Shardula Vikridita meter — one of the most demanding in Sanskrit prosody, with seventeen syllables per quarter-verse arranged in a complex pattern of long and short syllables — it is a work of extraordinary technical mastery. The precision of its versification is matched by the precision of its philosophical content: every image, every descriptive detail, every comparison is philosophically exact, conveying with the resources of poetic language what the corresponding philosophical prose would convey through argument and analysis.

The text’s central achievement is its sustained demonstration that physical beauty — the beauty of the Goddess’s form as described verse by verse in intimate, almost overwhelming sensuous detail — is not separate from metaphysical truth but is

124
The Cosmic Choreography

its most perfect expression. In Western philosophical aesthetics, this position is associated with the Neoplatonists (who argued that physical beauty is a reflection, however dim, of the transcendent beauty of the divine) and with Hegel (who argued that art is the sensuous presentation of the Idea). But in Shankaracharya’s version, the claim is stronger and more precise: physical beauty is not a dim reflection of metaphysical truth but its direct, complete manifestation in the medium of form. The Goddess’s body is beautiful because it is Brahman; it is Brahman because it is perfectly beautiful. Beauty and truth are not merely analogous but identical at the highest level.

This philosophical aestheticism has direct implications for the tradition of the 108 Karanas. If beauty is a direct manifestation of Brahman — not merely a symptom or signal of it but its actual self-expression in the medium of form — then the 108 Karanas, as forms of embodied beauty executed with complete technical mastery and genuine artistic integrity, are not merely representations or symbols of the cosmic dance but genuine instances of it. When a great dancer executes the Talapushpaputa with perfect grounded equanimity, perfect gesture, and luminous inner awareness, she is not imitating Brahman’s creative act; she is performing it. The boundary between art and reality, between imitation and actuality, dissolves — which is precisely the dissolution of Maya that Shankaracharya’s philosophy describes.

This understanding — that the most perfect art is not an imitation of reality but a genuine instance of it — is what gives the Natya Shastra’s claim that Natya is a fifth Veda its deepest meaning. The Vedas are not merely texts about Brahman; they

125
Shankaracharya

are, in the oral tradition, actual instances of Brahman-sound — the resonance of consciousness itself made audible in the medium of Sanskrit phonemes. Similarly, the 108 Karanas are not merely descriptions of Brahman’s cosmic dance but actual instances of it — Brahman’s own movement becoming audible and visible in the medium of a human body informed by the wisdom of the tradition. This is the deepest sense in which Shankaracharya’s philosophy and the Natya Shastra’s performance theory converge: both understand the highest human activity as not merely pointing toward Brahman but as being Brahman’s own self-expression through the medium of human consciousness and form.

4.5The Four Mathas and the Institutionalisation of Advaita Vedanta

One of Shankaracharya’s most enduring institutional achievements was the establishment of four cardinal monasteries (Mathas) at the four geographical extremities of the Indian subcontinent: Sringeri in the south, Dwaraka in the west, Puri in the east, and Badrinath in the north. This strategic placement was not merely organizational but philosophical: it expressed Shankara’s conviction that the Advaitic truth is not the property of any particular region, community, or lineage but belongs to the entire subcontinent’s spiritual heritage, and that its institutional expression should be as comprehensive and universal as the truth itself.

126
The Cosmic Choreography

The four Mathas have each developed their own distinctive emphases within the broad framework of Advaita Vedanta, and these emphases are relevant to understanding the relationship between Shankara’s philosophy and the performing arts traditions. The Sringeri Sharada Peetham in Karnataka, as the southernmost Matha and the one most directly connected to the Tamil and Andhra performance cultures, has historically maintained the closest relationship to the classical arts traditions. The Peetham’s patronage of the Carnatic musical tradition and classical dance has been an important dimension of its cultural programme throughout its history, and several of the Sringeri Acharyas have written philosophical commentaries that engage explicitly with the aesthetics of the classical arts.

The Kanchi Kamakoti Peetham — which some traditions regard as a fifth Matha established by Shankara, though this claim is contested by the other four Mathas — is located in Kanchipuram, one of the great temple cities of South India and a centre of classical dance scholarship and practice from at least the Pallava period. The Kanchipuram tradition’s proximity to the Chola period temple architecture that produced the most important sculptural programmes of the 108 Karanas makes it a particularly important institutional link between Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition and the Natya Shastra’s performance tradition.

The relationship between the Mathas and the performing arts is also visible in the devotional traditions associated with each Matha’s tutelary deity. The Sringeri Peetham’s devotion to the Divine Mother in her form as Sharada (a form of Saraswati)

127
Shankaracharya

connects it to the tradition of sacred music and dance that is Saraswati’s domain. The Puri Peetham’s association with Jagannath — one of the most culturally dynamic and artistically fertile of India’s divine figures, associated with the famous Rath Yatra chariot festival and the Odissi classical dance tradition — makes it a direct institutional link between the Advaita Vedanta tradition and one of India’s most vibrant dance forms.

The philosophical significance of this institutional connection between the Advaita Vedanta Mathas and the performing arts traditions is that it demonstrates the tradition’s own self-understanding of the relationship between philosophy and art. The Mathas did not maintain their connection to the arts as a concession to popular taste or as a fund-raising strategy; they understood this connection as philosophically essential. The classical arts, in the Matha tradition’s understanding, are not ornamental additions to the philosophical tradition but vehicles of the same truth that the philosophical tradition articulates through argument and analysis — vehicles that reach dimensions of human experience that argument and analysis alone cannot access.

This institutional dimension of the relationship between Shankaracharya’s tradition and the performing arts provides important context for understanding the philosophical synthesis this book traces. The synthesis is not merely a theoretical possibility articulated in the texts of Shankara and Abhinavagupta; it has actual institutional expression in the living traditions of the Mathas and their associated arts. The 108 Karanas are performed today in the context of temples that are, in

128
The Cosmic Choreography

many cases, under the patronage and philosophical guidance of traditions that trace themselves directly to Shankaracharya. The living transmission of the Karana vocabulary occurs within an institutional framework that has, for over a millennium, understood performing arts as a vehicle of the same truth that Shankara articulated in his philosophical commentaries.

4.6Shankaracharya’s Poetics: Form, Beauty, and the Communication of Truth

Shankaracharya’s philosophical poetry is not merely philosophy in verse but a genuine poetic achievement that demands aesthetic analysis alongside philosophical interpretation. The Soundarya Lahari, the Sivananda Lahari, the Bhaja Govindam, the Dakshinamurti Stotra, and the Nirvana Shatakam are works of art as well as works of philosophy, and understanding their artistic dimensions is essential to understanding their philosophical dimensions — for in Shankara’s work, as we shall argue, the medium and the message are inseparable.

The metrical variety of Shankara’s devotional compositions reflects a sophisticated understanding of the relationship between poetic form and philosophical content. The Soundarya Lahari’s primary meter, Shardula Vikridita (literally 'the gait of a tiger'), has nineteen syllables per quarter-verse arranged in a complex pattern that creates a sense of powerful, rhythmic movement — appropriate for a poem that is, among other things, a description of the Divine Mother’s dance. The Bhaja Govindam, by contrast,

129
Shankaracharya

is composed in a relatively simple, strongly rhythmic meter that lends itself to popular singing — appropriate for a poem whose philosophical message is aimed at the widest possible audience and whose central injunction is to abandon intellectual cleverness in favour of direct devotion.

The relationship between meter and philosophical content in Shankara’s work is not merely aesthetic but epistemological. In the Indian philosophical tradition, sound itself is understood as a vehicle of meaning at a level that transcends the semantic content of words: the quality of a verse’s sound — its meter, its alliteration, its internal rhythms — communicates dimensions of meaning that the words alone cannot convey. The Shiva Tandava Stotram’s driving Jagati meter communicates the dynamic, unstoppable energy of the Tandava dance at a level that the words' semantic content supplements but cannot replace. A reader who hears or recites the Shiva Tandava Stotram without knowing Sanskrit is already receiving a significant portion of its philosophical meaning through the medium of its sound.

The use of specific ornaments (Alamkaras) in Shankara’s philosophical poetry also deserves attention. The Simile (Upama), the Metaphor (Rupaka), and the Hyperbole (Atishayokti) are Shankara’s most frequently deployed ornaments, and their philosophical significance goes beyond mere literary decoration. In the Advaitic philosophical framework, the Simile — comparing one thing to another while maintaining the distinction between them — corresponds to the conventional level of understanding in which Brahman and the world are seen as related but distinct. The Metaphor — identifying one thing

130
The Cosmic Choreography

with another — corresponds to the philosophical level of understanding in which Brahman and the world are seen as identical in essence. And the Hyperbole — asserting something beyond the bounds of ordinary quantitative possibility — corresponds to the transcendent level of understanding in which ordinary categories of quantity and quality cease to apply.

The Soundarya Lahari’s primary ornamental strategy — the sustained, systematic description of the Divine Mother’s physical beauty — constitutes what the Indian poetic tradition calls Vastu-Varnana (description of a thing), but elevated to a philosophical principle. Every verse employs the resources of Sanskrit poetic tradition — its elaborate tradition of bodily description, its conventions of comparison to natural phenomena, its vocabulary of aesthetic appreciation — but at the same time transforms this tradition by treating the described body as the body of Brahman itself, making the conventional aesthetic appreciation of beauty into a philosophical recognition of the non-dual truth. This dual operation — working simultaneously within and against the conventions of Sanskrit love poetry — is the source of the Soundarya Lahari’s extraordinary aesthetic power and philosophical depth.

Understanding Shankara’s poetics in this way illuminates why the performing arts tradition would have found in his work such a congenial philosophical partner. The classical Indian dance tradition’s use of the body’s expressive vocabulary to communicate philosophical and spiritual truths operates on exactly the same principle: it works within the conventions of aesthetic appreciation (using the same vocabulary of movement,

131
Shankaracharya

gesture, and expression that secular performance employs) while simultaneously transforming those conventions by situating them within a framework of philosophical understanding that reveals their deeper spiritual dimensions. Shankara’s devotional poetry and classical Indian dance are not merely analogous activities; they are parallel deployments of the same fundamental insight: that the highest truth can be communicated through aesthetic beauty, that beauty and truth are ultimately not separate, and that the most complete human statement of the non-dual reality is one that speaks simultaneously to the senses, the emotions, and the philosophical intellect.

4.7Shankara’s Dialogues and the Art of Philosophical Transmission

The traditional accounts of Shankaracharya’s philosophical debates — with Mandana Mishra, Prabhakara, and numerous other opponents — provide fascinating material for understanding the relationship between the performative and philosophical dimensions of his work. These debates, which the traditional biographies describe in elaborate detail, were not merely intellectual contests but cultural performances: public events in which the philosophical traditions of India were enacted before audiences of scholars, kings, and curious laypeople, and in which the quality of the debaters' performance — their ability to respond instantly, to deploy the resources of the tradition with elegance and precision, to maintain composure and clarity under

132
The Cosmic Choreography

pressure — was as important as the intellectual content of their arguments.

The traditional accounts consistently describe Shankara’s debating style in terms that closely parallel the classical dance tradition’s descriptions of the highest level of performance. He is described as responding to opponents with the speed and precision of a trained dancer — his arguments arriving at exactly the right moment, with exactly the right force, in exactly the right form to dissolve the opponent’s position. His philosophical improvisation — the ability to generate new arguments on the spot in response to unexpected objections — is described in terms that parallel the classical musician’s or dancer’s Manodharma: the spontaneous, inspired response that arises from complete mastery of the tradition combined with complete freedom from its constraints.

The formal structure of the Indian philosophical debate (Vada) has close parallels with the formal structure of classical dance performance. Both begin with a period of preparation and invocation; both proceed through a structured sequence of phases (the initial statement of position, the development of argument, the response to objection, the resolution); and both conclude with a formal acknowledgment of the outcome. The qualities required of the ideal debater — complete mastery of the tradition’s technical vocabulary, the ability to deploy that vocabulary spontaneously and precisely in response to the situation, and the quality of equanimity that allows full engagement without personal investment in the outcome — are the same qualities required of the ideal classical performer.

133
Shankaracharya

This parallel between philosophical debate and classical performance illuminates an important dimension of Shankaracharya’s relationship to the performing arts. His philosophical activity was itself a kind of performance — a public enactment of the non-dual truth in the medium of philosophical argument. And conversely, the classical performance of the 108 Karanas can be understood as a kind of philosophical argument — a demonstration in the medium of embodied movement of the truth that Shankara demonstrated in the medium of philosophical discourse. Both are public enactments of the same non-dual insight; both require the same quality of complete technical mastery combined with complete freedom from that mastery; and both, at their highest, produce in the audience the same quality of direct, immediate recognition that is simultaneously an aesthetic and a philosophical experience.

The tradition’s understanding of great philosophical teaching as a form of performance — and of great performance as a form of teaching — is captured in the concept of Pravachana (discourse), which in the Indian tradition designates a form of teaching that is simultaneously intellectually precise and aesthetically refined, simultaneously philosophically rigorous and devotionally inspiring. The great Pravachana is a performance event in the full sense: it has a specific temporal form, a specific spatial context, and a specific quality of embodied presence that distinguishes it from mere lecture or mere recitation. And the best classical dance performance is a form of Pravachana in the movement medium: a teaching in the grammar of the body that communicates, with a precision beyond words, the same truth

134
The Cosmic Choreography

that the verbal Pravachana communicates in the grammar of language.

4.13The Philosophical Vision and Its Contemporary Relevance

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta.
