At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not

135
Shankaracharya

separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by

136
The Cosmic Choreography

reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human

137
Shankaracharya

consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

4.14Manuscript Traditions and Textual History

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical

138
The Cosmic Choreography

relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the

139
Shankaracharya

two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple

140
The Cosmic Choreography

sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

4.8Shankara’s Contribution to Sanskrit Literature

Shankaracharya’s contribution to Sanskrit literature extends far beyond his philosophical commentaries into the domains of stotric poetry, didactic verse, and philosophical kāvya (literary poetry). His literary corpus — however much of it may belong to his immediate disciples rather than to him personally — represents one of the most extensive and influential bodies of Sanskrit writing associated with any single name, spanning everything from the most technically demanding philosophical prose to the most accessible devotional song.

The literary sophistication of Shankara’s compositions is evident in their metrical variety alone. The Soundarya Lahari employs the demanding Shardula Vikridita meter; the Sivananda Lahari uses a range of meters suited to its devotional purposes; the Bhaja Govindam employs the simple, rhythmically driving Dindima meter; the Nirvana Shatakam uses a relatively rare variant of the Drutavilambita meter. This metrical variety reflects a deliberate matching of form to content — each composition’s meter contributing to its

141
Shankaracharya

philosophical and emotional meaning in ways that a less sophisticated literary craftsman could not achieve.

The literary tradition of Sanskrit has always understood the relationship between philosophical content and literary form as non-accidental. The Alankara tradition — the theory of literary ornamentation and figures — describes how specific literary devices (metaphor, alliteration, paranomasia, sustained simile) are not merely decorative but contribute to the communication of meaning at levels that ordinary discursive prose cannot reach. Shankara’s compositions consistently employ these literary devices with philosophical precision: his metaphors are not random comparisons but carefully chosen images that embody, in miniature, the complete philosophical insight they are intended to convey.

The relationship between Shankara’s literary and philosophical achievements is itself a demonstration of the thesis this book traces. His ability to communicate the non-dual truth simultaneously through rigorous philosophical argument and through the most refined literary beauty is itself an instance of the synthesis between philosophical depth and aesthetic excellence that the relationship between the Natya Shastra and Advaita Vedanta represents at the level of tradition and practice. In his person, as in the classical dance tradition at its highest, philosophy and art, rigorous analysis and spontaneous beauty, are not in tension but are mutually reinforcing expressions of the same single insight: that consciousness is one, beautiful, and free.

142
CHAPTER V

Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

“Shiva, only when united with Shakti, has the power to create. Otherwise, He is not even capable of movement.”

— Soundarya Lahari, Verse 1

5.1The Soundarya Lahari: Structure and Significance

The Soundarya Lahari — Wave of Beauty — is universally regarded as the crown jewel of Shankaracharya’s devotional poetry and one of the supreme achievements of the entire Sanskrit literary tradition. The text consists of one hundred verses in the Shardula Vikridita and other complex meters, addressed to the Divine Mother — Tripura Sundari, Lalita, Parvati — in her aspect as the supreme Shakti, the dynamic power of consciousness that underlies and animates all of creation. The text is traditionally divided into two major sections: the Ananda Lahari (Wave of Bliss, verses 1-41), which focuses on the metaphysical and tantric dimensions of the

143
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

Goddess, and the Soundarya Lahari proper (verses 42-100), which describes her physical beauty in exquisite and philosophically precise detail.

The opening verse of the Soundarya Lahari is perhaps the most philosophically concise statement of the entire Advaita Shakta position: 'Shiva Shaktya yukto yadi bhavati shaktah prabhavitum, na chedevam devo na khalu kushalah spanditumapi' — 'Shiva, only when united with Shakti, has the power to create; otherwise, even this God is not capable of the slightest movement.' This verse establishes the fundamental metaphysical structure that will organise the entire text: Shiva (pure consciousness, the Nirguna Brahman) and Shakti (dynamic power, the creative energy of consciousness) are not two separate realities but two aspects of the single non-dual reality. Without Shakti, Shiva cannot move; without Shiva, Shakti has no ground to move from. The dance of Shiva — the Ananda Tandava, the cosmic dance expressed through the 108 Karanas — is precisely this union of Shiva and Shakti, consciousness and energy, being and becoming.

The Ananda Lahari section (verses 1-41) develops this metaphysical framework with extraordinary philosophical depth. These verses deal with the most abstruse dimensions of the Shakta Tantric tradition — the Shri Chakra or Shri Yantra (the geometric diagram encoding the Goddess’s cosmic structure), the fifty letters of the Sanskrit alphabet as emanations of the divine creative power, the various levels of manifestation from pure consciousness through increasingly dense levels of cosmic structure to the physical world. For our purposes, what is most

144
The Cosmic Choreography

significant is the pervasive movement imagery in these verses: the Goddess is never static but always in dynamic relationship with Shiva, always in the process of emanating, sustaining, and withdrawing the cosmos, always dancing.

The Soundarya Lahari proper (verses 42-100) shifts to a description of the Goddess’s physical beauty, moving systematically from the top of her head to the soles of her feet in a pattern familiar from Sanskrit devotional poetry (the Kesadi-pada or Padadi-kesa description). But unlike superficially similar descriptions in secular Sanskrit love poetry, these verses are philosophically precise: every detail of the Goddess’s appearance encodes a specific metaphysical truth. The lustre of her hair encodes the nature of Tamas as it is transformed by Sattva; the brilliance of her forehead encodes the quality of pure awareness; the grace of her gait encodes the quality of consciousness moving through the world with effortless ease. The physical description is simultaneously a philosophical treatise.

Throughout the text, movement imagery is central and sustained. The Goddess does not merely exist; she moves, dances, sways, trembles, flows, leaps, and dissolves. Her movement is not random but expressive — every gesture of the cosmic body encodes a specific quality of divine consciousness. This sustained movement imagery is not decorative but constitutes Shankaracharya’s most sustained and direct engagement with the philosophical tradition of the Natya Shastra: the Soundarya Lahari is, among many other things, a philosophical commentary on the 108 Karanas, reading the complete vocabulary of sacred movement as a text of Advaitic wisdom.

145
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

5.2Key Verses and Their Karana Correspondences

A systematic analysis of the Soundarya Lahari reveals, as noted in our Executive Summary, at least seventeen verses whose imagery corresponds with striking precision to specific Karanas from the Natya Shastra system. In this section, we examine the most significant of these correspondences in detail, building toward an argument for the deliberate philosophical character of Shankaracharya’s movement imagery.

Verse 1’s description of the union of Shiva and Shakti as the precondition of all movement corresponds, at the structural level, to the Natya Shastra’s foundational claim that the Karana is the union (samayoga) of hands and feet — that is, that movement is itself a union, a coordination of apparently separate elements into a single event. Just as no movement is possible without the union of Shiva and Shakti, no Karana is possible without the union of hasta and pada. The metaphysical and the technical converge on the same insight: the deepest nature of movement is unity.

Verse 10, which describes the Goddess as a wave of bliss (Ananda Lahari) flowing from the union of Shiva and Shakti, corresponds most directly to the Karana called Nikuttaka — the vibrating, trembling movement that embodies the Spanda or primordial pulsation of consciousness. Shankara’s image of the wave is precisely apt: Nikuttaka embodies not a single, discrete movement but a continuous, rhythmic oscillation — a wave of movement that, like the Ananda Lahari described in verse 10, arises spontaneously from the

146
The Cosmic Choreography

nature of consciousness itself and flows through the body without beginning or end.

Verse 41, which describes the Goddess’s foot touching the earth and the trembling of the world in response to that divine touch, corresponds to the Karana called Talapushpaputa — the offering gesture in which both hands cup upward toward the touched foot of the Goddess. The image of the earth trembling at the Goddess’s touch encodes the philosophical insight that manifestation itself is a response to consciousness — that the world arises as a kind of trembling recognition of the divine presence that grounds and permeates it. The Talapushpaputa Karana encodes the same insight in movement: the offering gesture acknowledges the divine ground that the standing position (Sthana) embodies.

Verse 53 — the verse that most directly invokes the 108 Karanas through its description of the Urdhva Tandava — describes the Divine Mother watching Shiva’s dance and eventually joining it. This verse is of central importance for our entire study because it explicitly brings together the two traditions whose relationship we are tracing: the Natya Shastra’s Tandava tradition and Shankaracharya’s Advaitic devotional tradition. The verse describes Parvati-Shakti not as a passive spectator of Shiva’s dance but as an active participant — eventually dancing with him, eventually merging with him in the dance until it is impossible to say where Shiva’s dance ends and Shakti’s begins. This image of the indistinguishable dance of Shiva and Shakti is Shankaracharya’s most precise visual formulation of the Advaitic insight: the apparent duality of consciousness and energy, of the

147
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

absolute and the relative, dissolves in the recognition of their essential unity.

Verse 61, describing the Goddess’s gait as she walks through the cosmic garden, uses imagery of extraordinary grace and naturalness: her steps are like the gait of a young elephant (gajagamini — one of the most celebrated compliments in Sanskrit poetry), her movement effortless and perfectly proportioned. This correspondence to the Gajahasta Karana is not merely visual but philosophical: the gait of the Goddess encodes the quality of consciousness moving through the world with complete ease, without effort, without resistance, without the distortion of ego-assertion. This is the quality that Shankaracharya calls Sahaja — the 'natural' or 'spontaneous' quality of consciousness that has recognised its own nature and therefore moves through the world without the unnecessary friction of self-consciousness.

5.3The Aesthetic Theology of Beauty

What distinguishes the Soundarya Lahari from other Sanskrit devotional texts — and what makes it uniquely relevant to our study — is its sustained insistence on the spiritual validity of aesthetic experience as such. In most Indian philosophical traditions, including many strands of the Vedantic tradition itself, the path to liberation involves progressive disengagement from sensory experience — a turning inward from the apparent beauty of the world toward the subtler and finally unsurpassable beauty

148
The Cosmic Choreography

of pure consciousness. The world’s beauty is acknowledged as real at the conventional level but is seen as a veil that ultimately needs to be penetrated rather than a truth that needs to be celebrated.

Shankaracharya’s Soundarya Lahari takes a different and more philosophically daring position. The beauty of the Goddess’s form — described in verse after verse with an intimacy and sensuous precision that has made the text uncomfortable for some readers of the Advaita tradition — is not a veil concealing the truth but the truth itself in its most perfect formal expression. The Goddess is beautiful because she is Brahman; her beauty is the clearest, most direct, most unobstructed manifestation of Brahman’s own nature as Ananda (bliss). The world’s beauty, seen rightly, does not lead away from Brahman but toward it — indeed, seen with sufficient depth, the world’s beauty is Brahman.

This theological aestheticism has profound implications for the 108 Karanas and their philosophical significance. If the beauty of form is a direct manifestation of Brahman — not merely a pointer toward it but its actual self-expression — then the beautiful movements of classical dance, the graceful configurations of the Karanas executed with complete mastery, are themselves manifestations of Brahman. The dancer is not imitating the Goddess; she is, in the moment of perfect execution, being the Goddess — being the beautiful, dynamic, conscious expression of the divine that the Soundarya Lahari describes. This is not hubris but humility of the deepest kind: the recognition that the dancer herself is Brahman, and that her dance is Brahman’s own movement.

149
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

The tradition of Devadasi practice — the system through which the most refined classical dance forms were performed in the temple context, by women who were dedicated to the deity and understood their performance as a form of worship — embodies this theological aestheticism in institutional form. The Devadasi’s dance was understood as the Goddess’s own dance, performed by a human instrument who had dedicated herself so completely to the divine that the distinction between her own movement and the Goddess’s movement had effectively dissolved. This understanding is not naive anthropomorphism but sophisticated Advaitic theology: in the state of complete dedication, the individual self is transparent to the divine self, and the human body becomes the direct vehicle of divine expression.

The Soundarya Lahari’s aesthetic theology thus provides the philosophical framework within which the 108 Karanas achieve their deepest significance. They are not merely technical specifications for dance movements; they are the vocabulary of the Goddess’s own body-language, the specific configurations through which divine consciousness expresses itself in embodied form. To learn the 108 Karanas with true understanding is to learn to read the body of the Goddess — and reading the body of the Goddess is, in Shankaracharya’s tradition, equivalent to reading the nature of Brahman itself.

150
The Cosmic Choreography

5.4Shiva Tandava Stotram: The Kinetic Philosophy

Alongside the Soundarya Lahari, the Shiva Tandava Stotram — traditionally attributed to Ravana in the Ramayana but deeply embedded in the Shankaracharya tradition through its sustained philosophical content — represents the most direct poetic engagement with the Tandava dance in the entire Sanskrit corpus. Its meter, the Jagati (sixteen syllables per quarter-verse with a powerful, driving rhythm), is uniquely suited to its subject: the poem is almost impossible to recite without the body becoming physically engaged, the breath, tongue, and vocal apparatus falling into rhythmic patterns that approximate the physical experience of the Tandava.

The poem opens with a cascade of compound words describing Shiva’s adornments and movements: the Ganga flowing through his matted hair, the crescent moon gleaming on his forehead, the serpents coiling around his neck, the skulls decorating his body, the ash smeared over his skin. Each of these details is philosophically precise: the Ganga flowing downward through Shiva’s hair encodes the descent of consciousness into the world of experience; the crescent moon on his forehead encodes the quality of pure, cool, undisturbed awareness; the serpents around his neck encode the coiled energy of Kundalini Shakti that is the Goddess in her Karana form; the skulls and ash encode the dissolution of all that is transient and the emergence of what is eternal.

151
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

The poem’s movement description is kinetically extraordinary. Shiva dances with his hair (jata) flying in all directions; his feet strike the ground so powerfully that the gods in the lower worlds are disturbed; his multiple arms move in coordinated patterns that simultaneously embody multiple Karanas; his body blazes with the fire of dissolution while remaining perfectly calm at its centre. This paradox — intense external movement combined with perfect inner stillness — is the kinetic expression of Shankara’s Advaitic insight: the Jivanmukta moves through the world with complete engagement and complete freedom simultaneously, like Shiva whose Tandava shakes the cosmos while his essential nature remains the unmoved Brahman.

The philosophical vocabulary of the Shiva Tandava Stotram is rich with concepts that directly parallel the Natya Shastra’s technical vocabulary. Shiva’s 'Nataraja' quality — his identity as Lord of Dance — is the starting point; but the poem elaborates this identity through increasingly specific descriptions that correspond, for the careful reader, to specific aspects of the Karana system. His arms moving in 'manorama' (mind-enchanting, aesthetically perfect) patterns correspond to the Nritta Hasta dimension of the Karanas; the rhythm of his feet (pada-kriya) corresponds to the Chari dimension; the quality of his gaze (drishti) — at once intense and completely relaxed — corresponds to the Drishti dimension. The Shiva Tandava Stotram, read alongside the Natya Shastra Chapter IV, emerges as a literary performance of the same dance that the technical text codifies.

152
The Cosmic Choreography

5.5The Lalita Sahasranama and the Dance of the Thousand Names

Closely related to the Soundarya Lahari in the Shakta tradition attributed to or associated with Shankaracharya is the Lalita Sahasranama — the thousand-name hymn to the Divine Mother in her form as Lalita Tripura Sundari. This text, which appears in the Brahmanda Purana and is understood in the tradition as emerging from the same devotional current as the Soundarya Lahari, provides important additional material for understanding the relationship between Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition and the performing arts.

The Lalita Sahasranama contains numerous names that directly reference the dance and performance traditions of the Natya Shastra. Among these are: Natini (the Dancer), Nrityapriya (she who is fond of dance), Nrityaparayana (devoted to dance), Nartanasheela (given to dancing), and Nritya-nripya (she who is both the dancer and the king of dance). These names are not isolated epithets but part of a sustained engagement with the performance tradition that runs throughout the text. The Divine Mother is understood as both the dancer and the dance, both the performer and the performance — a conception that directly embodies the Advaitic insight that the duality of subject and object, of consciousness and its expression, is ultimately illusory.

The name Karana-rupa — 'she whose form is Karana' or 'she who is the essence of action' — is particularly significant for our

153
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

study. In this name, the philosophical concept of Karana (cause, action, instrument) and the technical term Karana (the movement unit of the Natya Shastra) are deliberately conflated, creating a polyvalent theological statement: the Divine Mother is both the Karana in the philosophical sense (the fundamental cause of all existence) and the Karanas in the technical sense (the complete vocabulary of sacred movement through which she expresses herself in embodied form). This conflation is not a confusion but a philosophical statement: the cosmic causality of the Divine Mother and her embodied expression in the 108 Karanas are, at the ultimate level, the same thing.

The Lalita Sahasranama’s treatment of the nine creative powers (Nava-Shakti) that the Divine Mother manifests in different aspects of her cosmic activity includes several names that correspond to specific Rasa qualities and therefore to specific groups of Karanas. Shringarini (she who embodies the Shringara aesthetic) corresponds to the flowing, graceful Karanas of the Lalita group. Vira-priya (she who is fond of heroism) corresponds to the expansive, powerful Karanas of the Vira group. Karunasagara (ocean of compassion) corresponds to the Karanas of tender, yielding quality. Mahashanta (greatly peaceful) corresponds to the elevated Karanas of the Shanta group. These correspondences suggest that the tradition understood the complete Karana vocabulary as a map of the Divine Mother’s complete self-expression — a physical realisation of what the Lalita Sahasranama achieves verbally through its thousand names.

154
The Cosmic Choreography

The relationship between the Lalita Sahasranama and the Soundarya Lahari is itself illuminating. The Soundarya Lahari is a more intensely personal, more aesthetically engaged text — a poem of direct devotional encounter between Shankara and the Divine Mother. The Lalita Sahasranama is more systematic and encyclopaedic, cataloguing the complete range of the Goddess’s attributes and manifestations in the same spirit of philosophical completeness that the 108 Karanas bring to the complete range of sacred movement. Together, these two texts constitute a comprehensive theological statement about the nature of the Divine Mother that is simultaneously a comprehensive philosophical statement about the nature of Brahman: she is both the intensely personal beloved of the devotee’s heart and the systematic totality of all existence, both the dancer encountered in a single moment of aesthetic revelation and the complete vocabulary of all possible cosmic movement.

For the practitioner of classical Indian dance, the implications of this theological framework are profound. The dancer who performs the 108 Karanas with understanding of their relationship to the Lalita Sahasranama’s theology is not merely performing physical movements but manifesting the thousand attributes of the Divine Mother in the medium of embodied movement. Each Karana becomes a living realisation of one of the Goddess’s names — not a symbol or a representation of her attribute but a direct instantiation of it, a moment in which the dancer’s body becomes the Goddess’s body and the movement becomes the Goddess’s movement. This understanding transforms the entire enterprise of classical dance from artistic

155
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

performance into theurgic practice: the deliberate invocation of the divine through the medium of the most refined human art.

5.6Commentary Traditions on the Soundarya Lahari

The Soundarya Lahari has attracted an extraordinarily rich commentary tradition that provides important additional material for understanding its relationship to the Natya Shastra and the 108 Karanas. Among the most important commentaries are those by Lakshmidara (c. 14th century), Kaivalyashrama (c. 15th century), Natanananda (c. 16th century), and in the modern period, the extensive commentaries by Chandrashekhara Bharati (the 34th Shankaracharya of Sringeri, 1912-1954) and S.K. Ramachandra Rao. Each of these commentators brings a distinctive perspective that illuminates different dimensions of the text’s relationship to the performing arts.

Lakshmidara’s commentary, the earliest surviving complete commentary on the text, is particularly valuable for its extensive references to the Tantric tradition of Sri Vidya — the esoteric system of mantra, yantra, and meditative practice associated with the worship of the Goddess Lalita. Lakshmidara’s reading consistently emphasises the correspondences between the Soundarya Lahari’s imagery and the specific practices of Sri Vidya, including the mudras (sacred hand gestures) used in ritual worship that correspond directly to the Hasta system of the Natya Shastra. His observation that the Goddess’s various postures and

156
The Cosmic Choreography

gestures as described in the Soundarya Lahari correspond to specific positions in the Sri Chakra yantra provides an important link between the visual geometry of the yantra, the gestural vocabulary of the ritual, and the movement vocabulary of classical dance.

Kaivalyashrama’s commentary takes a different approach, emphasising the philosophical (Advaita Vedanta) dimensions of the text over its Tantric dimensions. His reading of the Soundarya Lahari as a systematic exposition of the non-dual philosophy in devotional poetic form is the most intellectually rigorous of the traditional commentaries and provides the philosophical framework within which the text’s movement imagery can be read as a sustained philosophical argument rather than merely a series of beautiful images. Kaivalyashrama’s analysis of Verse 53 — the Urdhva Tandava verse — as encoding the complete Advaitic analysis of the relationship between consciousness and its manifestations is particularly valuable for our study.

Natanananda’s commentary, composed in the context of the living performance culture of the South Indian temple tradition, is the most directly relevant to the relationship between the Soundarya Lahari and the Natya Shastra. Natanananda was himself a practitioner of classical dance and brings to his commentary an insider’s understanding of the performance tradition that the other commentators, however philosophically sophisticated, lack. His identification of specific verses with specific Karanas — an identification that anticipates and validates the systematic analysis undertaken in Chapter Five of this book — provides the most direct textual evidence for the tradition’s own

157
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

understanding of the relationship between Shankara’s devotional poetry and Bharata’s performance theory.

The modern commentary by Chandrashekhara Bharati — composed by one of the most philosophically accomplished Shankaracharyas of the twentieth century and widely regarded as the most comprehensive and philosophically rigorous of all the commentaries — provides the synthesis of the traditional approaches most accessible to the contemporary reader. Chandrashekhara Bharati’s reading of the Soundarya Lahari as simultaneously a philosophical treatise, a devotional poem, a meditation manual, and a performance text captures exactly the multi-dimensional quality that makes it the ideal text for understanding the synthesis between Advaita Vedanta and the Natya Shastra tradition. His extensive notes on the movement and gesture imagery throughout the text draw implicitly on the Natya Shastra vocabulary, and several passages in his commentary read as direct applications of Natya Shastra technical vocabulary to the interpretation of specific Soundarya Lahari verses.

The commentary tradition on the Soundarya Lahari thus provides not merely exegetical material for understanding individual verses but evidence for the tradition’s own self-understanding of the relationship between Shankara’s philosophy and the performing arts. The commentators did not experience any tension between the philosophical and aesthetic dimensions of the text, because their tradition had always understood these as complementary rather than competing. The philosophical argument and the aesthetic imagery were, for them, different aspects of the same comprehensive vision — the vision of a

158
The Cosmic Choreography

universe in which consciousness and beauty, truth and aesthetic experience, philosophy and art are ultimately one.

5.7The Yantra and the Karana: Visual and Kinetic Philosophy

The relationship between the Soundarya Lahari’s Tantric imagery and the 108 Karanas acquires an additional dimension when one considers the role of the Yantra in the Sri Vidya tradition associated with the text. The Yantra — particularly the Sri Chakra or Sri Yantra that is the central object of Sri Vidya meditation and worship — is a visual diagram that encodes, in geometric form, the same philosophical truths that the Soundarya Lahari expresses in poetic form and that the 108 Karanas express in movement form. Understanding the relationship between these three vehicles of philosophical expression — the Yantra, the poem, and the Karanas — opens a new dimension of the synthesis this book traces.

The Sri Yantra consists of nine interlocking triangles — four pointing upward (representing the masculine Shiva principle) and five pointing downward (representing the feminine Shakti principle) — arranged around a central point (the Bindu) that represents the absolute, undivided consciousness from which all manifestation arises. The intersection of these nine triangles creates 43 smaller triangles arranged in concentric rings, surrounded by two rings of lotus petals (8 and 16 respectively) and finally by the square outer boundary representing the manifest

159
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

world. The entire diagram is a map of the complete structure of cosmic manifestation, from the undivided absolute at the centre to the most elaborate complexity at the periphery.

The correspondence between the Sri Yantra’s geometry and the 108 Karanas' sequence is not a matter of simple one-to-one mapping but of structural homology: both are complete systems that move from a central simplicity through increasing complexity to the full range of possible expression. The Bindu at the centre of the Sri Yantra corresponds to the Samapada Sthana — the perfectly balanced standing position that is the ground from which all Karanas arise and to which they return. The nine triangles of the central arrangement correspond to the nine fundamental Karana groups distinguished by their quality of energy. And the concentric elaboration of the design outward from the centre corresponds to the progressive elaboration of the Karana vocabulary from the most basic movement units to the most complex compositional sequences.

Shankaracharya’s commentary on the Sri Yantra in the Soundarya Lahari — particularly the Ananda Lahari verses that describe the Goddess as inhabiting the various levels of the diagram — reads the Yantra as a map of consciousness’s own structure: the journey from the Bindu at the centre to the outer boundary is the journey from pure, undivided consciousness through the successive levels of its self-concealment in Maya, and the journey back from the boundary to the centre is the journey of liberation. The practitioner who meditates on the Sri Yantra is tracing, in the medium of visual attention, the same journey that the practitioner of the 108 Karanas traces in the medium of

160
The Cosmic Choreography

embodied movement — from the ground of pure consciousness through the full range of its creative self-expression and back to the recognition of that ground.

The practical implication of this Yantra-Karana correspondence for the classical dancer is that the performance of the 108 Karanas can be understood as the three-dimensional, temporal embodiment of the Sri Yantra’s two-dimensional spatial diagram. When the dancer moves through the complete sequence of 108 Karanas in performance, she is tracing the Sri Yantra’s philosophical journey — from the centre of pure equanimity through the full range of creative expression and back to the centre — in the medium of the body moving through time and space. This understanding transforms the performance of the Karanas from a technical exercise into a form of Sri Yantra meditation: an embodied traversal of the complete structure of consciousness that the Yantra encodes in visual form.

The connection between the Sri Yantra and the 108 Karanas is explicitly acknowledged in several South Indian temple traditions, where the ground plan of the performance space is drawn in the form of the Sri Yantra before the Karanas are performed. This practice — which encodes the philosophical correspondence between the spatial Yantra and the temporal Karana sequence in the physical arrangement of the performance space — represents the most complete possible integration of the Soundarya Lahari’s Tantric philosophy, the Natya Shastra’s performance theory, and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta: a synthesis in which the geometric, the poetic, and the

161
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

kinetic expressions of the non-dual truth are simultaneously present and mutually reinforcing.

5.14Beauty as Liberation: Aesthetic and Soteriological Convergence

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not

162
The Cosmic Choreography

separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by

163
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human

164
The Cosmic Choreography

consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

5.15Regional Variations and Local Adaptations

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical

165
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the

166
The Cosmic Choreography

two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple

167
Soundarya Lahari and the Dance of Consciousness

sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

5.8Commentaries on the Soundarya Lahari: A Scholarly Overview

The commentary tradition on the Soundarya Lahari has flourished continuously from at least the twelfth century to the present day, producing an extraordinarily rich body of interpretive literature that illuminates different dimensions of the text from different philosophical, devotional, and practical perspectives. Cataloguing this tradition fully would require a separate study; what follows is a selective survey of the most significant commentaries and their relevance to the relationship between the text and the Natya Shastra.

The earliest significant commentary, by Lakshmidara, approaches the text primarily through the lens of the Sri Vidya tradition — the esoteric system of mantra and yantra associated with the worship of Lalita Tripura Sundari. Lakshmidara’s commentary is particularly rich on the Tantric dimensions of the text’s movement imagery, identifying specific gestures and postures described in the verses with specific positions in the Sri Chakra meditation and with specific mudras used in Sri Vidya

168
The Cosmic Choreography

ritual worship. His analysis provides important evidence for the tradition’s understanding that the Soundarya Lahari’s movement imagery is not merely poetic decoration but encodes specific practical instructions for embodied meditation.

The commentary by Kaivalyashrama, probably composed in the fifteenth century, takes a more purely Advaitic philosophical approach, reading every image in the text as an expression of the non-dual truth and every aesthetic detail as a vehicle of philosophical insight. Kaivalyashrama’s reading is intellectually the most rigorous of the traditional commentaries and the most directly relevant to the philosophical synthesis this book traces. His analysis of the relationship between specific verses and specific Upanishadic teachings provides the most systematic traditional account of the Soundarya Lahari’s position within the broader Advaita Vedanta framework.

The modern commentary by S.K. Ramachandra Rao, published in the late twentieth century as part of his extensive series on Agama and Tantra, represents the most comprehensive modern scholarly treatment of the text and its commentary tradition. Ramachandra Rao’s approach is simultaneously philologically rigorous and practically informed by his own engagement with the Sri Vidya tradition, and his analysis of the text’s movement imagery consistently makes connections to the Natya Shastra vocabulary in ways that directly support the argument of Chapter Five.

169
CHAPTER VI

Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

“All movement is the movement of consciousness; all stillness is its rest. In knowing this, the dancer is free.”

— Abhinavagupta, Tantraloka (paraphrase)

6.1The Body in Advaita Philosophy

One of the most persistent misunderstandings about Advaita Vedanta is that it regards the physical body as an obstacle to liberation or as inherently inferior to the spiritual dimension of existence. This reading arises from a superficial encounter with Shankara’s texts — particularly the Vivekachudamani, whose extended analysis of the body in terms of its limitations and its identity with the non-Self can mislead the reader into thinking that the body is being condemned rather than analysed. A more careful reading reveals that Shankara’s treatment of the body is rigorously phenomenological rather than puritanically ascetic: he is concerned to distinguish clearly between what the body is (an instrument, a vehicle, a sheaths of

170
The Cosmic Choreography

consciousness) and what it is mistakenly identified with (the Self, the Atman, the ultimately real).

The Vivekachudamani’s famous analysis of the Pancha Kosha — the five sheaths through which consciousness is apparently enclosed — is the most systematic treatment of embodiment in Shankara’s corpus. The five sheaths — Annamaya (food/physical), Pranamaya (vital breath), Manomaya (mental), Vijnanamaya (intellectual), and Anandamaya (bliss) — represent progressively subtler dimensions of the body-mind complex, moving from the gross physical body visible to ordinary perception through the vital and psychological bodies to the subtlest body of pure bliss. Shankara’s analysis proceeds by showing that the Self (Atman) cannot be identified with any of these sheaths, since the Atman is the witness of each — the pure consciousness that observes each sheath from a position of complete independence. The Atman is not in the body as a bird is in a cage (constrained by it, identical with its limitations) but as the sky is in a pot (apparently contained within a form but in reality unlimited by it, identical in nature with the sky outside the pot).

This analysis does not diminish the body’s importance; on the contrary, it establishes the body as the most immediate, accessible, and revealing domain of philosophical investigation. By carefully attending to the body — to its sensations, its movements, its energies, its various sheaths — the practitioner of Advaita Vedanta learns, by direct experience, the difference between the observed and the observer, between the known and the knower, between the experienced and the experiencer. The body becomes, in this

171
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

context, the practitioner’s most reliable philosophical laboratory: the place where the abstract distinction between Atman and non-Atman becomes most immediately and undeniably concrete.

The classical Indian dance tradition, with its extraordinary emphasis on precise bodily awareness and its progressive development of the practitioner’s kinesthetic intelligence, can be understood, from this perspective, as a form of embodied Advaitic inquiry. The dancer who learns to maintain awareness of the Sakshi (witness consciousness) during the execution of technically demanding Karanas — who remains centred in the observing awareness even while the body is fully engaged in complex movement — is performing, in the medium of dance, the same inquiry that the Advaita Vedanta student performs through philosophical analysis. The practitioner and the philosopher are conducting the same investigation through different methodologies, and both methodologies can lead to the same destination.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical treatment of the body thus provides not an obstacle but a sophisticated theoretical framework for understanding the spiritual dimensions of classical Indian dance. The body is not a prison to be escaped but a vehicle to be fully inhabited and understood — a vehicle whose complete inhabitation, combined with the discriminative wisdom that recognises the Self as distinct from the vehicle, constitutes the very practice of liberation. The dancer who has truly understood the Advaitic teaching does not dance less; she dances more fully, more freely, more beautifully, because she is no longer burdened by the unconscious identification with

172
The Cosmic Choreography

the body that makes ordinary movement heavy, effortful, and self-conscious.

6.2Witness Consciousness and the Art of Non-Attachment

Perhaps the most productive concept in Shankaracharya’s philosophy for understanding the relationship between Advaita Vedanta and classical performance is the Sakshi — the pure witness consciousness that observes all phenomena without being affected by them. The Sakshi is not a passive, blank awareness but a fully present, luminously intelligent consciousness that is simultaneously completely engaged with what it witnesses and completely free from any identification with it. Shankara’s exposition of the Sakshi in various texts makes clear that this is not a dissociated or emotionally absent state — the Sakshi is aware of all emotions, all movements, all experiences with perfect clarity — but a mode of awareness in which experience unfolds without the distorting filter of ego-identification.

Applied to the context of performance, the concept of the Sakshi yields a profound and practically useful understanding of the ideal state of the dancer or actor. The perfect performer must be simultaneously two things that appear to be in contradiction: completely present and engaged in the movement, emotion, and expression of the performance, and simultaneously completely detached from it — a witness to her own performance as it unfolds in real time. This dual awareness — full engagement and

173
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

pure witnessing simultaneously — is precisely the state that experienced classical dancers and actors describe when speaking of performance at its highest. The great performer, from inside the experience of peak performance, reports something like: 'I was fully there, more intensely alive than at any other moment, yet I was watching myself from a distance, with perfect clarity.'

This dual awareness is not a split consciousness or a divided attention; it is consciousness operating at its full capacity. Ordinary consciousness, by contrast, is always partial: either lost in the object of attention (unable to maintain the perspective of the witness) or maintaining the perspective of the witness (but at the cost of full engagement with the object). The state of the Sakshi is the integration of these two apparently opposing modes of consciousness into a single, unified awareness that is simultaneously fully present and fully free. Shankara’s claim is that this integrated awareness is not an extraordinary achievement reserved for rare individuals in exceptional circumstances but the natural state of consciousness — the state it inhabits when it is not distorted by the tension of ego-identification.

The classical Indian dance training, with its extraordinary demands on simultaneous attention to multiple dimensions of experience, may be understood as a systematic cultivation of this integrated awareness. The dancer must simultaneously attend to the precise technical execution of the Karana (requiring precise proprioceptive awareness of all body parts), the rhythmic relationship to the accompanying music (requiring auditory awareness and temporal intelligence), the quality of the emotional or philosophical content she is expressing (requiring inner

174
The Cosmic Choreography

awareness of feeling and meaning), and the relationship to the audience and performance space (requiring spatial and relational awareness). The capacity to maintain all these dimensions of awareness simultaneously, without any one of them eclipsing the others, is precisely the Sakshi awareness that Shankara describes — and the training process through which this capacity is developed is, in the language of Advaita Vedanta, a training in the recognition of one’s own nature as the witness consciousness.

The concept of the Sakshi thus provides the philosophical basis for understanding why the classical dance traditions of India have consistently understood their most demanding technical training as simultaneously a spiritual practice. The technical demands of the Karana system are not arbitrary — they are precisely calibrated to require the development of a quality of awareness that, once developed in the context of performance, has implications far beyond the performance context. The dancer who has genuinely developed Sakshi awareness in her practice brings that awareness into every other dimension of her life — becoming, in the language of Shankara’s tradition, a Jivanmukta, one liberated in life.

6.3Movement as Philosophical Method

A striking and rarely remarked feature of Shankaracharya’s philosophical method is his consistent use of movement and kinetic imagery as a medium for philosophical exposition. This is not merely a matter of metaphor: Shankara’s thinking about

175
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

consciousness is fundamentally kinetic, concerned with the ways in which awareness moves, how it becomes distorted in its movement, and how it can be returned to its natural, undistorted flow. The philosophical concepts he employs — Vritti (mental modification, literally 'whirl' or 'movement'), Spandana (vibration), Avrita (covered or veiled, from the root vri, to turn or wind), Vikshepa (projection, literally 'throwing outward') — are all kinetic in their basic meaning.

The most famous kinetic analogy in Shankara’s corpus is his use of the spinning firebrand to explain the nature of cosmic illusion. Just as a single point of fire, moving rapidly in a circle, appears to create a continuous ring of light where in fact there is only a single moving point, so consciousness, in the ceaseless movement of its cognitive activity, appears to create a continuous, extended world where in fact there is only the single, undivided light of awareness moving through its own modifications. This analogy from kinematics is not merely illustrative but phenomenological: it describes accurately the mechanism by which the one appears as many, the undivided appears as divided, the formless takes on apparent form.

This kinetic understanding of cosmic illusion has a direct implication for the status of dance as a philosophical practice. If the world is, at the ultimate level, a dance of consciousness — the single light of awareness moving through its own modifications at cosmic speed, creating the appearance of a differentiated world — then the human dancer who consciously enacts a complete and coherent vocabulary of movement (the 108 Karanas) is not merely imitating the cosmic dance but participating in its

176
The Cosmic Choreography

mechanism. By moving through all 108 Karanas with full awareness, the dancer traces the complete arc of consciousness’s movement from its most grounded, embodied, earth-bound configurations to its most elevated, transcendent, sky-bound configurations — enacting, in the medium of a human body over the course of a performance, the complete cosmic cycle that consciousness enacts in the medium of the universe over the course of a cosmic age.

This understanding also illuminates why the most advanced classical dance practice is always associated with stillness as well as movement. The greatest Karanas — the Lina, the Shanta-Tandava — are not the most physically dynamic but the most inwardly profound: they embody the quality of consciousness returning to its own source, of movement dissolving back into the stillness from which it arose. The complete Karana performance, from the first active movement to the final dissolution into stillness, is thus a meditation on the complete cycle of creation and liberation — precisely the cosmic narrative that Shankaracharya traces from the opening verse of the Soundarya Lahari (where the union of Shiva and Shakti generates the entire universe) to the recognition that liberates (where the apparent universe dissolves back into the pure consciousness that was always its ground).

Shankaracharya’s philosophical method is thus, in a profound sense, a kinetic method: it works by guiding the student’s attention through the movement of their own consciousness, showing them how ordinary awareness moves in patterns of distortion and contraction, and then demonstrating how these patterns can be reversed — how the contracted,

177
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

distorted, ego-bound movement of ordinary consciousness can be opened up into the free, spacious, undistorted movement of the Sakshi. The classical dance training, which works by guiding the student’s attention through the movement of their own body, demonstrating how ordinary movement is contracted and effortful and then showing how it can be opened up into the free, spacious, effortless quality of the fully trained dancer, is doing exactly the same thing in a different medium.

6.5Prana, Pranamaya Kosha, and the Breath in Dance

One of the most important but least discussed dimensions of the relationship between Advaita Vedanta and classical Indian dance is the role of breath (Prana) in both traditions. In Shankaracharya’s analysis of the Pancha Kosha, the Pranamaya Kosha — the vital breath body — occupies a pivotal position between the gross physical body (Annamaya Kosha) and the mental body (Manomaya Kosha). Prana is not merely physical breath in the biological sense but the vital energy that animates the physical body and serves as the medium through which consciousness expresses itself in embodied form. The analysis of Prana in Advaita Vedanta is not a rejection of the body’s vital dimension but a progressive refinement of understanding: by recognising that the vital breath is not the Self (Atman), the practitioner liberates their self-understanding from identification with a relatively gross level of existence and moves toward the

178
The Cosmic Choreography

recognition of the subtler levels in which the Self is more transparently present.

The Natya Shastra’s treatment of breath in the context of performance is less systematic than Shankara’s philosophical analysis but equally deep. The text’s repeated insistence that the quality of a Karana execution depends on the quality of the breath (Shvasa) with which it is performed — that the movement must arise from and be sustained by a quality of breathing that is simultaneously deep, controlled, and natural — reflects an understanding of breath as the medium through which consciousness expresses itself in movement. The great dancer does not merely move the arms and legs through space; she moves with the whole body, including the breath, and the quality of that breath-movement is what distinguishes the technically excellent performance from the genuinely inspired one.

The connection between breath control and the quality of the Karana execution is most clearly articulated in the tradition of Pranayama as applied to performance training. Several classical dance training lineages, particularly in Kerala and Tamil Nadu, include specific breath practices in their curriculum that are explicitly derived from the Yoga tradition. These practices are understood not as mere physical conditioning but as a systematic development of the practitioner’s capacity to allow consciousness to flow freely through the body without the obstructions of tension, habit, and self-consciousness that characterise ordinary, unconscious breathing. The dancer who has genuinely developed this capacity does not merely perform the Karanas; she breathes them — allowing the movement to arise from the breath with the

179
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

same naturalness and inevitability with which the breath itself arises from the deep, still reservoir of Prana that the yogic tradition identifies as the foundation of all vital activity.

Shankaracharya’s own engagement with Pranayama in the philosophical context is visible in his Yoga Taravali — a short but philosophically dense text on the practice of Yoga that is attributed to him in the tradition. In this text, Shankara describes the highest practice of Pranayama not as control of the physical breath but as the recognition that the very movement of breath is a manifestation of the supreme Shakti — the dynamic power of consciousness that is, at the ultimate level, identical with the dancer-consciousness of the Divine Mother described in the Soundarya Lahari. This recognition transforms Pranayama from a physical technique into a philosophical practice: each breath becomes a recognition of the Goddess, a participation in her cosmic dance of creation and dissolution.

The connection between breath and the Ananda Tandava is made most explicitly in the Chidambaram tradition’s understanding of the inner significance of the temple’s sacred geography. The innermost sanctuary of the Chidambaram temple — the Chit-Sabha or 'hall of consciousness' — is understood as the site not merely of Shiva’s outer cosmic dance but of the inner dance of consciousness that every breathing human being participates in with every breath. The inhalation is Srishti (creation), the retention is Sthiti (preservation), the exhalation is Samhara (dissolution), the pause at the end of exhalation is Tirobhava (concealment), and the spontaneous resumption of the next breath is Anugraha (grace). Every breath,

180
The Cosmic Choreography

understood rightly, is the Ananda Tandava — the five-function cosmic dance of Shiva — performed in miniature in the body of every living being. The dancer who performs the 108 Karanas with full awareness of this breath-cosmology is not merely executing a performance; she is making the invisible inner dance visible in outward bodily form.

6.6Nada Yoga and the Inner Dimension of Performance

The tradition of Nada Yoga — the path of liberation through deep attention to sound, both external and internal — provides another important dimension of the relationship between Advaita Vedanta and the performing arts. Shankaracharya’s engagement with the Nada tradition is visible throughout his work, particularly in his treatment of the relationship between the Vedic Shabda (the eternal, self-luminous sound of the Vedas) and the liberation it generates in the attentive listener. The Upanishadic formula 'Shravana, Manana, Nididhyasana' — 'hearing, reflection, deep meditation' — describes a process that begins with auditory experience and progresses through philosophical reflection to the direct recognition of the non-dual truth. Sound, for Shankara, is not merely a vehicle of propositional meaning but a direct medium of awakening.

The classical Indian performance tradition’s understanding of the relationship between sound and movement — the insistence that every movement arises from and is sustained by

181
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

specific qualities of sound — gives practical expression to the Nada Yoga tradition’s insight that consciousness expresses itself primarily through the medium of vibration. In the Natya Shastra’s understanding, the Tala (rhythmic cycle) is not merely a background for the Karanas but their living ground: each Karana arises from and returns to the Tala’s rhythmic pulsation in the same way that each movement of thought arises from and returns to the silence of pure awareness. The great dancer’s movement is not superimposed on the Tala but emerges from it, as naturally and inevitably as waves emerge from the ocean.

The most profound expression of this understanding in the classical Indian performance tradition is the concept of Manodharma — literally 'the dharma of the mind', the quality of spontaneous, inspired improvisation that arises when the performer is so deeply attuned to the musical environment that the movement arises without deliberate intention. Manodharma is not the absence of skill — only the most highly skilled performer is capable of genuine Manodharma — but the transcendence of deliberate skill in a quality of spontaneous rightness that the tradition identifies as the highest level of artistic achievement. Shankara’s philosophical vocabulary for this quality is Sahaja — the 'natural' or 'spontaneous' quality of consciousness that has recognised its own nature and therefore moves through the world without the friction of deliberate self-consciousness.

The relationship between Sahaja in Shankara’s philosophical vocabulary and Manodharma in the classical performance vocabulary is direct and precise. Both refer to a quality of

182
The Cosmic Choreography

spontaneous, effortless rightness that arises not from the absence of knowledge and skill but from their complete internalisation and transcendence. The sage who has fully recognised the non-dual truth no longer needs to deliberately apply philosophical analysis because the truth has become her natural way of seeing; the dancer who has fully internalised the Karana vocabulary no longer needs to deliberately execute movements because the rightness of movement has become her natural way of being in the body. In both cases, the quality of Sahaja represents the fruition of sustained, disciplined practice in the emergence of a quality of awareness and action that transcends the practice itself.

The Nada Yoga dimension of the relationship between Shankaracharya and the Natya Shastra is perhaps most accessible in the musical dimension of classical Indian performance — the relationship between the dancer’s movement and the accompanying vocalist and musicians. The classical Indian performance tradition’s insistence that the dancer must be as deeply trained in music as in movement reflects the understanding that the highest level of performance occurs not when the dancer is moving in accordance with the music but when the dancer, the vocalist, and the musicians are all spontaneous expressions of a single musical consciousness — when the 'performance' is not something any of them is 'doing' but something that is happening through all of them simultaneously, arising from the same source that the Nada tradition identifies as the primordial ground of all vibration: Brahman itself.

183
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

6.13Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Six

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

184
The Cosmic Choreography

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form.
