This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana,

185
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The

186
The Cosmic Choreography

scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

6.15Consciousness and the Moving Body: Further Dimensions

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the

187
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

188
The Cosmic Choreography

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

189
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

6.16Commentarial Interpretations Across Centuries

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary,

190
The Cosmic Choreography

and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the

191
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive

192
The Cosmic Choreography

analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

6.7The Pancha Kosha and the Five Levels of Dance Mastery

Shankaracharya’s Pancha Kosha analysis — the description of the five sheaths through which consciousness is apparently enclosed — provides a precise framework for understanding the five levels of mastery that the classical dance tradition recognises in the development of a performer. Just as the Koshas move from the grossest (the food body) through progressively subtler levels to the subtlest (the bliss body), the levels of dance mastery move from the grossest (physical control of the movement forms) through

193
Advaita Vedanta and the Aesthetics of Movement

progressively subtler levels to the subtlest (the quality of pure awareness that animates the most refined performance).

The first level of mastery corresponds to the Annamaya Kosha: the physical body’s capacity to produce the correct external forms. At this level, the dancer has learned the Adavus and Karanas sufficiently to execute them recognisably, but the execution is laborious, effortful, and lacks internal quality. The body knows the shapes but has not yet internalised them. The second level of mastery corresponds to the Pranamaya Kosha: the vital body’s capacity to animate the physical forms with genuine energy. At this level, the dancer executes the forms with genuine physical energy and rhythmic vitality, but the emotional and intentional dimensions are still underdeveloped. The third level corresponds to the Manomaya Kosha: the mental body’s capacity to fill the forms with genuine emotional and aesthetic content. At this level, the dancer brings genuine Bhava (emotional state) to the execution, and the performance begins to communicate meaning beyond mere form.

The fourth level of mastery corresponds to the Vijnanamaya Kosha: the intellectual body’s capacity to understand and consciously deploy the tradition’s complete philosophical vocabulary. At this level, the dancer not only feels the Bhava but understands its philosophical significance, not only executes the Karana but comprehends its cosmological meaning. And the fifth and highest level corresponds to the Anandamaya Kosha: the bliss body’s capacity to inhabit the performance from a place of pure, undistorted awareness. At this level, the distinction between the performer and the performance dissolves in a quality of pure

194
The Cosmic Choreography

expression that the tradition calls Sattvika: not merely skilled, not merely emotionally authentic, but transparently luminous with the quality of awareness itself.

The parallel between this five-level analysis of dance mastery and the Pancha Kosha framework of Advaita Vedanta is not a casual analogy but a structural identity: both are describing the same progressive refinement of awareness through successively subtler levels of the body-mind complex, moving from identification with the grossest level toward recognition of the pure consciousness that underlies all levels. The classical dance tradition’s implicit understanding of performance as a path through the Koshas toward the recognition of the Atman that underlies them is the most direct possible embodiment of the Advaita Vedanta insight — an insight that Shankaracharya articulated in philosophical language and that the dance tradition enacts in the language of the body in motion.

195
CHAPTER VII

Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

“Rasa is the universal aesthetic experience that arises when the individual aesthetic experience dissolves into the impersonal. It is Brahmananda in an indirect form.”

— Abhinavagupta, Abhinavabharati

7.1The Rasa Sutra and Its Interpretations

Bharata Muni’s Rasa Sutra — 'Vibhava Anubhava Vyabhichari Samyogad Rasa Nishpattih' — is the most commented-upon sentence in the Indian aesthetic tradition, having generated over two millennia of philosophical analysis, artistic application, and spiritual interpretation. Its apparent simplicity is deceptive: each of the four major terms in the sutra — Vibhava, Anubhava, Vyabhichari Bhava, and the crucial Nishpattih — has been the subject of extensive disagreement among commentators, and the overall philosophical meaning of the sutra has been read in radically different ways by different schools of interpretation.

196
The Cosmic Choreography

The most philosophically sophisticated and most relevant for our study is the interpretation offered by Abhinavagupta in his Abhinavabharati — the tenth-century Kashmiri philosopher’s commentary on the Natya Shastra that simultaneously illuminates Bharata’s text and transforms it into a vehicle for his own non-dual philosophical vision. Abhinavagupta’s key innovation is his interpretation of the term Nishpattih: rather than reading it as merely 'production' or 'arising' (as earlier commentators had done), he reads it as Anubhavana or Sakshat-Karana — direct experience, immediate recognition, the same terms used in the Advaita Vedanta tradition to describe the direct experience of Brahman.

For Abhinavagupta, Rasa is not merely a psychological effect produced in the spectator by the performance; it is a form of genuine aesthetic cognition — an experience in which the spectator’s ordinary, ego-bound consciousness is temporarily dissolved and replaced by a mode of awareness that he compares directly to the experience of Brahman: universal, impersonal, blissful, undistorted by desire or aversion. The spectator experiencing Rasa is, for the duration of that experience, in the state that the Advaita Vedanta student seeks through philosophical inquiry: the state of the Sakshi, the pure witness, the universal consciousness that observes without identification.

This interpretive move by Abhinavagupta — his identification of the highest aesthetic experience with the experience of Brahman — is the most important single contribution to the philosophical synthesis that this book traces. It establishes, with the authority of the greatest commentator in

197
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

the Natya Shastra tradition, that the Natya Shastra’s aesthetic theory and the Advaita Vedanta’s soteriology are not merely analogous but are descriptions of the same fundamental experience viewed from different angles: the aesthetic angle (where it appears as Rasa) and the philosophical angle (where it appears as Brahman-recognition).

The practical implications of this identification are enormous. If the experience of Rasa in the theatre is a genuine, if temporary and indirect, form of Brahman-recognition, then the great performer who reliably generates authentic Rasa in her audience is performing an act of spiritual significance equivalent to that of the great philosopher who guides his students to genuine Brahman-recognition through philosophical inquiry. Both are doing the same thing through different media: dissolving the spectator’s or student’s ego-bound awareness into the universal, impersonal, luminous awareness that is the true nature of every human being.

7.2The Nine Rasas and Their Philosophical Dimensions

Bharata enumerates eight primary Rasas — Shringara (erotic/romantic), Hasya (comic), Karuna (pathetic/sorrowful), Raudra (furious), Vira (heroic), Bhayanaka (terrifying), Bibhatsa (disgusting), and Adbhuta (wondrous) — each with its corresponding Sthayi Bhava (permanent emotional state), its Vibhavas (determinants), its Anubhavas (physical consequents),

198
The Cosmic Choreography

and its associated Vyabhichari Bhavas (transitory states). Abhinavagupta adds a ninth Rasa — Shanta (tranquil/peaceful) — arguing that Bharata’s eight Rasas are variations and combinations of a more fundamental aesthetic ground-state whose quality is peace, equanimity, and the dissolution of all emotional tension into pure awareness.

The philosophical significance of the eight Rasas for understanding the 108 Karanas lies in the correspondence between the Rasa system’s taxonomy of emotional-aesthetic experience and the Karana system’s taxonomy of movement. Just as the eight Rasas (plus Shanta) constitute a complete map of the aesthetic-emotional range of human experience, the 108 Karanas constitute a complete map of the movement-range of the human body-consciousness. And just as the Rasas are not merely categories of ordinary emotion but purified, universalised, impersonalised aesthetic versions of those emotions, the Karanas are not merely ordinary movements but purified, formalised, cosmologised versions of ordinary bodily gestures. The Karana is to ordinary movement what the Rasa is to ordinary emotion: the same fundamental human material, but elevated, purified, and made transparent to its divine ground.

The Shringara Rasa — the aesthetic of love, beauty, and erotic delight — is the queen of the Rasas in Indian aesthetic tradition, associated with the colour green, the deity Vishnu, and the season of spring. It is said to permeate all other Rasas and to be the ground from which all other aesthetic experiences arise and to which they return. The Karanas associated with Shringara quality are the most graceful, flowing, intimate, and beautiful:

199
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

movements of soft extension, gentle turning, delicate articulation of the fingers, soft and receptive gaze. These are the Karanas most closely associated with the Soundarya Lahari’s descriptions of the Divine Mother’s movement — the aesthetic of divine beauty embodied in physical form.

The Vira Rasa — the aesthetic of heroism, courage, and noble action — is associated with the colour golden-yellow and the deity Indra. It corresponds to the most expansive, powerful, dynamic Karanas: the warrior stances, the leaping movements, the configurations of strong extension and decisive gesture. These are the Karanas most closely associated with the Vivekachudamani’s descriptions of the spiritual warrior (Vira) who conquers the demons of Avidya, Kama, and Krodha through the weapons of discrimination and dispassion. The Shiva Tandava Stotram’s description of Shiva’s dance draws heavily on Vira Rasa qualities — the fierce energy, the unstoppable momentum, the cosmic power of the divine dance.

The Shanta Rasa — the aesthetic of peace, equanimity, and the dissolution of all emotional tension into pure awareness — occupies the most important position in the context of this study. Abhinavagupta’s argument for Shanta as the ninth and supreme Rasa is explicitly philosophical: the aesthetic experience of Shanta corresponds to the philosophical experience of Brahman — pure, self-luminous awareness, without agitation, without desire, without fear. The person experiencing Shanta Rasa in the theatre or in the dance performance is experiencing, in an indirect and transient form, what the Advaitic sage experiences permanently: the bliss of pure being. The Karanas associated with Shanta

200
The Cosmic Choreography

quality — the Lina, the Shanta-Tandava, the most elevated of the Urdhva Karanas — are therefore the Karanas that most directly embody Shankaracharya’s philosophical ideal.

7.3Ananda — The Ultimate Ground of Aesthetic Experience

Shankaracharya’s philosophy reserves a special and foundational place for Ananda — bliss — as the most fundamental quality of Brahman. Brahman is Sat-Chit-Ananda: Being, Consciousness, Bliss. Of these three fundamental qualifications, Ananda is in some ways the most accessible to direct human experience, since even ordinary happiness is understood as a dim reflection of the infinite bliss that is Brahman’s inherent nature. The Taittiriya Upanishad, whose Anandavalli section Shankara comments on with particular depth, traces a hierarchy of blisses from the ordinary pleasures of the human to the progressively more intense and pure blisses of the celestial beings, finally arriving at the infinite bliss of Brahman that infinitely exceeds all finite pleasures.

This Ananda dimension of Brahman provides the ultimate philosophical context for understanding both the Natya Shastra’s performance theory and the 108 Karanas. The Ananda Tandava — the Dance of Bliss that Shiva performs at Chidambaram, whose vocabulary is the 108 Karanas — is not merely a beautiful performance or even a profound spiritual practice; it is the self-expression of Ananda itself, the playful, joyful, spontaneous self-revelation of pure Being through the medium of movement. The

201
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

cosmic dance is Brahman’s own bliss made visible, audible, and kinetically tangible.

Abhinavagupta’s identification of Rasa-experience with Brahman-recognition gains its deepest meaning in this Ananda context. The Rasa experience is defined by its quality of pure pleasure — a pleasure that is different in kind, not merely in degree, from ordinary sensory pleasure. Ordinary pleasure is always tinged with anxiety (will it last? will it return?), always coloured by the particular preferences and aversions of the individual ego. Rasa pleasure is none of these things: it is pure, disinterested, universal, untinged by personal desire, without beginning and without end within the experience itself. This quality is exactly the quality of Ananda as Shankaracharya describes it: pure, universal, self-sustaining bliss that is the very nature of consciousness and therefore the deepest nature of every experiencing being.

The practical teaching that emerges from this analysis is of great importance for both the practitioner of classical dance and the student of Advaita Vedanta. For the dancer: the goal of performance is not to produce emotions in the audience but to generate the conditions for Rasa experience — the conditions under which the audience member’s ordinary ego-consciousness dissolves into the universal aesthetic awareness that is, philosophically, a direct taste of Brahman. This requires not merely technical mastery but a quality of presence, of inner luminosity, of complete absorption in the performance, that the Indian tradition calls Sattvika Abhinaya — the highest level of expressive quality, whose basis is not technique but awareness. For

202
The Cosmic Choreography

the student of Vedanta: the aesthetic experience of Rasa — particularly Shanta Rasa — is not a distraction from philosophical inquiry but a genuine, if transient and indirect, form of Brahman-recognition that can serve as a powerful catalyst for the deeper inquiry that leads to permanent recognition.

The connection between Ananda and the 108 Karanas is further illuminated by the cosmological significance of the number 108, as discussed in Chapter One. The 108 Karanas represent the complete range of the cosmic dance — the full vocabulary of Brahman’s Ananda-expression in the medium of movement. A performer who has genuinely mastered all 108 Karanas has, in the language of the Karana tradition, traversed the complete range of Brahman’s self-expression in embodied form. This complete traversal is not merely a technical achievement but a philosophical one: the performer has, through the medium of the body’s movement, moved through the complete range of Brahman’s creative self-expression and arrived at the still point from which all movement arises and to which all movement returns — the Ananda that is Brahman’s innermost nature and the dancer’s truest self.

203
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

7.5The Problem of Bibhatsa and Raudra: Dark Rasas and Non-Dual Philosophy

A challenging dimension of the relationship between Rasa theory and Advaita Vedanta is raised by the 'dark' Rasas — particularly Bibhatsa (disgust/repulsion) and Raudra (fury/wrath) — whose aesthetic qualities seem at first sight to be in tension with the non-dual philosophy’s insistence on the ultimate identity of all phenomena with Brahman. If Brahman is pure consciousness, if all phenomena are ultimately expressions of that pure consciousness, and if the aesthetic experience of Rasa is, as Abhinavagupta argues, a direct participation in Brahman’s blissful self-awareness, then how do we account for the 'negative' Rasas — the aesthetic experiences of disgust, terror, and rage that seem to involve precisely the opposite of the blissful equanimity that the non-dual tradition identifies as the mark of liberation?

Abhinavagupta’s answer to this question is philosophically subtle and draws directly on the Advaitic framework. He argues that the 'negative' Rasas — Bibhatsa, Raudra, Bhayanaka, and Karuna — are not really negative in the ultimate sense. They are negative only from the perspective of the ego-bound consciousness that is invested in pleasant and unpleasant, desirable and undesirable, as real categories of experience. From the perspective of the Sahridaya (the ideal spectator of refined aesthetic sensitivity), even these 'negative' Rasas are experienced as forms of Ananda — forms of aesthetic delight that arise precisely because the spectator is not personally invested in the emotional

204
The Cosmic Choreography

states they are witnessing but can appreciate them with the same quality of pure, disinterested awareness with which they appreciate Shringara or Shanta.

This argument has a direct practical implication for the 108 Karanas. Among the 108 Karanas are movements that embody qualities corresponding to the 'dark' Rasas: the fierce, powerful movements associated with Raudra, the sharp, penetrating movements that evoke Bhayanaka, the contracted, heavy movements that suggest Bibhatsa. A complete performance of the 108 Karanas must include these movements with the same quality of full expression that it brings to the graceful Shringara movements or the elevated Shanta movements. The dancer who omits or softens the 'dark' Karanas in favour of more conventionally beautiful movements is not making the performance more beautiful but less complete — less true to the full range of consciousness that the Karana vocabulary is designed to express.

The Nataraja iconography provides the most philosophically authoritative statement on this question. Shiva’s dance at Chidambaram includes not only the graceful gestures of Sthiti (preservation) and the elevated posture of transcendence but also the Damaru drum of Srishti (with all the creative violence that emergence from formlessness implies) and the fire of Samhara (with all the dissolution and destruction that this implies). The complete Nataraja embodies both the beautiful and the terrible aspects of the cosmic process, and the tradition is explicit that this completeness is not a concession to darkness but an expression of the non-dual truth: from the perspective of pure consciousness,

205
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

the creation and the destruction, the beautiful and the terrible, are equally expressions of the single divine energy that pervades all things.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical response to the problem of evil — the apparent existence of suffering, injustice, and ugliness in a world that Advaita Vedanta claims is ultimately nothing but blissful consciousness — runs along similar lines. The apparent negativity of suffering, ugliness, and evil is a function of the perspective of Maya-bound consciousness, which perceives some experiences as pleasurable and others as painful, some phenomena as beautiful and others as ugly. From the perspective of the liberated consciousness that has recognised its identity with Brahman, all phenomena are equally expressions of the single, self-luminous awareness that is the ground of all existence — which is not to say that suffering is not real at the conventional level but that it is not ultimately real, and that the recognition of its non-ultimate reality is the beginning of liberation from its apparent grip.

The practical implication of this philosophical position for the performer of the 108 Karanas is the same as its implication for the Advaita Vedanta student: the path to freedom lies not through avoidance of the 'dark' experiences but through the full, conscious, aware engagement with the entire range of experience — moving through it with the quality of the Sakshi, the pure witness, who is fully present to every experience without being bound by any of it. The dancer who can perform the Raudra Karanas with the same quality of pure, disinterested awareness that she brings to the Shringara Karanas is demonstrating, in the

206
The Cosmic Choreography

medium of embodied movement, the same quality of universal equanimity that Shankaracharya identifies as the mark of the Jivanmukta — the person liberated in life.

7.6Contemporary Rasa Theory and Cross-Cultural Aesthetics

The contemporary relevance of Rasa theory extends far beyond the domain of Indian classical arts. Over the past century, scholars of aesthetics, performance theory, and cross-cultural philosophy have increasingly recognised in Rasa theory a sophisticated alternative to the dominant Western aesthetics, one that addresses fundamental questions about the nature of aesthetic experience that Western philosophy has struggled to answer satisfactorily. The engagement between Rasa theory and Western aesthetics — from Ananda Coomaraswamy’s pioneering studies in the early twentieth century through contemporary scholars including Dolf Zillmann, Arthur Berger, and Srinivasa Ayya Srinivasan — has been one of the most productive interdisciplinary dialogues in contemporary humanities scholarship.

The most productive point of engagement between Rasa theory and Western aesthetics is the question of aesthetic distance — the question of what determines whether an experience of strong emotion in the theatre or concert hall is aesthetically pleasurable rather than merely distressing or overwhelming. Western aesthetics, from Aristotle’s concept of catharsis through

207
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

Kant’s theory of the sublime and Bullough’s concept of 'psychical distance', has struggled to explain this phenomenon satisfactorily. Rasa theory’s solution — the concept of Sadharanikarana (universalisation) through which personal emotion is transformed into impersonal aesthetic experience — is arguably the most sophisticated and psychologically accurate account of what actually occurs in genuine aesthetic experience.

The relationship between Rasa theory and the Western phenomenological tradition — particularly Merleau-Ponty’s analysis of embodied aesthetic experience — has been explored by several contemporary scholars with productive results. Merleau-Ponty’s insistence that aesthetic experience is fundamentally an experience of the lived body, not merely of the mind’s response to external stimuli, resonates deeply with the Natya Shastra’s understanding of the Karana as a psychophysical event that engages the spectator’s body as well as their mind and emotions. The mirror neuron research that provides a neurological basis for the spectator’s embodied participation in the performer’s states supports and deepens this Merleau-Pontian reading of Rasa.

The application of Rasa theory to contemporary performance practices — including contemporary dance, immersive theatre, and performance art — raises interesting questions about the relationship between the tradition’s specific cultural context and its potentially universal aesthetic insights. Contemporary choreographers including Chandralekha, Akram Khan, and Shobana Jeyasingh have drawn explicitly on Rasa theory in their work, finding in it a framework for understanding the aesthetic experience of movement that is both culturally

208
The Cosmic Choreography

specific and universally resonant. Their work demonstrates that the Rasa theory of the Natya Shastra, developed within the specific context of classical Indian performance, contains insights about the nature of aesthetic experience that are applicable to the full range of contemporary performance practice.

From a Shankaracharya perspective, the contemporary relevance of Rasa theory is not surprising. If Rasa experience is, as Abhinavagupta argues, a form of Brahman-recognition — a direct, if transient and mediated, experience of the non-dual awareness that is the ultimate nature of every human consciousness — then Rasa theory is not culturally specific but universal: it describes something that every human being is capable of, regardless of their cultural background, because it describes something that every human consciousness is, at its deepest level. The cross-cultural validity of Rasa theory is, from this perspective, a reflection of the cross-cultural validity of the Advaitic insight that Rasa theory aesthetically embodies: the insight that consciousness is one, that its deepest nature is blissful awareness, and that the highest human art is that which makes this blissful awareness directly experienceable in the medium of aesthetic form.

209
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

7.14Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Seven

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

210
The Cosmic Choreography

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana,

211
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The

212
The Cosmic Choreography

scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

7.16Aesthetic Experience as Spiritual Practice: Concluding Analysis

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the

213
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

214
The Cosmic Choreography

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

215
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

7.17Philosophical Debates and Their Resolution

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S.

216
The Cosmic Choreography

Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in

217
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily

218
The Cosmic Choreography

selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

7.7The Sthayi Bhavas and Their Philosophical Foundations

The Natya Shastra’s concept of Sthayi Bhava — the 'permanent' or 'abiding' emotional state that underlies and organises each Rasa — is philosophically significant in ways that have not been fully appreciated in the scholarly literature. The term Sthayi derives from the root stha, 'to stand, to be established', which is the same root as Sthana (the standing position that grounds each Karana) and Pratishtha (the philosophical concept of the established ground of being). The Sthayi Bhava is not merely one emotional state among many but the emotional ground — the abiding

219
Rasa Theory and Its Advaitic Dimensions

quality of feeling from which the particular transient emotions of a performance arise and to which they return.

Each of the eight primary Rasas has its corresponding Sthayi Bhava: Rati (love/attachment) underlies Shringara, Hasa (humour/playfulness) underlies Hasya, Shoka (grief) underlies Karuna, Krodha (anger) underlies Raudra, Utsaha (enthusiasm) underlies Vira, Bhaya (fear) underlies Bhayanaka, Jugupsa (disgust) underlies Bibhatsa, and Vismaya (wonder) underlies Adbhuta. Abhinavagupta adds Shama (tranquility/equanimity) as the Sthayi Bhava underlying the ninth Rasa, Shanta — and this addition is philosophically crucial for our study.

The Sthayi Bhava of Shanta — Shama — is not an emotion in the same sense as Rati, Hasa, or Shoka. It is rather the absence of the distorting emotions: the quality of pure, undistorted equanimity that remains when all the specific emotional colours have been dissolved. This is precisely the quality that Shankaracharya identifies as the Shat-Sampat virtue of Sama — the first of the six virtues of the qualified Vedanta student — described as the 'subduing of the mind', the quality of consciousness that has been stilled from its habitual agitation without being suppressed into dullness. Shama is not the absence of awareness but its most complete presence: awareness without the distortion of emotional reactivity, pure consciousness without the veil of personal preference and aversion.

The identification of Shanta Rasa’s Sthayi Bhava with the virtue of Sama in the Advaita Vedanta tradition creates a direct bridge between the two traditions' approaches to the same quality of consciousness. The dancer who embodies Shanta Rasa in

220
The Cosmic Choreography

performance is embodying, in the aesthetic medium, the same quality of equanimous awareness that the Vedanta student cultivates as the prerequisite for philosophical recognition. And the philosopher who has cultivated the virtue of Sama is inhabiting, in the philosophical domain, the same quality of undistorted awareness that the Shanta Rasa embodies in the aesthetic domain. Both are approaching the same Brahman from different directions, speaking the same truth in different languages.

221
CHAPTER VIII

The Tandava

Cosmological Dimensions

“The Tandava is not a dance performed by Shiva; it is what Shiva is — pure consciousness in its ceaseless self-expression.”

— V. Raghavan, Studies in Sanskrit Drama

8.1The Five Functions of the Cosmic Dance

The theological significance of the Tandava in the Shaiva tradition rests on its identification with the Panchakriya — the five cosmic functions of Shiva that together constitute the complete cycle of cosmic existence: Srishti (creation/emission), Sthiti (preservation/maintenance), Samhara (dissolution/withdrawal), Tirobhava (concealment), and Anugraha (grace/liberation). These five functions are not sequential stages in a cosmic timeline but simultaneous, eternal activities of divine consciousness — eternally creating, eternally maintaining, eternally dissolving, eternally concealing, and eternally liberating, all at once, in every moment.

222
The Cosmic Choreography

The Nataraja icon — the most perfectly realised visual expression of the Tandava theology — encodes the five functions with extraordinary precision and economy. The upper right hand holds a small drum (Damaru) whose two-headed form symbolises the duality of manifestation and whose sound symbolises the primordial Nada from which creation emerges: this is Srishti. The upper left hand holds a flame that simultaneously illuminates and consumes: this is Samhara, dissolution. The lower right hand is raised in the Abhaya mudra — fearlessness, protection, the gesture of one who preserves what has been created: this is Sthiti. The left leg is raised in the Urdhva Tandava configuration, the raised foot suggesting the elevation above ordinary existence that constitutes Maya or concealment: this is Tirobhava. And the lower left hand, pointing to the raised foot in the Gajahasta gesture, indicates that the very concealment is itself a form of grace — that the veil of Maya is Shiva’s compassionate gift to beings who are not yet ready for the full light of unmediated reality: this is Anugraha.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical system maps onto this iconographic scheme with remarkable precision. Srishti corresponds to Shankara’s analysis of Brahman’s projection of the world through Maya — the creative emanation of apparent diversity from the undivided ground of being. Sthiti corresponds to Shankara’s analysis of Brahman as the sustaining ground of all apparent existence — the consciousness without which nothing could exist even apparently. Samhara corresponds to the philosophical dissolution of the apparent world in the recognition of its identity with Brahman — the liberation event

223
The Tandava

viewed from the cosmic perspective. Tirobhava corresponds to Shankara’s concept of Avidya — the concealment of Brahman’s nature by the veil of ignorance. And Anugraha corresponds to the liberating power of Brahma-vidya — the knowledge that removes the veil and reveals the truth that was always already present.

The 108 Karanas, as the vocabulary of Shiva’s Tandava, collectively embody the full range of these five cosmic functions. Some Karanas are clearly Srishti in quality: expansive, outward, creating new forms in space. Others are Sthiti: balanced, sustained, maintaining a configuration in perfect equilibrium. Others are Samhara: contracting, withdrawing, dissolving from form back into formlessness. Others are Tirobhava: concealing, veiling, drawing a veil across the clarity of the previous movement. And some are unmistakably Anugraha: liberating, opening, revealing — the Karanas in which the dancer seems to become transparent to the light that shines through her, in which the technical mastery disappears into spontaneous grace.

Understanding the 108 Karanas in terms of the Panchakriya provides a powerful framework for understanding not merely individual Karanas but the overall structure of a complete Karana performance. A performance that genuinely embodies the wisdom of the tradition will not be a random or merely aesthetic sequence of movement but a complete philosophical statement — a movement through the full cycle of creation, preservation, dissolution, concealment, and liberation that mirrors, in miniature and in human time, the eternal cycle that Shiva’s Tandava enacts at the cosmic scale.

224
The Cosmic Choreography

8.2Shankaracharya’s Reading of Nataraja

While Shankaracharya does not write a systematic treatise on the Nataraja iconography, his various hymns to Shiva — particularly the Shiva Tandava Stotram, the Nirvana Shatakam, the Dakshinamurti Stotra, and the Shivananda Lahari — collectively constitute a sustained philosophical meditation on the meaning of the cosmic dance. Crucially, Shankara does not treat the Nataraja mythology as a cosmological narrative separate from philosophical inquiry; rather, he reads the cosmic dance as the Advaitic truth of consciousness embodied in iconic form — a visual philosophy that communicates non-dual insight through the medium of sacred art.

The Nirvana Shatakam — 'I am not the body, I am not the mind, I am not the intellect, I am not the ego...' — is perhaps the most direct poetic expression of the Nataraja philosophy in Shankaracharya’s corpus. Each verse systematically removes one more identification — one more apparent weight that the ego-dancer carries — until the final verse arrives at the pure recognition: 'Ananda rupam amritam yad vibhati, Chidananda rupah Shivoham Shivoham' — 'The blissful form, the immortal, that which shines — consciousness-bliss form, I am Shiva, I am Shiva.' This progressive removal of identification is precisely the inner movement of the Urdhva Tandava: as each false identification falls away, the foot of consciousness rises higher, lighter, more free, until the final verse achieves the fully elevated position of Nataraja’s raised leg.

225
The Tandava

The Dakshinamurti Stotra presents the other pole of the Nataraja teaching: where the Nirvana Shatakam focuses on the transcendent, liberated aspect (the raised leg, the consciousness beyond all limitation), the Dakshinamurti Stotra focuses on the teaching aspect (the lower right hand in Jnana Mudra, the gesture of wisdom pointing to the recognition of non-duality). The great teacher of Advaita — Shiva as Dakshinamurti, seated beneath the fig tree, teaching in silence — is presented as the still point at the centre of the cosmic dance: the pure awareness from which all movement arises and to which all movement returns, the dancer who is simultaneously the most perfectly still and the most perfectly dynamic.

The synthesis of these two aspects — the transcendent liberation of the raised leg and the immanent teaching of the Jnana Mudra — is precisely the synthesis that the 108 Karanas embody as a system. The Karanas that embody Urdhva quality (elevated, transcendent, sky-moving) correspond to the Nirvana Shatakam aspect of the teaching; the Karanas that embody Bhu quality (grounded, immanent, earth-moving) correspond to the Dakshinamurti aspect. A complete performance of the 108 Karanas — moving through both aspects in their full range — is a complete philosophical statement: both the transcendent freedom of the liberated consciousness and its compassionate immanent presence in the world of beings who have not yet recognised their own freedom.

This synthesis has practical implications for contemporary dance practice. A performance of the Karanas that emphasises only the technically spectacular Urdhva (elevated) Karanas at the

226
The Cosmic Choreography

expense of the quieter, more grounded Karanas is philosophically incomplete: it presents transcendence without immanence, liberation without teaching, the raised leg of Nataraja without his lower right hand’s gesture of wisdom and protection. A complete and philosophically mature performance of the Karana vocabulary will give equal attention to both poles — grounding and elevation, stillness and dynamism, the Dakshinamurti’s teaching silence and the Nataraja’s blissful cosmic movement.

8.5Lasya and Tandava: The Dance of Complementarity

The cosmic dance of Shiva is not understood in the Indian tradition as a solo performance but as a duet: Shiva’s dynamic, powerful Tandava finds its complement and completion in the graceful, tender Lasya of Parvati-Shakti. This complementarity is not merely aesthetic — the alternation of masculine vigor and feminine grace — but metaphysical: it embodies the non-dual truth that the absolute consciousness of Shiva and the dynamic creative power of Shakti are not two separate realities but aspects of a single, non-dual whole whose full expression requires both aspects simultaneously.

The Natya Shastra’s treatment of Lasya — the feminine dance style — is less extensive than its treatment of Tandava, but it makes clear that Lasya is not merely a gentler version of Tandava but a complete and independent vocabulary that encodes different but equally essential philosophical insights. Where Tandava embodies

227
The Tandava

the qualities of creation, transformation, and transcendence — the qualities associated with the dynamic principle of divine consciousness — Lasya embodies the qualities of sustenance, beauty, and immanence — the qualities associated with the creative and nurturing principle of divine power. Together, Tandava and Lasya constitute the complete vocabulary of cosmic self-expression.

Shankaracharya’s treatment of this complementarity in the Soundarya Lahari is among the most philosophically subtle aspects of that text. The Verse 1’s famous statement that Shiva without Shakti is incapable of even the slightest movement is not merely a statement about the metaphysical relationship between consciousness and energy; it is also a statement about the aesthetic relationship between Tandava and Lasya: neither the dynamic masculine movement nor the graceful feminine movement, taken alone, is the complete expression of the divine. Only when both are present simultaneously — when the power of the Tandava and the grace of the Lasya are perfectly united — is the full truth of the non-dual consciousness expressed in movement.

Contemporary Bharatanatyam, in its full classical form, embodies this complementarity through the balance it maintains between the vigorous Nritta sections (which draw primarily on the Tandava vocabulary of the Karanas) and the expressive Abhinaya sections (which draw primarily on the Lasya vocabulary of gesture and expression). The ideal classical Bharatanatyam performance is not predominantly one or the other but a continuous dynamic between them — a sustained embodiment of the Shiva-Shakti complementarity that the

228
The Cosmic Choreography

Soundarya Lahari’s first verse describes. The Karanas that the performer executes in the Nritta sections are Tandava Karanas; the gestures she employs in the Abhinaya sections are Lasya Hastas; and the highest quality of performance is the one in which these two vocabularies are so deeply integrated that the distinction between them disappears in a unity that embodies both.

The philosophical implication of this complementarity for the student of Advaita Vedanta is directly stated by Shankaracharya in the Soundarya Lahari: the apparent duality of Shiva and Shakti, of consciousness and energy, of the absolute and the relative, is not a real duality but a dynamic unity. The Tandava and the Lasya are not two dances but one dance seen from two perspectives — just as Brahman and Maya are not two realities but one reality seen from two perspectives (the absolute perspective of pure consciousness and the conventional perspective of the world of appearance). The practitioner who understands this non-dual unity through the medium of dance — who can move between the Tandava and Lasya vocabularies with the fluid ease of someone who has recognised their common source — has, in the embodied medium of performance, realised the insight that Shankaracharya articulates philosophically in the first verse of the Soundarya Lahari.

This analysis has practical implications for the training of classical dancers. A training programme that focuses exclusively on the Tandava vocabulary of the Karanas at the expense of the Lasya dimensions of gesture and expression — or, conversely, one that emphasises the expressive Abhinaya at the expense of the

229
The Tandava

technical rigour of the Nritta Karanas — is philosophically incomplete. The complete classical training should develop both vocabularies to the highest level simultaneously, in the understanding that their integration is not merely an aesthetic achievement but a philosophical one: the dancer who has truly integrated Tandava and Lasya in her body-consciousness has, in the medium of embodied practice, realised the Advaitic insight of the non-dual unity of consciousness and energy.

8.6The Panchakriya in Individual Practice and Universal Manifestation

The five cosmic functions of Shiva — Srishti, Sthiti, Samhara, Tirobhava, and Anugraha — are not only cosmological categories but categories of individual experience. In every moment of conscious existence, all five functions are operating simultaneously: consciousness is continuously creating new experiences (Srishti), maintaining the continuity of awareness (Sthiti), dissolving past experience (Samhara), concealing its own infinite nature behind the finite appearance of the moment’s content (Tirobhava), and providing the grace of its own self-revealing nature to any consciousness attentive enough to receive it (Anugraha). The cosmic dance of Shiva is not a mythological narrative about events in some other time and place but a description of what is happening in every moment of conscious experience.

230
The Cosmic Choreography

Shankaracharya’s philosophical analysis of the three states of consciousness — waking (Jagrat), dreaming (Svapna), and deep sleep (Sushupti) — and the fourth state (Turiya) that underlies and permeates them provides the most systematic account of the Panchakriya at the individual level. The waking state corresponds to the manifest phase of the Panchakriya — the phase in which Srishti, Sthiti, and Samhara are most visibly operative as the world of experience is created, maintained, and dissolved moment by moment. The dreaming state corresponds to the Tirobhava aspect — the phase in which the apparent solidity of the waking world is revealed as a construction of consciousness, as the dream world proves to be equally convincing as an experience while it lasts and equally insubstantial when it ends. The deep sleep state corresponds to the temporary cessation of manifest activity — the phase in which the Panchakriya rests in its source before the next cycle begins. And Turiya — the fourth, the ever-present ground — corresponds to the unmanifest absolute from which all five cosmic functions arise and to which they return.

The 108 Karanas, understood in terms of the Panchakriya, constitute a complete map of consciousness’s activity in its individual as well as its cosmic dimension. The opening Karanas of the sequence — those grounded, emerging, creative movements that embody the quality of Srishti — correspond to the dawn of consciousness in the waking state, the emergence of the individual’s awareness from the deep sleep of rest. The middle Karanas — those sustained, balanced movements that embody the quality of Sthiti — correspond to the sustained engagement with the world of experience that characterises the mature waking

231
The Tandava

state. The dynamic, transformative Karanas of the sequence’s middle section — those spinning, turning, dissolving movements that embody Samhara — correspond to the moments of insight and transformation through which the practitioner’s consciousness undergoes the continuous dissolution and renewal that is the spiritual path. The concealing Karanas — those contracted, veiling movements that embody Tirobhava — correspond to the moments of doubt, confusion, and forgetting that are part of every genuine spiritual journey. And the transcendent, elevated Karanas of the sequence’s culmination — those Urdhva movements that embody Anugraha — correspond to the moments of grace in which the divine reveals itself through the veil of individual experience.

The performer who understands this correspondence between the Panchakriya and the Karana sequence approaches each performance as a complete spiritual journey — a miniature version of the complete cycle of cosmic manifestation and liberation that the Nataraja’s dance expresses at the cosmic scale. Each performance is a complete spiritual biography: from the first grounded movement (corresponding to the emergence of individual consciousness from its cosmic source) through the middle phases of engagement, transformation, and concealment, to the final elevated gestures (corresponding to the dissolution of individual consciousness back into its cosmic source in the recognition of liberation). This understanding transforms the entire experience of performing the 108 Karanas from artistic production into spiritual autobiography.

232
The Cosmic Choreography

The practical implications of this understanding for the dancer’s preparation and state of mind are profound. The preparation for a performance of the 108 Karanas, properly understood, involves not merely physical and technical preparation but a philosophical preparation: the practitioner must consciously enter the cycle of the Panchakriya, recognising herself as simultaneously the dancer who will perform the Karanas and the Shiva-consciousness whose cosmic dance the Karanas embody. This recognition — which is, in Shankara’s language, a moment of Aparoksha Anubhuti (direct non-mediated experience of the non-dual truth) — is what transforms technical performance into genuine sacred art. The dancer who begins a performance of the 108 Karanas from this state of recognition is not merely performing Shiva’s dance; she is Shiva’s dance — not a representation or imitation of the cosmic consciousness but its direct expression in the medium of a human body informed by the wisdom of the tradition.

8.15Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Eight

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the

233
The Tandava

practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is

234
The Cosmic Choreography

actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana, moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace,

235
The Tandava

in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce.
