This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

236
The Cosmic Choreography

8.17Cosmic Dance, Human Body, Divine Consciousness

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

237
The Tandava

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one

238
The Cosmic Choreography

tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing

239
The Tandava

to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

8.18Iconometric Analysis and Its Philosophical Meaning

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are

240
The Cosmic Choreography

less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram

241
The Tandava

— as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple

242
The Cosmic Choreography

sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

8.7The Kailasha Tradition and Alternative Tandava Accounts

While the Chidambaram tradition has been the primary focus of this chapter’s analysis of the Tandava’s cosmological dimensions, other important regional traditions offer alternative accounts of the cosmic dance that illuminate different aspects of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The Kailasha tradition — centred on Mount Kailasha in the Himalayas as the primary site of Shiva’s cosmic dance — presents a different geographical and theological context for the same fundamental insight.

In the Kailasha tradition, Shiva’s dance is understood primarily in terms of the Samhara (dissolution) function rather than the Ananda (bliss) function that the Chidambaram tradition emphasises. The harsh, austere landscape of Kailasha — the eternal snows, the extreme cold, the remoteness from human habitation — provides a very different aesthetic context for the cosmic dance than the lush, humid, culturally rich environment of Chidambaram in Tamil Nadu. The dance of Shiva at Kailasha

243
The Tandava

is the dance of the Great Renouncer, the Mahayogi, the one who has dissolved all attachment in the fire of supreme awareness.

Shankaracharya’s own biography connects him to both traditions. Born in the warm south of Kerala, he composed his most sensuous and aesthetically rich devotional poetry (the Soundarya Lahari) in the tradition associated with Chidambaram’s Ananda Tandava. But he also established his northernmost Matha at Joshimath, near Badrinath in the high Himalayas — in the spiritual geography of Kailasha — and composed works like the Nirvana Shatakam that reflect the austere, renunciatory aesthetic of the Kailasha tradition. This geographical and aesthetic range is not a contradiction but a reflection of the same non-dual insight expressed in different registers: the blissful, aesthetic, creative expression of the Chidambaram Ananda Tandava and the austere, renunciatory, liberating expression of the Kailasha Samhara Tandava are not opposed but complementary aspects of the complete cosmic dance.

The 108 Karanas, understood against this dual background, encompass both poles of the cosmic dance. The Lalita (graceful) Karanas of the sequence embody the Chidambaram Ananda quality — flowing, beautiful, aesthetically refined. The Raudra (fierce) Karanas embody the Kailasha Samhara quality — powerful, austere, dissolving. A complete performance of the 108 Karanas that genuinely embodies both poles is, in the tradition’s understanding, the complete expression of the cosmic dance in its full range — the complete Tandava of Shiva

244
The Cosmic Choreography

that the Chidambaram and Kailasha traditions each illuminate from their respective angles.

245
CHAPTER IX

Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

“The temple is the cosmos made comprehensible; the sculpture is the text made visible; the dance is both — the cosmos comprehended in a living body.”

— Stella Kramrisch, The Hindu Temple

9.1The Temple as Philosophical Programme

South Indian temple architecture — particularly the elaborately adorned Dravida-style temples of the Chola, Pallava, and Vijayanagara periods — represents one of the most extraordinary achievements of human civilisation: a systematic materialisation in stone, space, and iconographic programme of the most sophisticated philosophical and cosmological understanding of the tradition. The great South Indian temple is not merely a religious building but a three-dimensional philosophical text, a sacred diagram at architectural scale, a physical manifestation of the same non-dual vision that Shankaracharya articulated in philosophical language.

246
The Cosmic Choreography

The spatial organisation of the South Indian temple encodes the Advaitic understanding of reality as a series of progressively subtler layers of manifestation surrounding an innermost core of absolute reality. The outermost precincts of the temple complex — the most accessible, the most open to the general public, surrounded by markets and ordinary life — correspond to the grossest level of material existence. As one moves inward, through successive enclosures (prakaras) and ever more imposing gateways (gopurams), the architectural density and iconographic complexity increase while the space becomes progressively more intimate, more focused, more concentrated. Finally, in the innermost sanctuary (garbhagriha, literally 'womb-chamber'), the architectural complexity is suddenly stripped away: the chamber is small, dark, and simple, housing either a highly refined form of the deity or — in the extraordinary case of Chidambaram — nothing at all, or rather, the formless absolute concealed behind a golden curtain.

This architectural journey from the complexity of the periphery to the simplicity of the centre enacts, in spatial terms, the philosophical journey that Shankaracharya describes in the Vivekachudamani: from the complex, apparently differentiated world of ordinary experience through progressive levels of understanding to the simple, luminous, undivided ground of pure consciousness. The worshipper who moves through the temple complex in pradakshina (circumambulation) is performing a spatial meditation — a pilgrimage through the layers of appearance toward the innermost reality that is their common ground.

247
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

Within this spatial programme, the sculptural renderings of the 108 Karanas occupy a position of unique philosophical significance. At Chidambaram — the supreme Nataraja temple, the most important Shaiva pilgrimage site in South India, and the place most directly associated with the tradition of the 108 Karanas — all 108 Karanas are depicted in sculptural panels arranged along the walls of the Kanaka Sabha (the golden-roofed hall adjacent to the innermost shrine). These panels are not random decorative elements but a carefully organised iconographic programme whose sequence and placement reflect the same philosophical understanding of the Karana system that we have been tracing throughout this study.

The worshipper who moves through the Kanaka Sabha, attending to the Karana panels in sequence, is receiving a teaching in the complete vocabulary of sacred movement without a single spoken word. The stone Karanas teach through pure visual presence — through the beauty and power and philosophical precision of their forms — just as the Dakshinamurti of the Natya tradition teaches through the quality of his silence. This silent teaching in stone is, in a profound sense, the most faithful possible transmission of the Karana tradition: it communicates not merely the external form of the Karanas but their inner quality, their philosophical depth, their cosmological significance, all at once and without reduction.

248
The Cosmic Choreography

9.2Sculptural Analysis: Chidambaram, Thanjavur, and Darasuram

The three most important sites for the sculptural transmission of the 108 Karanas are the Nataraja Temple at Chidambaram, the Brihadeeswara Temple at Thanjavur, and the Airavatesvara Temple at Darasuram. Each site presents the Karanas in a distinctive artistic style and theological context that illuminates different aspects of the philosophical synthesis this book traces.

The Chidambaram panels — dating primarily from the Chola period (c. 900-1200 CE) — are executed in a style of extraordinary refinement and technical mastery. The sculptors have solved the fundamental challenge of representing dynamic movement in static stone with solutions of remarkable elegance: through the careful arrangement of drapery, jewellery, and ornament to suggest the momentum of interrupted movement; through the use of multiple arms (in some panels) to represent successive positions in a movement sequence; and above all through the quality of the figures' inner life, conveyed through the precise modelling of facial expression, the orientation of the gaze, and the subtle torsion of the torso. These are not merely beautiful figures but figures that seem about to move — images of consciousness arrested at the peak of its physical expression.

The Thanjavur Brihadeeswara panels, dating from the reign of the great Chola king Rajaraja I (c. 985-1014 CE), show a more monumental, architectural approach to the Karanas. The larger scale of the Thanjavur figures allows for greater anatomical detail

249
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

and more complex compositional arrangements. Scholars including Kapila Vatsyayan have noted that the Thanjavur panels show a closer correspondence to the technical descriptions in the Natya Shastra than the Chidambaram panels, suggesting that the Thanjavur sculptural programme was created with explicit reference to the textual tradition and with the aim of providing a precise visual codification of the technical vocabulary.

The Darasuram Airavatesvara Temple panels, dating from the reign of Rajaraja II (c. 1143-1173 CE), introduce a quality of lyrical expressiveness into the Karana iconography that goes beyond both Chidambaram’s refinement and Thanjavur’s monumentality. The Darasuram figures move with a quality of spontaneous joy — a quality that the Tamil Shaiva tradition calls Ananda — that is precisely the quality of the Ananda Tandava itself. These sculptures seem to embody Shankaracharya’s most intimate and devotional understanding of the divine dance: not the cosmic drama of the Shiva Tandava Stotram nor the metaphysical precision of the Nirvana Shatakam, but the simple, pure, uncontainable joy of Brahman’s self-expression through the medium of beautiful movement.

The art historical analysis of these three sites reveals something important about the nature of the tradition’s philosophical understanding: it is not static but dynamic, evolving over time in response to the developing philosophical understanding of the tradition. The Chidambaram panels embody the early Chola period’s emphasis on technical mastery and philosophical precision; the Thanjavur panels embody the high Chola period’s emphasis on cosmological grandeur and systematic codification;

250
The Cosmic Choreography

the Darasuram panels embody the late Chola period’s emphasis on devotional warmth and aesthetic joy. Together, they constitute a complete statement of the tradition’s philosophical range — precisely the range that this study has been tracing from the technical precision of the Natya Shastra through the cosmological grandeur of the Tandava theology to the devotional warmth of Shankaracharya’s Soundarya Lahari.

9.5The Vijayanagara Period and the Systematisation of Temple Dance

The Vijayanagara Empire (c. 1336-1646 CE) represents the most important political and cultural context for the consolidation and systematisation of the relationship between temple architecture, temple iconography, and classical dance performance in South India. The Vijayanagara kings were among the greatest patrons of the arts in Indian history, and their patronage was explicitly philosophically motivated: they understood the arts as vehicles of the same Advaitic truth that the Shankaracharya tradition had articulated, and they invested enormous resources in the creation of artistic programmes that embodied this understanding in the most refined and comprehensive way possible.

The great temple complexes built under Vijayanagara patronage — including the Virupaksha Temple at Hampi, the Vittala Temple complex, the Hazara Rama Temple, and numerous others throughout the empire’s vast territory —

251
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

represent the culmination of the tradition of using temple architecture and iconography as philosophical programmes. The Vijayanagara architects and sculptors had, by the fourteenth century, at their disposal the complete legacy of the Chola, Pallava, and Hoysala sculptural traditions, as well as the philosophical framework provided by the Shankaracharya tradition’s Advaita Vedanta. The result was a synthesis of extraordinary comprehensiveness and refinement.

The Vijayanagara period also witnessed the most systematic institutional development of the relationship between the Devadasi tradition and the philosophical traditions of the temples. The Devadasi system — through which women were dedicated to the temple deity and understood their dance as a form of ritual worship — reached its most elaborate and philosophically self-conscious form during the Vijayanagara period. The systematic training programmes developed in this context drew explicitly on both the Natya Shastra’s technical prescriptions and the Advaita Vedanta tradition’s philosophical framework, producing performers who were simultaneously technically accomplished, philosophically trained, and genuinely understood their practice as a path of liberation.

The philosophical training of Devadasi performers in the Vijayanagara period is documented in several texts of the period, including the Sangita-ratnakara of Sarangadeva and various regional dance manuals that drew on the Natya Shastra tradition while adapting it to the specific cultural contexts of different regional performance traditions. These texts consistently embed their technical prescriptions within a philosophical framework

252
The Cosmic Choreography

that is explicitly Advaitic: the correct execution of a Karana is described not merely in terms of the physical form but in terms of the quality of consciousness that should accompany it — a quality that is invariably described using the vocabulary of Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta.

The legacy of the Vijayanagara synthesis is visible in the living traditions of South Indian classical dance today. Contemporary Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, Odissi, and Mohiniyattam all contain elements whose origins can be traced to the Vijayanagara period’s synthesis of Natya Shastra technical tradition and Advaita Vedanta philosophical framework. The choreographic forms, the musical accompaniment structures, the training methodologies, and above all the philosophical self-understanding of these traditions all bear the imprint of the Vijayanagara systematisation. Understanding this historical context is important for appreciating what contemporary classical Indian dance actually is: not an archaic survival from an ancient past but a living synthesis of philosophical and artistic traditions that has been continuously renewed and refined across many centuries of creative engagement.

9.6Reading the Temple as Philosophical Text

The great South Indian temple complexes that house the sculptural programmes of the 108 Karanas are not merely art historical monuments but active philosophical texts that continue to teach today for any reader attentive to their language.

253
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

Learning to read the temple as a philosophical text requires developing a specific kind of visual literacy — the capacity to engage with sculptural and architectural forms in the same way that one engages with written philosophical texts: following the logic of their arrangement, attending to the relationships between different elements, recognising the conceptual vocabulary they employ, and allowing the work of understanding to unfold progressively over many visits and periods of extended contemplation.

The most important principle for reading the temple as a philosophical text is the principle of spatial hierarchy. The temple’s spatial organisation — from its most open, most accessible, most externally facing elements to its most closed, most restricted, most internally facing elements — corresponds precisely to the hierarchy of levels of understanding that Shankaracharya describes in his philosophical works. The outermost gopuram (gateway tower), with its overwhelming density of sculptural imagery covering every available surface, corresponds to the level of ordinary experience: overwhelming in its multiplicity, visually compelling, but without clear internal organisation from the perspective of the uninitiated viewer. The intermediate courts and halls, with their more carefully organised iconographic programmes, correspond to the level of philosophical analysis: the apparent multiplicity of phenomena begins to resolve itself into recognisable patterns and categories. And the innermost sanctuary — where the complexity suddenly strips away to the simplicity of either a single image or, at Chidambaram, the astonishing 'nothing' of the Akasha Linga —

254
The Cosmic Choreography

corresponds to the level of direct non-dual recognition: the recognition that beneath all the multiplicity there is only the simple, luminous, undivided ground of pure consciousness.

The Karana panels of Chidambaram, arranged along the walls of the Kanaka Sabha adjacent to the innermost shrine, occupy a particularly significant position in this spatial hierarchy. They are placed between the complexity of the outer sculptural programmes (which include images of deities, mythological narratives, and devotional figures in great variety) and the simplicity of the innermost shrine (which contains, at its ultimate interior, nothing visible at all). This placement encodes a specific philosophical statement: the 108 Karanas represent the complete vocabulary of the phenomenal world’s self-expression — all the forms that consciousness takes in its creative self-manifestation — and their spatial proximity to the Akasha Linga’s 'formless absolute' emphasises that these forms are not separate from the formless but its direct expression, identical with it at the ultimate level.

The sequential arrangement of the 108 Karana panels — which begin with the most grounded, earthbound movements near the entrance to the Kanaka Sabha and progress to the most elevated, transcendent movements near the innermost shrine — traces the same philosophical journey that this entire book has been describing: from the grossest level of embodied consciousness to the most refined, from the most heavily material configurations of the body to the most transparently spiritual, from the earthward orientation of ordinary consciousness to the skyward aspiration of the consciousness approaching liberation. The

255
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

worshipper who moves through this sequence of panels in pradakshina (circumambulation) — or who contemplates a reproduction of the complete sequence in the context of philosophical study — is following a path that the tradition understands as genuinely transformative: a path whose transformative power derives not from the intellectual content of the images but from their capacity to engage and reshape the perceiver’s embodied consciousness through the medium of aesthetic experience.

The experience of reading the Chidambaram Karana panels and the experience of reading Shankaracharya’s philosophical texts are, from this perspective, more similar than they might appear. Both require a quality of sustained, attentive engagement that is simultaneously intellectual and aesthetic, analytical and receptive. Both work through a progressive disclosure of meaning that moves from apparent complexity toward revealed simplicity. And both, at their highest, produce in the engaged reader or viewer a quality of direct, non-mediated recognition that the tradition identifies as Aparoksha Anubhuti — the direct experience of the non-dual truth that is the goal of both the philosophical tradition and the artistic tradition: the same recognition, approached through different media, opening onto the same infinite space of pure, blissful, undivided awareness.

256
The Cosmic Choreography

9.16Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Nine

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

257
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana,

258
The Cosmic Choreography

moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The

259
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

9.18Iconography as Living Philosophy

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated

260
The Cosmic Choreography

experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

261
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

262
The Cosmic Choreography

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

9.19Inscriptional Evidence and Historical Documentation

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary,

263
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the

264
The Cosmic Choreography

Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive

265
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

9.7The Natya Mandapa: Performance Space as Cosmological Map

The Natya Mandapa — the performance hall specified in the Natya Shastra’s second chapter — is not merely a practical space for theatrical productions but a cosmological diagram: a physical space whose dimensions, proportions, and orientation are determined by philosophical principles that encode the same understanding of cosmic order that the 108 Karanas encode in the medium of movement. Understanding the Natya Mandapa as a cosmological diagram illuminates both the spatial context of the

266
The Cosmic Choreography

Karana performances and the relationship of that spatial context to Shankaracharya’s philosophical framework.

The Natya Shastra specifies three sizes of Natya Mandapa — Jyeshtha (large, 96 x 48 angulas), Madhyama (medium, 64 x 32 angulas), and Avara (small, 32 x 16 angulas) — in proportions that maintain a 2:1 ratio of length to width. This 2:1 ratio is not arbitrary: it reflects the same binary logic of cosmic manifestation that underlies both the Sri Yantra’s geometry and the Samkhya philosophy’s duality of Purusha and Prakriti. The performance space is literally constructed as a diagram of the cosmic duality that the performance will progressively dissolve in the recognition of the underlying non-dual unity.

The placement of the stage (Rangapitha) at the eastern end of the Natya Mandapa, with the audience in the western half, encodes a directional cosmology: the performers face west (toward the setting sun, toward the world of ordinary experience) while their inspiration comes from the east (the direction of the rising sun, the direction of the sacred, the direction from which Vedic revelation comes). The performer stands at the threshold between the sacred and the ordinary, embodying the transition between them — which is precisely the philosophical position of the classical dancer as described throughout this study: standing at the threshold between the divine and the human, embodying the passage between Maya and Brahman in the medium of physical movement.

The altar (Devakhanda) at the centre of the stage — the small area at the midpoint of the performance space that is consecrated to the presiding deity — is the spatial equivalent of the Bindu at

267
Temple Iconography and the 108 Karanas

the centre of the Sri Yantra: the point of absolute concentration from which all the complexity of the performance radiates and to which it ultimately returns. The performer who passes through this central point in the course of executing a Karana — whose movement takes her through the exact centre of the consecrated space — is, in the tradition’s understanding, passing through the axis mundi, the cosmological centre of the universe. Each Karana that passes through this centre is an encounter with the absolute ground of the performance space, just as each moment of genuine Brahman-recognition is an encounter with the absolute ground of consciousness.

268
CHAPTER X

Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

“What the words cannot say, the gesture says; what the gesture cannot express, the silence says — and all three arise from the same source.”

— Traditional saying, Kerala Kutiyattam tradition

10.1The Semiotics of Sacred Gesture

The Sanskrit word Mudra encompasses a domain of embodied meaning whose richness and philosophical depth have no precise equivalent in Western semiotic tradition. In its most common usage in the context of classical Indian performance, Mudra refers to the hand gestures that constitute the most immediately visible and communicatively rich component of the dancer’s bodily vocabulary. But the word also refers, in other contexts, to the physiological locks (Bandha Mudras) used in Hatha Yoga to direct and concentrate vital energy; to the symbolic hand configurations used in ritual worship (Puja Mudras); to the gestures depicted in Buddhist and

269
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

Jain iconography; and more generally to any configuration of the body — or of space itself — that 'seals' a particular quality of consciousness and makes it visible.

This diversity of usage is philosophically significant. In all its uses, Mudra carries the sense of a seal or stamp — an impression that both expresses and fixes a particular quality of consciousness, making it visible to others and simultaneously reinforcing its presence in the practitioner. The Mudra is thus simultaneously expressive (communicating a quality of consciousness to an observer) and performative (bringing about the quality of consciousness it expresses in the practitioner). This double function — simultaneously representational and transformative — is precisely the function that Shankaracharya claims for the genuine knowledge of Brahman: it is simultaneously a cognition (a recognition of what is true) and an event (the liberation that consists in that recognition).

The Natya Shastra devotes three complete chapters to the systematic description of hand gestures, progressing from the twenty-four single-hand gestures (Asamyuta Hastas) through the thirteen combined gestures (Samyuta Hastas) to the thirty pure-dance gestures (Nritta Hastas). This systematic enumeration produces a vocabulary of 67 primary gesture-types that, in various combinations and contexts, is capable of expressing virtually any concept, image, deity, emotion, or philosophical truth in the universe of classical Indian thought and experience. The classical dancer who has mastered this complete gesture vocabulary has, in a very real sense, mastered the complete expressive range of the tradition — has learned to speak, with her

270
The Cosmic Choreography

hands, the entire language of Indian philosophical and spiritual culture.

The philosophical significance of this mastery goes beyond mere technical competence. In the Indian philosophical tradition, the hands are understood as the organs of action (Karma Indriyas) most directly connected with consciousness: while the feet move the body through space, the hands express the quality of consciousness inhabiting that body. The specific configuration of the fingers, the orientation of the palm, the tension or relaxation of the hand muscles — all these subtleties communicate, to the attentive observer, the exact quality of awareness from which the gesture arises. A gesture executed with perfect outer form but without the corresponding inner quality is immediately recognisable as technically competent but spiritually empty; a gesture executed with full inner quality but imperfect outer form is recognisable as genuinely informed but technically incomplete. The highest level of performance requires both dimensions simultaneously — the outer form perfectly expressing the inner quality, and the inner quality fully inhabiting the outer form.

Shankaracharya’s own use of gesture — as evidenced by the iconographic tradition of his representation and by his descriptions of the Jnana Mudra and other gestures in his philosophical texts — reflects a deep understanding of this double function of Mudra. His description of the Jnana Mudra (thumb touching index finger, remaining three fingers extended) as the supreme philosophical gesture is not merely iconographic tradition but a carefully argued philosophical position: the circle

271
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

formed by thumb and index finger represents the union of Jivatman and Paramatman, the individual self and the supreme Self, that constitutes liberation; the three extended fingers represent the three states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep) that are transcended in liberation; and the overall quality of the gesture — alert, open, neither grasping nor releasing — represents the quality of the liberated sage’s engagement with the world: fully present, fully responsive, without identification or attachment.

10.2The Hasta Vocabulary and Its Philosophical Dimensions

Each of the 67 primary hand gestures described in the Natya Shastra carries a specific range of meanings, which the tradition categorises according to both its technical description and its philosophical significance. A comprehensive philosophical analysis of the complete hasta vocabulary would itself require a full-length study; for our purposes, we focus on the gestures most directly relevant to Shankaracharya’s philosophical imagery.

The Anjali Hasta — both hands joined in the prayer gesture — is the most universally recognised gesture in the Indian tradition and appears in multiple Karanas. Its philosophical significance in Shankaracharya’s tradition is foundational: the Anjali is the gesture of recognition, of the individual self acknowledging its relationship to the divine. In the Advaitic interpretation, the Anjali is not the gesture of a separate self

272
The Cosmic Choreography

prostrating before a superior being but the gesture of consciousness recognising its own divine nature — the gesture in which subject and object, worshipper and worshipped, are revealed as the same. The Anjali Hasta appears in several of the most important Karanas, always carrying this quality of simultaneous devotion and recognition.

The Pataka Hasta — the flat-hand gesture with fingers extended and joined — is one of the most versatile gestures in the classical vocabulary, used in hundreds of different contexts to represent everything from a cloud to a flag to a forest to divine protection. Its philosophical significance lies in its quality of open receptivity: the extended, open palm is the gesture of consciousness that has released its grasping and is available to whatever arrives. This quality of open receptivity — neither grasping nor pushing away, neither clinging nor rejecting — is precisely the quality of the Sakshi awareness that Shankaracharya describes as the natural state of liberated consciousness.

The Abhaya Hasta — the raised palm facing outward in the gesture of protection and fearlessness — is among the most philosophically significant gestures in the entire vocabulary, carried by virtually every major deity in the Hindu, Buddhist, and Jain traditions. In Shankaracharya’s tradition, Abhayam (fearlessness) is one of the primary characteristics of the Brahman-knower — the one who has recognised the infinite, indestructible nature of the Atman and therefore has nothing to fear from any finite, transient phenomenon. The Vivekachudamani’s description of the Jivanmukta includes fearlessness as a primary quality: 'Na jata-mriti-shanka tasya cha' — 'For him, there is no

273
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

fear of birth or death.' The Abhaya Hasta in the Karana context embodies this fearlessness not as an intellectual position but as an embodied quality — a quality of the whole body that arises naturally when consciousness has recognised its own indestructibility.

The Shukhatunda Hasta — the gesture in which the index finger points upward while the other fingers are loosely closed — is the gesture most directly associated with philosophical teaching and pointing. It appears iconographically in images of the great philosophical teachers — Shankara himself is sometimes depicted with this gesture — and in the Karana tradition it appears in the context of Karanas associated with Adbhuta (wonder) and philosophical revelation. The philosophical significance is obvious: the pointing finger directs attention upward — toward the transcendent, toward the source, toward the Brahman that is always present but not always recognised. In the Karana context, the Shukhatunda gesture transforms an otherwise purely technical movement into a philosophical statement, directing the observer’s attention toward the dimension of reality that transcends the movement itself.

10.4The Nritta Hastas and Their Tantric Dimensions

The thirty Nritta Hastas — the hand gestures specific to pure dance as described in the eleventh chapter of the Natya Shastra — occupy a special position in the classical Indian gesture

274
The Cosmic Choreography

vocabulary because they represent gestures that are purely expressive and communicative rather than narrative or descriptive. Where the Asamyuta and Samyuta Hastas of Chapters Nine and Ten can be used to 'say' specific things — to indicate a particular deity, emotion, action, or concept — the Nritta Hastas communicate qualities of consciousness rather than specific contents. They are the gesture vocabulary of pure, content-free aesthetic expression: the hands saying 'this is what it feels like to be alive to the beauty of existence' rather than 'I see a lotus' or 'Shiva dances'.

This purely expressive quality of the Nritta Hastas makes them the most directly relevant to Shankaracharya’s philosophical vocabulary. When Shankara describes the quality of the liberated sage’s engagement with the world — free from agenda, from desire, from aversion, simply present to whatever arises — he is describing a quality of conscious engagement that corresponds precisely to the quality of conscious expression embodied in the Nritta Hastas. The liberated sage does not engage with the world in order to achieve anything or avoid anything; she engages with it as pure, present, aesthetic consciousness — the same quality of engagement that the Nritta Hastas embody in the medium of gesture.

The Tantric dimensions of the Nritta Hastas emerge from their relationship to the mudra traditions of esoteric practice. Several of the Nritta Hastas described in the Natya Shastra correspond precisely to the mudras used in specific Tantric rituals — rituals that are understood, in the Shakta Tantric tradition, as direct invocations of specific aspects of the Goddess’s cosmic

275
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

power. The Bhramara Hasta (bee gesture), the Sarpashirsha Hasta (snake-head gesture), and the Mushti Hasta (fist gesture), among others, appear in both the Natya Shastra’s dance vocabulary and the Tantra’s ritual vocabulary, with correspondences that suggest a common origin in a tradition of sacred gesture that predates both the classical dance codification and the Tantric ritual systematisation.

Shankaracharya’s engagement with Tantric practice is a complex and sometimes contentious topic in the scholarly literature. Traditional accounts of his life describe him as a Tantric initiate who received specific transmission in the Shakta Tantra from his guru Govinda Bhagavatpada — a claim that is supported by the explicitly Tantric dimensions of the Soundarya Lahari and the detailed knowledge of Tantric ritual practice visible in his devotional compositions. His philosophical position, while consistently Advaitic, does not require the rejection of Tantric practice but rather its philosophical reinterpretation: the Tantric rituals and their associated mudras are understood not as ends in themselves but as vehicles of the same non-dual recognition that philosophical inquiry seeks through a different route.

This Tantric dimension of Shankara’s relationship to the gesture tradition means that his engagement with the Nritta Hastas of the Natya Shastra is not merely aesthetic or philosophical but potentially liturgical: the gestures that the classical dancer employs in performance are, in this perspective, the same gestures that the Tantric practitioner employs in ritual, and both are vehicles of the same divine energy whose complete

276
The Cosmic Choreography

philosophical analysis Shankara provides in the Advaita Vedanta tradition. The dancer who performs the Nritta Hastas with full awareness of their Tantric dimensions is not merely making beautiful gestures but invoking, through the medium of embodied practice, the divine powers that the Tantric tradition associates with those gestures — powers that are, in the ultimate Advaitic analysis, nothing other than the various expressive modalities of the single, non-dual consciousness that is Brahman itself.

10.5The Eyes and the Drishti: Consciousness Looking at Itself

Of all the expressive instruments of the classical Indian dancer, none is more philosophically significant than the eyes. The Natya Shastra’s elaborate enumeration of thirty-six Drishtis (gaze types) — categorised according to their direction, quality, and associated emotional states — reflects an understanding that the eyes are not merely visual organs but the most direct outward expression of the quality of consciousness inhabiting the body. A great dancer can communicate the entire range of human emotional and spiritual states through the quality of her gaze alone: the eyes that convey Shanta Rasa are recognisably different from the eyes that convey Shringara, not merely in their direction or physical configuration but in the quality of awareness that animates them.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition assigns enormous significance to the quality of the gaze as an expression of the state

277
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

of consciousness. The eyes of the Jivanmukta — the person liberated in life — are described consistently throughout the Advaita Vedanta literature as having a specific quality: neither inward-turned (as in the concentrated gaze of meditation) nor outward-turning (as in the distracted gaze of ordinary ego-bound consciousness), but a specific quality of open, luminous, all-seeing awareness that sees everything with perfect clarity and perfect equanimity. This quality — which the tradition calls Brahmadrishti (the divine gaze) — is not a practiced technique but the natural expression of the awareness that has recognised its own nature as the infinite, luminous ground of all experience.

The thirty-six Drishtis of the Natya Shastra can be understood, from this philosophical perspective, as a typology of the ways in which consciousness can be present to itself through the medium of the eyes. The most elevated Drishti — the Sama Drishti or 'equal gaze' that looks straight forward with perfect equanimity — corresponds to the Brahmadrishti of the liberated sage: the gaze that sees everything equally, without preference or aversion, without the distortion of personal desire or fear. The most contracted Drishti — the concentrated gaze of intense inner focus — corresponds to the concentrated awareness of deep philosophical inquiry. And the most expansive Drishti — the gaze that encompasses the entire visual field without focusing on any particular element — corresponds to the spacious, panoramic awareness of the meditative state in which the distinction between the observer and the observed begins to dissolve.

The specific Drishti associated with each Karana is not arbitrary but encodes the philosophical quality of that Karana’s

278
The Cosmic Choreography

consciousness. The elevated Karanas of the Urdhva group are associated with an upward, sky-directed gaze that embodies the aspiration toward transcendence. The grounded Bhumi Karanas are associated with a downward or forward gaze that embodies the quality of presence and earthly engagement. The spinning, transformative Karanas are associated with a soft, unfocused gaze that embodies the quality of consciousness in transition, between states. And the Shanta Karanas — those most elevated, most peaceful movements that embody the quality of Brahman-recognition — are associated with the Sama Drishti, the equal gaze that looks at the world with perfect equanimity and luminous clarity.

Shankaracharya’s description in the Soundarya Lahari of the Divine Mother’s gaze — which he describes as a gaze so luminous and compassionate that it simultaneously illuminates everything it touches and leaves it entirely free — is the devotional counterpart to the philosophical analysis of Brahmadrishti. The Goddess looks at the world with the gaze of pure consciousness: seeing everything with perfect clarity, touched by everything she sees, disturbed by nothing, drawn toward nothing, repelled by nothing. This gaze is the ideal Sama Drishti of the classical dance tradition: the gaze of a consciousness so completely at home in itself that it can be fully present to every experience without being captured by any of it. The dancer who achieves this quality of gaze in her performance has achieved, in the medium of embodied practice, what Shankaracharya describes in the medium of philosophical analysis: the quality of awareness that is the natural expression of the non-dual recognition of Brahman.

279
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

10.16Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Ten

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

280
The Cosmic Choreography

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana,

281
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The

282
The Cosmic Choreography

scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

10.19The Gesture as Philosophical Statement

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated

283
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

284
The Cosmic Choreography

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

285
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

10.20Ritual Context and Temple Practice

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S.

286
The Cosmic Choreography

Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate.
