The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in

287
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily

288
The Cosmic Choreography

selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

10.6The Feet and Their Sacred Significance in Dance and Philosophy

The philosophical significance of the feet in both the Natya Shastra tradition and Shankaracharya’s philosophy deserves dedicated treatment beyond what the earlier analysis of the Pada component of the Karanas provided. In both traditions, the feet occupy a position of extraordinary symbolic and philosophical importance that goes well beyond their functional role in grounding and moving the body through space.

In the Natya Shastra tradition, the feet are not merely the body’s contact point with the ground but the primary

289
Mudra, Hasta, and the Language of Consciousness

instruments through which rhythmic communication between the dancer and the earth — and, through the earth, with the cosmic ground of being — is established and maintained. The Natya Shastra’s description of the Tala as arising from the clapping of hands and stamping of feet situates rhythm in the body’s relationship to both space (the air that the hands strike) and earth (the ground that the feet stamp). The dancer’s feet, in this understanding, are instruments of cosmic communion: through the rhythmic striking of the earth, the dancer participates in the cosmic rhythm that the Tala cycle encodes.

Shankaracharya’s tradition assigns profound philosophical significance to the feet of the divine figures described in its devotional literature. The feet of the Guru are the primary object of veneration in the Advaita tradition: Guru Paduka (the sandals of the teacher) are revered as the most direct material expression of the teacher’s presence, and the act of placing one’s head at the teacher’s feet (Pranipata) is the primary expression of the student’s surrendered receptivity to the transmission of Brahman-vidya. This veneration of the divine and guru feet is not superstition but philosophical practice: the feet, as the lowest and most humble part of the body, represent the principle of complete humility and complete receptivity — the quality of consciousness that has completely surrendered the ego’s elevation and pretension and is ready to receive the grace that liberates.

The feet of Shiva’s Nataraja icon embody both the philosophical significance of the feet in the performance tradition and the theological significance they carry in the Shankaracharya tradition. The right foot treads on Apasmara — the dwarf of

290
The Cosmic Choreography

ignorance — while the left foot is raised in the transcendent Urdhva Tandava position. The right foot is the foot of engagement, of presence, of the Guru who stands in the world to teach; the left foot is the foot of liberation, of transcendence, of the consciousness that has risen free from the grip of ignorance. Together, they embody the complete philosophical path: complete engagement with the world of experience (the right foot standing firm) combined with complete freedom from identification with it (the left foot raised free). The dancer who performs the Urdhva-Janu Karana with genuine understanding is embodying this complete path in her own body — one foot firmly grounded in the present moment of performance, the other raised in the recognition of the infinite freedom that is the deepest nature of the consciousness performing it.

291
CHAPTER XI

Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

“In the beginning was Nada — the primordial sound. All rhythm is its remembering; all silence, its origin.”

— Nada Bindu Upanishad

11.1Nada Brahman: The Universe as Sound

The concept of Nada Brahman — the universe as primordial sound, Brahman as the ground of all vibration — occupies a central position in Indian metaphysics that has no precise equivalent in Western philosophical traditions. The Nada Bindu Upanishad, one of the Yoga Upanishads particularly revered in musical and meditative traditions, begins with the statement 'Nada brahma' — sound is Brahman — and proceeds to describe the entire cosmos as a manifestation of sound at progressively grosser levels of vibration. The Aum (Om) — the primordial sound that precedes all other sounds — is understood not merely as a symbol of Brahman but as its direct sonic manifestation: to hear Aum

292
The Cosmic Choreography

in its deepest dimension, through sustained meditative practice, is to hear Brahman.

Shankaracharya was deeply attentive to this sonic dimension of reality, as evidenced by the extraordinary prosodic sophistication of his poetry and by his philosophical analysis of the relationship between sound (Shabda) and meaning (Artha) in his Vedantic commentary tradition. His analysis of Vedic Shabda — the eternal, uncreated, self-luminous sound of the Vedas — parallels his analysis of Brahman itself: just as Brahman is not created but self-existent, not dependent on anything outside itself for its existence, the eternal Shabda of the Vedas is understood as the direct manifestation of Brahman in the medium of sound, prior to any human act of composition or recitation.

This understanding of sound as a direct manifestation of Brahman has profound implications for the relationship between music, dance, and philosophy in the Indian tradition. The Natya Shastra’s insistence on the inseparability of dance and music — that the Karanas are not silent visual forms but movement arising from and sustained by rhythmic sound — reflects this metaphysical understanding. The relationship between the dancer’s movement (Nritta) and the musician’s sound (Sangita) is not merely the practical relationship of coordination but the ontological relationship of Shakti and Shiva: movement is the visible expression of what sound is the audible expression of — the same primordial vibration of consciousness manifesting in two different sensory media simultaneously.

The concept of Nada in the performance context goes beyond the audible dimension of music to include the inaudible, inner

293
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

sound that the practitioner attends to in deep states of meditative absorption. The Nada Yoga tradition — the tradition of using inner sound as the primary object of meditative attention — identifies a hierarchy of increasingly subtle inner sounds, beginning with the Anahata (unstruck) sound that arises spontaneously in deep meditation as a continuous, self-sustaining vibration, and progressing through progressively subtler levels until the meditator arrives at the Para Nada — the supreme sound, which is indistinguishable from the silence of pure consciousness itself.

The practitioner of classical dance who has developed the inner dimension of her practice will recognise this Nada dimension in the experience of peak performance. At the highest levels of absorption in the dance, the external sounds of the accompanying music are no longer experienced as coming from outside but as arising simultaneously with and from within the movement itself — as if the movement and the music are both expressions of the same inner vibration, the same Nada that is the ground of both. This experience — which many great dancers and musicians describe in strikingly similar terms, across different traditions and cultural contexts — is the experiential basis for the Natya Shastra’s metaphysical claim that Natya arises from the five Vedas and embodies the primordial Nada from which all creation emerges.

294
The Cosmic Choreography

11.2Tala as Cosmic Rhythm and Liberation

Tala — the rhythmic cycle that organises the temporal dimension of Indian classical music and dance — is one of the most philosophically rich concepts in the entire Natya Shastra tradition. The word itself has two primary meanings: the palm of the hand (as in the striking or clapping that originally marked rhythm) and the rhythmic cycle of music. This double meaning reveals the embodied basis of Indian rhythmic theory: rhythm is not an abstract temporal structure imposed from outside the performance but an event arising from the meeting of the human body (the clapping hand) with the musical fabric.

The structure of Tala in classical Indian music is fundamentally cyclic: a Tala consists of a specific number of beats arranged in a recurring pattern, and the performance proceeds through repeated cycles of this pattern indefinitely. This cyclic structure — fundamentally different from the linear temporality of most Western music — has profound philosophical implications. In a Tala-governed performance, time does not simply pass; it recurs. Each cycle of the Tala is a return to the starting point (Sam, the 'one' of the rhythmic cycle) — a recapitulation of the beginning in the context of everything that has happened since the last Sam. This structure of return — of moving through complexity back to simplicity, through development back to origin — mirrors the philosophical structure that Shankaracharya describes as the movement of liberation: moving through the apparent complexity of the world

295
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

of Maya back to the simple, luminous ground of Brahman that was always the starting point.

The moment of Sam in Indian classical music — the meeting point of the melodic and rhythmic cycles, the 'one' where everything comes together — is perhaps the most celebrated moment in the entire tradition of classical Indian performance. The dancer and musician who arrive at Sam simultaneously, after navigating the complex rhythmic and melodic pathways that have led away from and back to this point, experience a moment of resolution, of completion, of absolute rightness that the tradition associates with the aesthetic of Shanta Rasa and the philosophical recognition of Brahman. This is not a momentary event but a recurring one: Sam returns again and again, with increasing depth and richness as the performance develops, each return deepening the understanding of the original simplicity that it embodies.

Shankaracharya’s analysis of the three states of consciousness — waking (Jagrat), dreaming (Svapna), and deep sleep (Sushupti) — and the fourth state (Turiya) that underlies and permeates the other three, finds a precise analogy in the structure of Tala. The beats of the Tala cycle correspond to the various states of manifest experience; the Sam corresponds to the moment of pure, undivided consciousness that underlies and connects all states; and Turiya — the fourth, the ever-present ground — corresponds to the continuous pulse of the Tala itself, the rhythmic breath of consciousness that sustains the entire performance from beginning to end without itself being any particular beat or any particular moment.

296
The Cosmic Choreography

The philosophical significance of Tala for the 108 Karanas is that the Karanas are not merely spatial forms (configurations of the body in space) but temporal forms (configurations of consciousness in time). A Karana executed in one Tala context will have a completely different philosophical quality than the same Karana executed in a different Tala context, because the relationship between the specific movement-configuration and the recurring rhythmic cycle in which it is embedded determines its temporal meaning — its significance as a particular moment in the cycle of cosmic time. The complete mastery of the Karana system thus requires not merely spatial mastery (the ability to produce each Karana’s physical form with precision) but temporal mastery (the ability to embed each Karana in its appropriate Tala context and to understand its relationship to the rhythmic cycle of which it is a part).

11.4The 108 Talas and Their Correspondence with the 108 Karanas

The Sangita Ratnakara of Sarngadeva — the thirteenth-century compendium of Indian musical theory that represents the most comprehensive synthesis of the classical music and dance tradition — specifies 108 Talas as the complete vocabulary of rhythmic organisation, just as the Natya Shastra specifies 108 Karanas as the complete vocabulary of movement. This numerical identity is not coincidental: both systems are understood to be complete expressions of the same

297
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

cosmic musical consciousness in different media — one in sound/time, the other in movement/space.

The correspondence between specific Talas and specific Karanas, while not formally specified in either text, emerges naturally from the philosophical framework they share. The most fundamental rhythmic cycles — Adi Tala (the primary eight-beat cycle), Rupaka Tala (the six-beat cycle), and Khanda Chapu (the asymmetric five-beat cycle) — correspond to the most fundamental Karana groups in ways that are immediately apparent to the experienced practitioner. Adi Tala’s stable, expansive eight-beat structure corresponds to the grounded, balanced Karanas of the Bhumi group. Rupaka Tala’s more intimate, circular six-beat structure corresponds to the flowing, graceful Karanas of the Lasya group. And Khanda Chapu’s asymmetric, dynamic five-beat structure corresponds to the dynamic, transformative Karanas of the Tirthana group.

The philosophical significance of this correspondence becomes clear when one considers the Indian tradition’s understanding of number as a philosophical category. In the Vedic tradition, specific numbers are not merely quantitative but qualitative: they embody specific qualities of cosmic consciousness. The number eight (Ashta) is associated with the eight directions of space and with the octagonal cosmic geometry that maps the complete range of spatial orientation. The number six (Shad) is associated with the six seasons and with the cyclical completeness of temporal experience. And the number five (Pancha) is associated with the five elements and with the dynamic incompleteness of existence — the quality of always being in

298
The Cosmic Choreography

transition between states — that characterises the world of manifest existence.

When the Adi Tala’s eight-beat structure is combined with the Bhumi Karanas' grounded, spatially oriented quality, the result is a performance event that embodies the complete spatial orientation of the cosmic ground — the stable, all-directional awareness that Shankaracharya associates with the recognition of Brahman as the ground of all spatial experience. When the Rupaka Tala’s six-beat structure is combined with the Lasya Karanas' flowing, cyclic grace, the result embodies the complete temporal cycle of the Divine Mother’s cosmic creative activity — the continuous, graceful, cyclically complete dance of consciousness that the Soundarya Lahari’s wave imagery describes. And when the Khanda Chapu’s five-beat asymmetry is combined with the dynamic Tandava Karanas, the result embodies the dynamic incompleteness of the world process — the quality of always becoming, always transforming, never arriving at a final rest that characterises the Maya-world that Shankara describes as the dance of divine illusion.

The practical implication of this tala-karana correspondence for the performer is that the choice of Tala in which to perform a particular Karana is not merely an aesthetic decision but a philosophical one: each Tala-Karana combination embodies a specific quality of cosmic consciousness, and the performer’s understanding of this quality is what determines whether the performance is merely technically correct or genuinely philosophically expressive. The dancer who performs the Urdhva-Janu Karana in the context of Misra Chapu Tala — the

299
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

seven-beat cycle associated with the incomplete, searching quality of a consciousness still striving toward liberation — is making a different philosophical statement than the dancer who performs the same Karana in the context of Adi Tala’s stable, complete eight-beat cycle. Both may be technically correct; only the one who has understood the philosophical significance of the tala-karana relationship is performing in the fullest sense.

11.5Mantra, Svara, and the Sound Body of the Universe

The relationship between mantra (sacred sound formula), svara (musical note), and the universe’s sound body provides another important dimension of the connection between Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition and the Natya Shastra. The Indian philosophical tradition understands the universe as fundamentally constituted by sound: the Sanskrit alphabet’s fifty letters (or fifty-one, in some accounts) are understood as the complete set of the universe’s phonemic elements — the sound-atoms from which all manifest existence is constructed. This understanding is not a scientific hypothesis but a philosophical statement about the relationship between consciousness and its self-expression: the universe’s diversity arises through the same process by which human language arises through the combination of basic phonemic elements.

Shankaracharya’s engagement with this 'sound body' of the universe is extensive and philosophically precise. His commentary

300
The Cosmic Choreography

on the Mandukya Upanishad — which takes the syllable AUM as the sonic symbol of the four states of consciousness and the non-dual ground that underlies them — provides the most systematic account of the relationship between sound, consciousness, and liberation in his corpus. The three sounds that constitute AUM (A, U, M) are understood as corresponding to the three states of consciousness (waking, dreaming, deep sleep), and the silence that precedes, follows, and permeates the syllable — what the Upanishad calls the Amatra or 'immeasurable' — corresponds to the fourth state of pure consciousness that Shankara identifies as the ultimate truth.

This sonic philosophy has direct implications for the relationship between the Natya Shastra’s performance tradition and the non-dual philosophy. If the universe is constituted by sound, and if the human voice and the musical instruments of the classical tradition are vehicles of this same cosmic sound, then the performance event — in which the dancer’s movements arise from and correspond to the vocal and instrumental music — is not merely an aesthetic event but a cosmological one: a moment in which the complete range of cosmic sound-consciousness is made visible in the medium of embodied movement. The 108 Karanas, performed in the context of the complete vocabulary of Indian classical music, are the visual equivalent of the complete Sanskrit alphabet: they complete the sound-world of the performance by giving it visible, bodily form.

Shankaracharya’s own compositions were designed with explicit attention to their sonic dimensions. The Nirvana Shatakam’s use of the repeated phrase 'Shivoham Shivoham' (I

301
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

am Shiva, I am Shiva) at the end of each verse is not merely rhetorical but mantraic: the repetition of the name Shiva (which etymologically means 'that which is auspicious', 'the benevolent one', or, in the Advaitic interpretation, 'pure consciousness itself') is understood as a vehicle of the same recognition that the verse’s intellectual content conveys. The sound of the mantra works directly on consciousness, dissolving the ego’s false identification with limited existence in the same way that philosophical analysis dissolves it intellectually.

The connection between mantra and movement is fully realised in the context of temple ritual, where the dancer’s performance of specific Karanas is coordinated with the recitation of specific mantras by the presiding priest. In this context, the movement and the sound are not merely coordinated aesthetically but are understood as two aspects of a single cosmic act: the invocation of the divine through the complete expression of its nature in both visible (movement) and audible (mantra) form. The Karana and the mantra together constitute a complete sacred act — a moment in which consciousness simultaneously expresses itself in both its visible (Shakti, form, movement) and its audible (Shiva, sound, mantra) dimensions. This complete expression is, in the tradition’s understanding, the most direct possible vehicle of the non-dual recognition that both the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta identify as the ultimate goal of all human practice.

302
The Cosmic Choreography

11.17Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Eleven

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

303
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana,

304
The Cosmic Choreography

moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The

305
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

11.20Rhythm, Time, and the Recognition of Eternity

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the

306
The Cosmic Choreography

aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

307
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

308
The Cosmic Choreography

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

11.21The Theory and Practice of Sacred Sound

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S.

309
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in

310
The Cosmic Choreography

increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily

311
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

11.6The Seven Svaras and Cosmic Consciousness

The seven Svaras (musical notes) of the Indian classical music system — Sa, Ri, Ga, Ma, Pa, Dha, Ni — are not merely acoustic phenomena or arbitrary cultural conventions but, in the Indian philosophical understanding, direct expressions of cosmic consciousness in the medium of sound. The traditional accounts of the origins of the seven Svaras assign each one a specific natural source: Sa arises from the cry of the peacock, Ri from the cry of the chataka bird, Ga from the bleat of the goat, Ma from the cry of the heron, Pa from the song of the kokila (cuckoo), Dha from the neigh of the horse, and Ni from the trumpeting of the

312
The Cosmic Choreography

elephant. These natural origins are not merely poetic but philosophical: they assert that the seven fundamental intervals of the Indian musical system are inherent in the nature of the world, not invented by human musicians but discovered through careful attention to the sound-structure of creation.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition finds in the seven Svaras an expression of the seven-fold structure of consciousness described in the Mandukya Upanishad’s analysis of the syllable AUM. The three letters of AUM (A, U, M) correspond to the three states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, each associated with a specific quality of consciousness and a specific range of musical expression. The Amatra (the unmeasured silence that pervades and underlies the three letters) corresponds to the Turiya — the fourth state of pure consciousness — that the seven Svaras collectively arise from and return to in the complete expression of a musical phrase.

The connection between the seven Svaras and the 108 Karanas is established through the tradition’s understanding that each Karana embodies a specific quality of musical consciousness — a specific 'note' in the cosmic scale of embodied expression. This correspondence is not a simple one-to-one mapping (108 Karanas cannot be simply mapped onto 7 Svaras) but a structural homology: just as the seven Svaras constitute the complete vocabulary of musical consciousness from which all musical phrases are constructed, the 108 Karanas constitute the complete vocabulary of movement consciousness from which all choreographic phrases are constructed. Both vocabularies are complete, both are cosmologically grounded, and both are

313
Sound, Rhythm, and the Metaphysics of Tala

expressions of the same underlying awareness that Shankaracharya identifies as Brahman.

The practical implication of this Svara-Karana correspondence for the classical dancer is the understanding that the musical and movement dimensions of a performance are not separate — not music here and movement there, synchronised externally — but internally unified: the movement is the music made visible, and the music is the movement made audible. This understanding, once genuinely internalised, transforms the entire experience of performance: the dancer does not 'dance to the music' but 'dances as the music', her body becoming the visible form of the same cosmic consciousness that the accompanying instruments express in the medium of sound.

314
CHAPTER XII

The Living Tradition

Contemporary Practice and Transmission

“The tradition is not a museum piece; it is a living fire. Our task is not to preserve ashes but to pass on the flame.”

— Rukmini Devi Arundale, on the Bharatanatyam revival

12.1The Modern Revival and Its Philosophical Dimensions

The twentieth century witnessed a remarkable revival of classical Indian dance traditions that had been suppressed, marginalised, and denigrated during the colonial period. This revival — associated with figures including Rukmini Devi Arundale, E. Krishna Iyer, Balasaraswati, Yamini Krishnamurti, and many others — was not merely a restoration of artistic practice but a philosophical project: the reclaiming and reaffirmation of the spiritual and philosophical dimensions of classical performance that the colonial context had systematically denied. The colonial administration and its missionary allies had consistently portrayed classical Indian dance as either decadent

315
The Living Tradition

sensuality or superstitious ritual, systematically stripping it of the philosophical and spiritual significance that the Natya Shastra tradition and the Advaita Vedanta tradition had consistently attributed to it.

The revival’s philosophical dimension is most clearly visible in its explicit appeal to the authority of the Natya Shastra. Rukmini Devi Arundale’s founding of the Kalakshetra Foundation in 1936 was conceived explicitly as a project of reconstructing classical Bharatanatyam in accordance with the principles of the Natya Shastra — which she understood as a sacred text of the highest philosophical authority, equivalent in her view to the Upanishads. Her training at the feet of the great masters of the Pandanallur style gave her access to a living transmission of the tradition; her study of the Natya Shastra and related texts gave her the philosophical framework within which to understand that transmission. The combination produced a form of Bharatanatyam that was simultaneously technically rigorous, aesthetically refined, and philosophically grounded in the Advaitic tradition.

The explicit connection between Bharatanatyam revival and Advaita Vedanta was also developed by E. Krishna Iyer, the lawyer and dance enthusiast whose public performances of Bharatanatyam in the 1930s were a landmark in the tradition’s legitimisation. In his writings and lectures, Krishna Iyer consistently argued that classical Indian dance was a form of Yoga — a systematic path of self-discipline and awareness that, when practised with full understanding of its philosophical dimensions, could lead to the same liberation that the Vedantic tradition

316
The Cosmic Choreography

described through philosophical inquiry. This argument — that classical dance is a form of Nritya Yoga, a path to liberation through the medium of embodied movement — is precisely the argument that this entire book has been developing through its analysis of the Natya Shastra, the 108 Karanas, and Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition.

The figure of Balasaraswati deserves particular attention in this context because she represents a different and equally important strand of the revival: not the systematic reconstruction of the tradition in accordance with textual authority, but the living transmission of a practice whose philosophical depth was inseparable from its embodied immediacy. Balasaraswati’s dance — which she explicitly connected to the Bhakti tradition of devotion and to the Rasa theory of Abhinavagupta — was understood by her not as a restoration of historical forms but as a living expression of the eternal truth that the tradition had always transmitted. Her insistence that the greatest dance could not be taught from texts but only through the living encounter between teacher and student, body to body, heart to heart, is the clearest possible expression of the Guru-Shishya Parampara principle that is central to both the Natya Shastra and the Advaita Vedanta traditions.

The tension between Rukmini Devi’s textually grounded, systematically reconstructed approach and Balasaraswati’s orally transmitted, experientially immediate approach is not merely a historical debate but a philosophical one, reflecting the perennial tension in Indian intellectual culture between Shastra (authoritative text) and Sampradaya (living transmission).

317
The Living Tradition

Shankaracharya himself navigated this tension with characteristic subtlety: his voluminous commentaries on the major Vedantic texts demonstrate his commitment to textual authority and systematic philosophical analysis, while his devotional poetry and his establishment of the four cardinal Mathas (monasteries) demonstrate his equally strong commitment to living transmission, to the personal encounter between teacher and student that no text can replace.

12.2Padma Subrahmanyam and the Reconstruction of the 108 Karanas

Among the contemporary scholars and practitioners who have contributed most significantly to the understanding of the 108 Karanas, Padma Subrahmanyam occupies a position of unique importance. Her decades-long research project — combining meticulous philological analysis of the Natya Shastra, intensive study of the Chidambaram and Thanjavur sculptural programmes, and systematic practical reconstruction of the Karanas' physical form through her own training and teaching practice — produced the monumental two-volume work Karanas: Common Dance Codes of India and Indonesia (1997), which remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the Karana system available in English.

Subrahmanyam’s work demonstrates, with exhaustive scholarly and practical evidence, that the 108 Karanas as described in the Natya Shastra and as depicted in the South

318
The Cosmic Choreography

Indian temple sculptures are not merely historical artefacts but living possibilities — that they can be reconstructed, performed, and transmitted in the present, and that their philosophical and aesthetic qualities are as alive and relevant today as they were when Bharata Muni first codified them. Her choreographic works based on the Karanas — including the landmark production Margam, performed internationally from the 1970s onward — have brought the Karana system to the attention of audiences worldwide and have demonstrated, through performance, that the Karanas are not arcane museum pieces but vital, expressive, philosophically charged movement events capable of communicating across cultural and linguistic boundaries.

The philosophical dimensions of Subrahmanyam’s reconstruction project are as significant as its technical achievements. Her work consistently emphasises that the Karanas are not merely physical forms but embodied philosophical statements — that to perform a Karana correctly requires not merely the correct physical configuration but the correct quality of inner awareness, the correct relationship between the practitioner’s consciousness and the movement she is executing. This emphasis on the inner dimension of the Karanas — their quality as forms of embodied awareness rather than merely mechanical movement patterns — reflects precisely the understanding of the tradition that this study has been developing through its analysis of the relationship between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy.

Subrahmanyam’s discovery of the correspondence between the 108 Karanas of the Natya Shastra and the movement

319
The Living Tradition

vocabulary of classical Balinese and Javanese dance — a discovery that led to the comparative study published in her two-volume work — has important philosophical implications beyond its art historical significance. The fact that the same movement vocabulary appears in substantially identical form in traditions separated by thousands of miles of ocean and centuries of independent cultural development suggests that the Karanas are not culturally contingent but point toward something genuinely universal in the human experience of embodied consciousness. This universality is precisely what one would expect if the Karanas are, as this study argues, a map of the complete range of possibilities available to human consciousness in its embodied form — a map of something inherent in the human body-mind system rather than something imposed from outside by a particular cultural tradition.

The living practice of the Karana system today, as transmitted through practitioners including Subrahmanyam and her students, the Kalakshetra tradition, the various lineages of Bharatanatyam, Kuchipudi, and Odissi, and the temple traditions of South India, represents the most direct and authentic way of engaging with the philosophical synthesis that this book has been tracing. No amount of textual analysis or art historical study can substitute for the experience of moving through the Karanas with a teacher who has genuinely internalised their philosophical dimensions — the experience of inhabiting, from inside, the specific quality of consciousness-in-movement that each Karana embodies. This experiential dimension is what the tradition has always called Anubhava —

320
The Cosmic Choreography

direct experience — and it is what both the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy identify as the deepest level of knowledge: not knowledge about Brahman but knowledge as Brahman.

12.4Kalakshetra and the Philosophical Training of the Classical Dancer

The Kalakshetra Foundation, established by Rukmini Devi Arundale in Adyar, Chennai in 1936, represents the most sustained modern institutional attempt to realise the philosophical dimensions of classical Indian dance that the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s tradition have always claimed for it. Rukmini Devi’s founding vision was explicitly philosophical as well as artistic: she understood the Bharatanatyam she was systematising and teaching not merely as a refined artistic form but as a path of self-development and ultimately of spiritual realisation — a path that she described, in language directly reminiscent of both the Natya Shastra and the Advaita Vedanta tradition, as a form of Yoga.

The Kalakshetra curriculum, as developed by Rukmini Devi and subsequently refined by successive generations of teachers, integrates technical training in the Bharatanatyam vocabulary (including the Karana-based Nritta elements) with training in music, Sanskrit, Indian philosophy, and the devotional traditions of the classical arts. This integration is not merely cosmetic — a superficial addition of 'cultural content' to a primarily technical

321
The Living Tradition

training — but reflects a genuine understanding that the technical and philosophical dimensions of the tradition are inseparable. A dancer who does not understand the philosophical significance of the gestures she is executing cannot execute them with the quality that the tradition requires; conversely, a philosopher who does not understand the technical dimensions of the tradition cannot fully appreciate its philosophical depth.

The specific engagement of the Kalakshetra curriculum with the Shankaracharya tradition is visible in several dimensions. The devotional compositions of the Shankaracharya tradition — particularly the Soundarya Lahari, the Dakshinamurti Stotra, and the various stotras associated with the Sringeri Peetham — form an important part of the musical and devotional training at Kalakshetra. The philosophical framework provided by Advaita Vedanta is regularly invoked in the school’s teaching to explain the deeper significance of specific Karana executions, gesture sequences, and performance traditions. And the tradition of seeking the guidance of philosophical teachers from the Shankaracharya Mathas for the interpretation of difficult classical compositions has been maintained throughout the school’s history.

The specific contribution of Kalakshetra to the synthesis traced in this book is its demonstration that the philosophical dimensions of the classical tradition are not abstract theoretical claims but practical realities that can be transmitted through a living training programme. The dancers who have emerged from the Kalakshetra tradition — including figures such as Leela Samson, Anita Ratnam, and many others — have consistently

322
The Cosmic Choreography

demonstrated in their performances and their teachings that the philosophical depth of the classical tradition is not merely a historical attribute of a distant past but a living quality of contemporary practice. Their work has shown that the 108 Karanas, performed with full understanding of their philosophical dimensions within the training framework that Kalakshetra developed, do indeed produce the quality of performance that the Natya Shastra describes and that Shankaracharya’s tradition celebrates: a performance that is simultaneously technically rigorous, aesthetically beautiful, and spiritually illuminating.

The Kalakshetra model has influenced numerous other classical dance institutions across India and internationally, creating a network of institutions that collectively embody the philosophical synthesis this book traces. The Nrityagram Dance Village near Bangalore, the Attakkalari Centre for Movement Arts, the Natyarangam of the Chidambaram Nataraja Temple Trust, and many other institutions have each developed their own versions of a training programme that integrates technical excellence with philosophical understanding and devotional depth. The diversity of these institutional expressions reflects the same diversity that characterised the classical tradition’s historical development across multiple regional contexts — while the underlying unity reflects the same unity that the Advaita Vedanta tradition claims for the non-dual consciousness that underlies all apparent diversity.

323
The Living Tradition

12.5Digital Transmission and the Future of the Living Tradition

The digital revolution has created new possibilities and new challenges for the transmission of classical Indian dance traditions. On the positive side, digital technology has made possible a degree of documentation, preservation, and global dissemination of classical performance that would have been unimaginable a generation ago. High-definition video documentation of great masters' performances, online teaching platforms that connect students with teachers across geographical boundaries, and digital archives of notated Karana forms and their corresponding temple sculptures have all contributed to widening access to the classical tradition.

On the challenging side, the digital transmission of classical Indian dance raises profound questions about the relationship between embodied knowledge and its representation, between the living transmission of a tradition through the guru-shishya relationship and the necessarily partial, mediated transmission that digital media can provide. The Karana, as we have argued throughout this book, is not merely a physical form that can be captured in a video recording but a psychophysical event — a specific quality of unified consciousness-in-movement — whose essential quality cannot be fully transmitted through any representational medium, however sophisticated. This limitation of digital transmission is not a technological problem that better technology will eventually solve but a philosophical one: it reflects

324
The Cosmic Choreography

the fundamental nature of embodied knowledge as something that can only be fully transmitted through the direct encounter of bodies and consciousnesses.

Shankaracharya’s tradition makes an exactly analogous point about the limitations of textual transmission for the knowledge of Brahman. The texts of Advaita Vedanta — however sophisticated, however precisely articulated — can provide the intellectual framework and the conceptual vocabulary for understanding the non-dual truth, but they cannot transmit the direct experience of that truth. For that, the tradition insists, one needs a living teacher — a Brahma-nishtha Guru, a teacher who has themselves realised the truth — whose presence, teaching, and transmission can catalyse in the student the direct recognition that the texts can only prepare for. The text and the digital recording are analogous: both can prepare the ground, but neither can substitute for the direct encounter.

The most productive use of digital technology in the context of classical Indian dance transmission is therefore not as a substitute for the guru-shishya relationship but as a supplement to it: creating resources that can extend the reach of a living teacher’s transmission, preserve the forms of great masters' performances for study and contemplation, and provide theoretical frameworks that help students understand the philosophical dimensions of what they are learning in the embodied context. Digital archives of the Chidambaram Karana panels, computer-based reconstructions of specific Karanas from their sculptural representations, and online databases of the philosophical literature relevant to the tradition can all serve this

325
The Living Tradition

supplementary function without pretending to replace the irreplaceable living encounter.

The emergence of international networks of classical Indian dance practitioners and scholars — enabled in large part by digital communication technology — represents perhaps the most significant contribution of the digital revolution to the living tradition. These networks facilitate the exchange of knowledge, the comparison of regional traditions, the collaborative development of new choreographic work informed by traditional principles, and the construction of scholarly frameworks for understanding the tradition’s philosophical depth. They create, in effect, a global community of practice that embodies the same principle of unity-in-diversity that Advaita Vedanta describes philosophically: many practitioners, many traditions, many approaches — but all ultimately expressions of the same fundamental insight that the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy both articulate: that consciousness is one, that it expresses itself through the full range of human creative capacity, and that the highest human art is the one that makes this unity most transparently visible.

12.18Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Twelve

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The

326
The Cosmic Choreography

relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but

327
The Living Tradition

deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana, moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient

328
The Cosmic Choreography

alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same

329
The Living Tradition

recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

12.21The Tradition Speaks: Voices of Living Masters

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not

330
The Cosmic Choreography

separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by

331
The Living Tradition

reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human

332
The Cosmic Choreography

consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

12.22Training Methodologies Across Traditions

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical

333
The Living Tradition

relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the

334
The Cosmic Choreography

two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple

335
The Living Tradition

sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

12.6The Devadasi Tradition: Philosophical Analysis

The Devadasi tradition — through which women were dedicated to specific temple deities and understood their performance as both divine service and spiritual practice — has been the subject of intense scholarly, political, and social debate over the past century. The tradition’s suppression through colonial-era anti-nautch legislation and subsequent legal prohibition, followed by its rehabilitation in the scholarly literature as a sophisticated institution of sacred performance, reflects the complex politics of knowledge about the body, gender, and religious practice that have shaped both colonial and postcolonial engagements with Indian culture.

For the argument of this book, the most important dimension of the Devadasi tradition is its philosophical self-understanding as expressed in the textual and oral traditions preserved by Devadasi lineages. The Devadasi’s relationship to her patron deity was understood not merely as one of service but of identity: she was the deity’s consort, the living embodiment of the divine feminine principle that the Goddess represented, the human vehicle

336
The Cosmic Choreography

through whom the Goddess’s own dance was performed in the earthly realm. This understanding is directly continuous with the philosophical framework developed by Shankaracharya in the Soundarya Lahari: the Divine Mother’s dance through the medium of a consecrated human instrument is not a metaphor but an ontological reality, made possible by the complete dissolution of the individual performer’s ego in the larger consciousness of the divine.

The philosophical training that was part of the traditional Devadasi curriculum is documented in several texts from the Thanjavur and Tanjore courts, where the most refined forms of the tradition were maintained under royal patronage. This training included not only the technical dimensions of dance and music but systematic instruction in Sanskrit, in the philosophical traditions of Shaivism and Vaishnavism, and in the devotional literature of the Alvar and Nayanar saints. The Devadasi was expected to be not merely a technically accomplished performer but a philosophical practitioner — one who understood the tradition’s deepest dimensions and could embody them in performance.

The philosophical significance of this integrated training — combining technical mastery with philosophical understanding and devotional sincerity — is that it represents the most complete historical realisation of the synthesis this book traces. In the fully trained Devadasi practitioner, the 108 Karanas' technical vocabulary, Shankaracharya’s philosophical framework, and the devotional traditions of the temple were not separate dimensions of a complex training but aspects of a single, integrated practice of

337
The Living Tradition

sacred embodied knowledge.
