Whatever the social and ethical complexities of the institutional framework within which this integration occurred, the philosophical achievement it embodied remains significant: it demonstrates that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Advaita Vedanta is not merely a theoretical possibility but had actual historical expression in the lives and practices of real human beings who understood their embodied creative work as a path of liberation.

CHAPTER XIII

Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

“Every great dance tradition has discovered, through its own unique path, the same fundamental truth: that the body in motion can become transparent to the infinite.”

— Rudolf Laban, The Mastery of Movement

13.1Sacred Dance Across Traditions

The convergence of philosophy and performance that this study has traced in the Indian tradition is by no means unique to that tradition. Across cultures and centuries, the world’s great religious and philosophical traditions have discovered in dance and embodied movement a uniquely powerful vehicle for spiritual transformation and philosophical insight. The ancient Greek tradition of choral dance in the service of Dionysus and Apollo understood the dancing body as the site of divine possession and divine revelation; the Sufi whirling meditation of the Mevlevi tradition, instituted by Rumi in the thirteenth century, understands the turning movement of the

339
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

Sama as a direct participation in the cosmic rotation of the stars and the soul’s rotation around the divine axis; the sacred dances of the Balinese and Javanese traditions, as we have noted, share their fundamental movement vocabulary with the Indian Karana system. In each of these traditions, the dancing body is understood not merely as an aesthetic spectacle but as a sacred instrument — a vehicle through which the divine expresses itself and through which the dancer and audience can access dimensions of experience not available through ordinary, undisciplined bodily existence.

The philosophical frameworks developed to explain and justify the spiritual significance of sacred dance vary enormously across these traditions, reflecting the different metaphysical assumptions and cultural contexts of each. Yet beneath this philosophical diversity, a remarkable convergence of practical insight can be observed: across traditions, the most profound descriptions of the highest state of sacred dance describe a condition of simultaneous full engagement and complete freedom — a condition in which the dancer is maximally present and maximally free, fully inhabiting the movement and yet not bound by it, performing and yet also purely witnessing the performance. This condition — which Western psychology would call 'flow' and Indian philosophy would call Sakshi awareness or Jivanmukti — appears to be a genuine possibility of human consciousness that multiple traditions have independently discovered and systematically cultivated through the medium of sacred dance.

340
The Cosmic Choreography

The Sufi tradition of Sama (spiritual listening) and the associated practice of the whirling dance of the Mevlevi dervishes provides perhaps the most striking cross-cultural parallel to the Natya Shastra’s tradition of sacred performance. Rumi’s famous metaphor of the reed flute — the reed that cries for the reed bed from which it was cut — is a sonic analogy for precisely the condition that the Natya Shastra’s Sattvika Abhinaya describes: the performer in whom the inner longing (Bhava) has become so intense and authentic that it bursts through the technical form and creates an involuntary, uncontrolled expression of genuine spiritual yearning. The reed’s cry is Rumi’s Sattvika Abhinaya: the involuntary, authentic expression of genuine inner state that distinguishes the truly great performance from the merely competent one.

The Japanese Noh theatre tradition, which developed in the fourteenth century under the influence of the philosopher-aesthetician Zeami Motokiyo, offers another compelling parallel. Zeami’s concept of Hana (flower) — the ineffable quality of the greatest Noh performance that cannot be reduced to technique but must arise spontaneously from the full integration of technique, inner state, and transmitted wisdom — corresponds closely to the Natya Shastra’s concept of Sattvika Abhinaya and to Shankaracharya’s concept of Sahaja (the natural, spontaneous quality of consciousness that has recognised its own nature). Zeami’s insistence that the Hana quality cannot be taught directly but can only emerge from sustained practice under the right conditions parallels both Bharata’s understanding of the highest levels of performance

341
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

and Shankara’s understanding of the highest levels of philosophical realisation.

The African traditions of sacred dance — including the Vodou traditions of Haiti and West Africa, the Ngoma traditions of East and Southern Africa, and the various traditions of ritual dance associated with initiation ceremonies across the continent — represent a domain of embodied spiritual practice that Western scholarship has only recently begun to take seriously as philosophy. In these traditions, the highest states of dance are understood as states of divine possession — conditions in which the individual dancer’s ordinary consciousness is displaced by a divine or ancestral consciousness that moves and speaks through the dancer’s body. This model of possession is different in important respects from the Indian model of the Sakshi (pure witness) or the Advaitic model of Jivanmukti (liberation in life), but it shares with both the fundamental insight that the most profound states of dance involve a qualitative transformation of ordinary consciousness — not merely a skilled execution of learned movements but a fundamental shift in the quality of the awareness inhabiting and expressing itself through the moving body.

342
The Cosmic Choreography

13.2The 108 Karanas in Indonesian Dance: A Cross-Cultural Confirmation

The most directly relevant cross-cultural parallel for our study — and one of the most important discoveries in twentieth-century dance scholarship — is Padma Subrahmanyam’s demonstration of the correspondence between the 108 Karanas of the Natya Shastra and the classical dance traditions of Bali and Java in Indonesia. The cultural contact between India and Southeast Asia during the first millennium CE was extensive and well documented; Indian traders, scholars, and missionaries carried the texts, practices, and philosophical frameworks of the Indian tradition to the islands of what is now Indonesia, where they took root and developed in dialogue with existing indigenous traditions over many centuries.

Subrahmanyam’s comparative analysis, which formed the basis of her landmark publication Karanas: Common Dance Codes of India and Indonesia, demonstrates that the fundamental movement vocabulary of the Balinese Legong, the Balinese Baris, the Balinese Topeng, and the Javanese Wayang Wong and Serimpi traditions corresponds, at a deep structural level, to the Karana vocabulary of the Natya Shastra. The correspondence is not a matter of superficial stylistic similarity but of fundamental structural identity: the same combinations of foot position, leg movement, and hand gesture appear in both traditions, identified by cognate names and associated with cognate philosophical and spiritual meanings.

343
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

This cross-cultural confirmation has important philosophical implications. If the same movement vocabulary appears in substantially identical form in traditions separated by thousands of miles and centuries of independent cultural development, this is strong evidence that the vocabulary is not merely a cultural convention but reflects something more fundamental in human embodied experience. The Karanas, this evidence suggests, are not arbitrary cultural codes but genuine discoveries — systematic codifications of movement possibilities inherent in the human body-mind system that have been independently recognised and cultivated in multiple traditions.

The Balinese case is particularly instructive because the Balinese tradition has maintained the explicit connection between dance and Hindu philosophical practice to a degree that mainland Indian dance traditions, disrupted by colonial suppression and the forced separation of temple performance from its religious context, have had to laboriously reconstruct. In Bali, classical dance continues to be performed primarily in the temple context, as an offering to the gods — precisely the context for which the Natya Shastra specifies the Karanas. The Balinese dancer who performs the Legong or the Baris in the temple precincts is performing the same ontological act that the Devadasi of the South Indian temple performed before the colonial disruption of that tradition: offering the body as a vehicle for divine expression, making the cosmic dance visible in human form.

The philosophical tradition that the Balinese dance is embedded in — a form of Hindu philosophy deeply influenced by

344
The Cosmic Choreography

Advaita Vedanta — provides the most direct cross-cultural confirmation of the thesis that the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition are expressions of the same fundamental understanding. Balinese Hindu philosophy understands the dancer not as an individual artist expressing personal creativity but as a vehicle of divine consciousness — a medium through whom the cosmic dance of the gods becomes visible in the human world. This understanding is precisely the understanding that Shankaracharya’s tradition attributes to the highest level of sacred performance: the condition in which the individual dancer has become transparent to the divine consciousness that moves through her, and in which the distinction between the dancer, the dance, and the witnessed performance has dissolved in the recognition of the single consciousness that is all three.

13.4African and Oceanic Sacred Dance: Alternative Paradigms

The comparative study of sacred dance traditions across cultures reveals that the fundamental insights encoded in the 108 Karanas and articulated in Shankaracharya’s philosophy are not culturally specific but reflect something genuinely universal in the relationship between embodied consciousness and spiritual transformation. While the specific forms, vocabularies, and philosophical frameworks vary enormously across traditions, a comparative analysis reveals consistent structural

345
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

correspondences that point toward a common deep grammar of sacred movement.

The West African traditions of sacred dance — particularly the traditions associated with the Yoruba, Fon, and related cultures of what is now Nigeria, Benin, and surrounding areas — represent one of the world’s most elaborate and philosophically sophisticated systems of sacred embodied practice. The Yoruba tradition’s understanding of the Orisha (divine beings or principles) as forces that can take possession of the trained dancer’s body — making themselves present in human form through the vehicle of the dancer’s consciousness — is structurally analogous to the Indian tradition’s understanding of the Devadasi’s dance as the Goddess’s own dance performed through the medium of a dedicated human instrument.

The Polynesian and Pacific Islander traditions of sacred dance — including the Hawaiian Hula, the Tahitian 'Ori, and the complex dance traditions of Papua New Guinea — represent yet another family of sacred movement traditions that encode philosophical insights in the medium of embodied practice. The Hula tradition’s understanding of movement as a direct communication with the natural and divine forces of the environment — in which specific hand gestures invoke specific natural phenomena (the movement of the ocean, the growth of plants, the flight of birds) — corresponds at a deep level to the Natya Shastra’s understanding of the Hasta vocabulary as a language of consciousness’s relationship to its entire environment, both natural and divine.

346
The Cosmic Choreography

The Aboriginal Australian traditions of sacred dance — the Corroboree ceremonies that encode cosmological knowledge about the Dreamtime in the medium of embodied movement and song — represent perhaps the oldest continuous tradition of sacred dance on earth, with deep roots in a human relationship to embodied cosmic knowledge that predates all the traditions discussed elsewhere in this study. The structural resemblance between the Dreaming’s understanding of the physical landscape as the materialised expression of ancestral consciousness and the Natya Shastra’s understanding of the 108 Karanas as the materialised expression of Shiva’s cosmic dance is striking, suggesting that the fundamental insight connecting embodied movement to the deepest structures of cosmic consciousness may be genuinely archaic — a recognition that human beings have arrived at independently across vastly different cultural contexts throughout history.

The lesson of these cross-cultural comparisons for the main argument of this book is clear: the synthesis between the Natya Shastra’s performance theory and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta that this book traces is not merely a specific cultural achievement of the Indian tradition but an expression of something more fundamental in the relationship between consciousness, embodied movement, and the recognition of the non-dual ground of existence. The Indian tradition’s achievement is not to have discovered this insight — which has been independently discovered in virtually every human culture that has developed a sophisticated tradition of sacred practice — but to have articulated it with the greatest philosophical precision and

347
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

technical elaboration ever achieved in any culture. The 108 Karanas represent the most systematic, most philosophically elaborated, and most technically refined codification of the insight that sacred movement can be a vehicle of the highest truth — an achievement that deserves to be understood not merely as a regional cultural heritage but as a contribution to the universal human understanding of consciousness, embodiment, and liberation.

13.5The Philosophy of Form: Indian Aesthetics in Global Perspective

The question of why form matters — why the precise configuration of the hands in the Talapushpaputa Karana, or the exact angle of the raised knee in the Urdhva-Janu, or the specific direction of the gaze in the Gajahasta is philosophically important rather than merely technically precise — is one that any thoughtful student of the classical tradition must eventually confront. The Indian aesthetic tradition’s answer to this question is philosophically sophisticated and has implications that extend far beyond the domain of dance.

The fundamental principle is that form is not separate from meaning but is its embodiment. In the Western philosophical tradition, there is a persistent tendency to understand meaning as a property of mental states (beliefs, intentions, concepts) and form as an external expression of those mental states — a 'vehicle' for meaning that is, in principle, replaceable by any other vehicle

348
The Cosmic Choreography

that expresses the same meaning. On this view, the precise form of the Talapushpaputa Karana is a cultural convention, one of many possible ways of expressing the meaning 'devotional offering', and a different gesture that expressed the same meaning would be equally valid.

The Indian aesthetic tradition rejects this sharp distinction between form and meaning at the highest levels of artistic practice. For the Natya Shastra tradition and for Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition alike, the specific form of the Talapushpaputa Karana is not merely a vehicle for the meaning 'devotional offering' but the specific configuration of consciousness-in-movement in which the quality of devotional offering is most completely and precisely embodied. The form does not merely express the meaning; it is the meaning — the direct, non-representational embodiment of a specific quality of consciousness in the medium of physical gesture.

This philosophical position — that form and meaning are ultimately identical at the highest levels of artistic and philosophical expression — is the aesthetic counterpart of Shankaracharya’s metaphysical claim that Brahman and its manifestation are ultimately identical: that the world of form is not separate from the formless absolute but is its direct expression, identical with it at the ultimate level. Just as the world’s forms are not separate from Brahman (which would imply a real dualism) but Brahman’s own self-expression in the medium of Maya, so the forms of the 108 Karanas are not separate from the philosophical meanings they embody but the direct expression of those meanings in the medium of embodied movement.

349
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

This identity of form and meaning in the Karana tradition is what gives classical Indian dance its unique philosophical status. It is not merely a vehicle for philosophical ideas that could equally well be expressed through other vehicles; it is a form of philosophical practice in its own right — a way of thinking with the body that accesses dimensions of philosophical understanding that thinking with concepts alone cannot reach. The student who learns the Talapushpaputa Karana through the guru-shishya relationship — who inhabits the form with the full quality of awareness that the tradition requires — is not merely learning a technique or illustrating a concept but cultivating a specific quality of conscious being: the quality of devotional offering, of the self extending toward the divine with open, unguarded generosity. This quality, once genuinely cultivated through sustained practice, does not remain confined to the performance context but becomes a dimension of the practitioner’s ongoing way of being in the world — which is precisely what the Natya Shastra tradition means when it claims that the mastery of the Karana vocabulary is a path of liberation.

The global philosophical conversation about the nature of form, meaning, and consciousness that this analysis of Indian aesthetics invites is one of the most important intellectual contributions that the study of classical Indian performance can make to contemporary thought. At a moment when the Western philosophical tradition is increasingly questioning its own assumptions about the primacy of abstract, disembodied thought over embodied, situated practice, the classical Indian tradition’s integration of the highest philosophical sophistication with the

350
The Cosmic Choreography

most refined embodied practice offers a genuinely alternative vision: not philosophy and art as separate domains that occasionally illuminate each other, but philosophy as art and art as philosophy — a unified vision in which the dancing body and the contemplating mind are both expressions of the single, luminous, non-dual consciousness that is the ground and goal of all human inquiry.

13.19Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Thirteen

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the

351
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that

352
The Cosmic Choreography

produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana, moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied

353
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

13.22Global Presence of Ancient Wisdom

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of

354
The Cosmic Choreography

knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other

355
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that

356
The Cosmic Choreography

Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

13.23Documentation and Preservation Challenges

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and

357
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya,

358
The Cosmic Choreography

Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological

359
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

360
The Cosmic Choreography

13.6The Japanese Butoh Tradition: A Comparative Perspective

The Japanese Butoh dance tradition — which emerged in the late 1950s from the creative ferment of post-war Japan — offers one of the most philosophically productive cross-cultural comparisons for understanding the deepest dimensions of the 108 Karanas and their relationship to Shankaracharya’s non-dual philosophy. Butoh, which developed partly as a response to the existential devastation of World War II and the atomic bombings, explores the relationship between consciousness, embodiment, and transformation in ways that resonate deeply with both the Natya Shastra tradition and the Advaita Vedanta.

Butoh’s central preoccupation — with the relationship between the individual body and the cosmic forces that move through it, with death, transformation, and the dissolution of fixed identity — mirrors in a very different cultural register the same concerns that animate the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The Butoh performer’s cultivation of a quality of embodied attention that goes beyond personal expression into what practitioners describe as 'becoming the movement' rather than 'doing the movement' corresponds precisely to the quality of Tanmayata (complete absorption) that the Natya Shastra identifies as the mark of the highest level of performance.

The founder of Butoh, Tatsumi Hijikata, explicitly described his practice as an investigation into what he called 'the dead body

361
Global Perspectives and Comparative Studies

that walks' — the body in which the ordinary ego-consciousness has been dissolved and something larger, more primal, and more universal can express itself. This description, while arriving at the same insight from a very different cultural and philosophical direction, corresponds strikingly to Shankaracharya’s concept of the Jivanmukta — the person liberated in life — whose actions and movements arise not from the limited ego-self but from the infinite consciousness that has recognised itself as the ground of all activity.

The cross-cultural convergence between Butoh and the classical Indian traditions is not merely coincidental but reflects the universal quality of the insight both traditions are exploring: that the most profound forms of embodied artistic practice involve a fundamental shift in the quality of consciousness inhabiting the body, from the contracted, ego-bound, defensive consciousness of ordinary experience to the open, expanded, transparent consciousness that both traditions identify as the ground of genuine creative freedom. This shift — whether described in the language of non-dual philosophy, Tantric practice, or post-war existential investigation — is the same fundamental transformation that both Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta and the 108 Karanas' complete vocabulary of embodied consciousness are pointing toward.

362
CHAPTER XIV

Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

“The brain is not the organ of consciousness; it is one of consciousness’s many instruments. The dancer who knows this dances differently.”

— Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson & Eleanor Rosch, The Embodied Mind

14.1Neuroscience and the Dancing Body

Contemporary neuroscience has provided unexpected and philosophically significant support for some of the deepest claims of the Natya Shastra and Advaita Vedanta. The last three decades of neuroscientific research have produced a series of discoveries that collectively challenge the dominant Western understanding of consciousness as a product of brain activity — a view that would make nonsense of the claim that dance or philosophical inquiry can lead to genuine spiritual transformation — and suggest instead a more complex, more interesting

363
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

relationship between brain activity, embodied experience, and the nature of consciousness itself.

The discovery of mirror neurons in the early 1990s by Giacomo Rizzolatti and his colleagues at the University of Parma provided the first clear neuroscientific basis for understanding the mechanism of aesthetic empathy — the spectator’s direct experiential participation in the performer’s emotional and physical states. Mirror neurons are neural cells that fire both when an animal performs an action and when it observes the same action being performed by another member of its species. In humans, the mirror neuron system is considerably more complex and sensitive than in other animals, capable of simulating not merely physical actions but emotional states, intentions, and even abstract social meanings. When an audience member watches a skilled dancer perform the Shringara Karanas with full emotional presence, mirror neurons in the observer’s motor cortex, somatosensory cortex, and limbic system create a simulation of the dancer’s physical and emotional states — not a mere conceptual understanding of what the dancer is feeling but an actual, partial enactment of it in the observer’s own body-mind.

This neuroscientific finding provides strong support for Abhinavagupta’s theory of Rasa — his claim that the audience of a great performance experiences genuine Rasa rather than merely recognising it from the outside. The mechanism Abhinavagupta proposes — the spectator’s personal emotion being purified, universalised, and transformed into genuine aesthetic experience through the process of Sadharanikarana — corresponds, at a functional level, to the operation of the mirror neuron system

364
The Cosmic Choreography

combined with the higher-order cognitive processes of aesthetic attention and emotional regulation. The mirror neurons simulate the performer’s states; the aesthetic context of the performance (the theatrical space, the knowledge that one is watching a performance, the quality of the artistic execution) provides the conditions for the Sadharanikarana process; and the result is the experience of Rasa — universal, impersonal, aesthetically purified emotion that has been lifted out of the context of personal desire and aversion.

The Default Mode Network (DMN) — a set of interconnected brain regions that become active during self-referential thought, mind-wandering, and introspection — has been the subject of intensive research in the context of meditative practice. Advanced meditators — including practitioners of Zen, Vipassana, Tibetan Buddhist, and Advaita Vedanta meditation — consistently show distinctive alterations in DMN activity: specifically, a reduction in the excessive self-referential processing (the 'narrative self' activity) associated with the ordinary ego-bound mind, combined with an increase in a broader, more open, less self-centred mode of awareness. This pattern of neural activity corresponds, at the functional level, to what these traditions describe as the development of the Sakshi (witness) awareness — the shift from identification with the contents of experience to identification with the awareness that observes those contents.

Preliminary research on highly trained classical dancers and musicians suggests that advanced performers may show similar patterns of neural activity during peak performance states — a

365
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

reduction in the self-monitoring, error-checking, performance-anxiety activity associated with ordinary conscious control of skilled movement, and an increase in a broader, more integrated mode of awareness that performers consistently describe in terms closely parallel to the meditative traditions' descriptions of Sakshi awareness. This neurological evidence supports the claim — made by both the Natya Shastra tradition and the Advaita Vedanta tradition — that the highest states of artistic performance and the highest states of meditative practice converge on the same quality of awareness, approached from different directions but arriving at the same destination.

14.2Embodied Cognition and the Philosophical Body

The emergence of embodied cognition as a major research programme in cognitive science and philosophy of mind over the last three decades represents the most sustained Western intellectual challenge to the Cartesian dualism of mind and body that has dominated Western thought since the seventeenth century. The Cartesian model — which understands the mind as a disembodied computational system that uses the body as a tool for acting in the world — cannot account for the complexity, flexibility, and context-sensitivity of actual human cognitive performance. The embodied cognition research programme, beginning with the foundational work of Merleau-Ponty in phenomenology and developed in cognitive science by researchers

366
The Cosmic Choreography

including Francisco Varela, Evan Thompson, Eleanor Rosch, Mark Johnson, George Lakoff, and Andy Clark, argues instead that cognition is fundamentally shaped by, and grounded in, bodily experience.

This research programme has produced several findings of direct relevance for understanding the philosophical dimensions of classical Indian dance and the 108 Karanas. First, the research on conceptual metaphor by Lakoff and Johnson demonstrates that the most fundamental human concepts — including abstract philosophical concepts like space, time, causation, identity, and experience — are grounded in bodily experience rather than in disembodied computation. We understand 'more' as 'up' because we have bodies that grow vertically; we understand 'past' as 'behind' because we have bodies that face forward and move forward; we understand argument as 'war' or 'building' because we have bodies that fight and build. This means that changes in bodily practice — learning to inhabit the body differently, to move differently, to be aware of the body’s relationship to gravity and space and others differently — are not merely physical changes but cognitive changes, changes in the fundamental structures through which we understand and experience reality.

Applied to the practice of the 108 Karanas, this insight suggests that the classical Indian dance training is not merely developing physical skill but fundamentally restructuring the practitioner’s cognitive architecture. The student who learns to inhabit the Urdhva-Janu Karana with genuine understanding — who learns, through sustained practice, to experience the quality

367
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

of effortless elevation that the Karana embodies, to inhabit from inside the specific quality of consciousness in that configuration of the body — is not merely acquiring a new physical skill but developing a new cognitive structure: a new way of experiencing the relationship between heaviness and lightness, between limitation and freedom, between the earthward pull of physical existence and the upward aspiration of spiritual longing. This new cognitive structure, once developed, does not remain confined to the performance context but reorganises the practitioner’s experience more generally — changing the quality of her awareness in every domain of her life.

The research on proprioception — the body’s awareness of its own position, movement, and internal states — is also highly relevant. Classical Indian dance training involves the most extreme development of proprioceptive awareness available through any existing practice: the dancer must simultaneously attend to the precise position of every finger joint, the angle of every limb, the distribution of weight through the feet, the quality of tension in the core and peripheral muscles, the relationship of the body to the surrounding space, and the rhythmic relationship to the accompanying music — all at once, with no single element allowed to eclipse the others. This sustained cultivation of holistic proprioceptive awareness — awareness of the body as a unified, integrated, dynamic whole — is, from the perspective of the Advaita Vedanta tradition, a systematic practice of awareness itself: a training in the very faculty (discriminative awareness, Viveka) that Shankaracharya identifies as the primary instrument of liberation.

368
The Cosmic Choreography

The Advaita Vedanta tradition, despite its metaphysical insistence on the ultimately non-physical nature of the Self, has never been dismissive of the body as a site of spiritual practice. The tradition of Hatha Yoga — which many scholars believe to have developed within the Advaita Vedanta and Shaiva contexts — demonstrates that working through the body, with the body, as the body, can be a direct path to the same recognition that philosophical inquiry approaches through conceptual analysis. The 108 Karanas, understood in this context, represent the most complete and philosophically sophisticated system of Hatha Yoga ever developed — a system in which every asana (pose) is simultaneously a philosophical statement, a cosmological map, and a vehicle of direct experiential insight.

14.5Somatic Therapy and the Healing Dimensions of the Karana Tradition

The healing dimensions of classical Indian dance — the tradition’s understanding that the practice of the Karanas can not only develop artistic skill and philosophical understanding but also heal physical and psychological disorders — represent an important but insufficiently studied dimension of the tradition’s contemporary relevance. This healing dimension is not a modern addition to the tradition but is explicitly acknowledged in the Natya Shastra itself, which describes the therapeutic effects of specific Karanas and recommends them for practitioners suffering from specific physical or psychological conditions.

369
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

Contemporary somatic therapy — the broad field of body-centred therapeutic practices including approaches such as Somatic Experiencing, Sensorimotor Psychotherapy, Body-Mind Centring, and related approaches — has developed, largely independently of the Indian classical tradition, a sophisticated understanding of the relationship between chronic patterns of muscular tension and psychological trauma, and the potential of conscious embodied practice to dissolve these patterns and restore the body-mind’s natural capacity for healthy self-regulation. The convergence between these contemporary somatic approaches and the classical Indian tradition’s understanding of the body as a vehicle of both pathology and healing is striking and suggests that both traditions are addressing the same fundamental phenomena from different cultural perspectives.

The specific therapeutic applications of the Karana system that are most clearly supported by contemporary somatic theory involve the use of specific movement qualities to address specific patterns of body-mind dysfunction. The research on the relationship between chronic postural patterns and psychological states — beginning with Wilhelm Reich’s body armour theory and continuing through contemporary trauma therapy — supports the Natya Shastra’s understanding that the way a person habitually holds and moves their body both expresses and reinforces their characteristic psychological patterns. A person whose habitual posture is contracted, forward-slumped, and inwardly collapsed is not merely making a poor aesthetic choice but expressing and reinforcing a psychological pattern of depression,

370
The Cosmic Choreography

self-diminishment, and diminished vital engagement with the world.

The Karana tradition’s approach to transforming these patterns is not through the forcible correction of posture but through the cultivation of specific movement qualities that gradually introduce new possibilities into the body-mind’s repertoire. The Samapada Sthana — the perfectly balanced standing position — does not merely correct poor posture but introduces, through the body, the quality of balanced equanimity that the Advaita Vedanta tradition identifies as one of the primary marks of the liberated sage. Regular practice of this position, with the full quality of awareness that the tradition requires, gradually permeates the practitioner’s habitual body-consciousness, introducing the possibility of balance and equanimity as a lived bodily reality rather than merely an intellectual aspiration.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition makes an analogous point about the relationship between philosophical understanding and psychological healing. The recognition of the non-dual truth — the direct experience of one’s identity with the infinite, indestructible consciousness of Brahman — is not merely an intellectual achievement but a profound psychological healing: it dissolves the fundamental anxiety that arises from the false identification of the Self with the limited, mortal, vulnerable ego, and in dissolving this anxiety, it dissolves the entire structure of psychological defensiveness, contraction, and suffering that Shankara identifies as the consequence of Avidya (ignorance). The healing that comes from genuine philosophical practice is not a secondary benefit of philosophical understanding but its

371
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

direct consequence: in recognising the truth of one’s own nature, one is simultaneously healed of the psychological wound that false self-identification creates.

The convergence of these two healing perspectives — the somatic therapy’s understanding of how embodied practice can heal psychological patterns, and the Advaita Vedanta’s understanding of how philosophical recognition can heal existential suffering — suggests a genuinely integrative approach to human well-being that neither tradition fully articulates on its own but that their synthesis makes possible. The practice of the 108 Karanas, understood as simultaneously a somatic therapy (working directly with the body’s patterns of tension and release, contraction and expansion, grounding and elevation), a philosophical practice (cultivating the qualities of equanimity, spaciousness, and non-attachment that the Advaita tradition identifies as the marks of liberation), and a devotional practice (expressing and deepening the relationship between the individual practitioner and the divine consciousness that the tradition honours), represents one of the most complete integrative approaches to human healing and flourishing available in any culture’s traditions.

372
The Cosmic Choreography

14.6Meditation Research and the Contemplative Dimensions of Dance

The growing body of scientific research on the effects of meditation on brain structure, function, and subjective experience has created new frameworks for understanding the contemplative dimensions of classical Indian dance practice. Landmark studies by researchers including Richard Davidson, Sara Lazar, Antoine Lutz, and many others have demonstrated that sustained meditative practice produces measurable changes in brain structure and function — changes that correspond to the subjective changes that meditators report in their quality of attention, emotional regulation, and sense of self.

The most relevant findings for our study concern the relationship between meditative practice and the Default Mode Network (DMN), which as noted in Section 14.2 is consistently altered in experienced meditators in ways that correspond to the development of the Sakshi (witness) awareness that Shankaracharya identifies as the mark of philosophical maturity. Recent research has extended these findings to include other forms of sustained, attentive practice including yoga, tai chi, and improvisational music performance — all of which show DMN alterations similar to those produced by formal seated meditation.

Classical Indian dance, with its requirements of sustained, multi-dimensional attention during extended performance, would be predicted by this research to produce similar neural effects. Preliminary studies by researchers in India and

373
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

internationally have begun to investigate this prediction, with early results supporting the hypothesis that advanced classical dance practice produces alterations in neural function consistent with the development of expanded awareness, reduced self-referential processing, and increased capacity for sustained attention. These findings, while still preliminary, provide growing scientific support for the tradition’s claim that sustained classical dance practice is a genuine contemplative practice with genuine transformative effects on consciousness.

The specific mechanisms through which classical dance practice might produce these contemplative effects are multiple and synergistic. The intense proprioceptive training required by the Karana system cultivates a quality of body awareness that is functionally analogous to the body scan techniques used in Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction and related clinical interventions. The sustained attention to rhythmic patterns required by the Tala system cultivates a quality of temporal awareness that is functionally analogous to the attention training of formal meditation practice. The development of the Sakshi quality — the capacity to maintain witness awareness while fully engaged in technically demanding movement — is, as argued in Section 6.2, precisely the quality that meditation research has identified as the core contemplative competence being developed in advanced practitioners.

What the meditation research adds to the traditional understanding is a neurological account of why these effects occur — an account that, while necessarily incomplete and preliminary, provides independent scientific support for the tradition’s own

374
The Cosmic Choreography

claims. The tradition does not require this scientific support; its authority rests on the direct experience of generations of practitioners who have verified its claims through their own practice. But the convergence between the scientific findings and the tradition’s self-understanding is philosophically significant: it suggests that the tradition’s claims about the transformative effects of sustained classical dance practice are not merely cultural beliefs or metaphysical speculations but descriptions of real, measurable, reproducible changes in the practitioner’s neurological and psychological functioning. This convergence strengthens the case for taking the tradition’s philosophical claims seriously and for investing in the kind of rigorous, philosophically-informed practice that the tradition describes as necessary for their realisation.

14.20Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Fourteen

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of

375
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the

376
The Cosmic Choreography

natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana, moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce.

377
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

378
The Cosmic Choreography

14.23The Science and Spirituality of Sacred Movement

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

379
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one

380
The Cosmic Choreography

tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing

381
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

14.24Clinical Research and Therapeutic Applications

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S. Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are

382
The Cosmic Choreography

less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram

383
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

— as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple

384
The Cosmic Choreography

sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

14.7Interoception and the Inner Body of Classical Dance

Recent research in the neuroscience of interoception — the body’s awareness of its own internal states — provides a new framework for understanding one of the most philosophically significant dimensions of classical Indian dance training: the development of an extraordinarily refined inner bodily awareness that goes far beyond the proprioceptive awareness of position and movement to include awareness of subtle internal energetic states. This dimension of dance training has been recognised by practitioners as important since the earliest codifications of the tradition, but it has been difficult to discuss in the language of Western science without reducing it to mere vague metaphors.

Interoception research by A.D. Craig, Sahib Khalsa, and others has demonstrated that the insular cortex — a region of the brain that processes internal bodily sensations — plays a crucial role in self-awareness, emotional experience, and the sense of being a self inhabiting a body. Advanced meditators, who have developed highly refined interoceptive awareness through

385
Cognitive Science and Embodied Spirituality

sustained practice, show measurably enlarged and more active insular cortices. The quality of awareness they develop corresponds closely to what the classical Indian tradition describes as the awareness of the Pranamaya Kosha and Manomaya Kosha — the vital and mental sheaths that constitute the subtler dimensions of the body-mind complex.

The specific forms of interoceptive training involved in the Karana tradition — the sustained attention to the quality of breath and energy in each Karana, the development of sensitivity to the subtle relationship between the inner quality of awareness and the outer quality of movement — would be predicted by interoceptive research to develop precisely the kind of refined inner bodily awareness that advanced meditators show. This prediction is consistent with what experienced classical dancers report: that sustained Karana practice develops a quality of inner bodily awareness that eventually becomes the primary guide for the quality of movement, replacing the external visual or auditory feedback that beginning practitioners rely on.

From a Shankaracharya perspective, this development of interoceptive awareness is a dimension of the progressive refinement of awareness through the Pancha Koshas described in the Vivekachudamani. The practitioner who has developed the refined interoceptive awareness that sustained Karana training produces has moved their primary identification from the Annamaya Kosha (the gross physical body, whose movements are visible externally) to the Pranamaya Kosha (the vital body, whose energetic quality is perceptible only through refined inner attention). This shift is not a departure from embodiment but its

386
The Cosmic Choreography

deepening: the practitioner is becoming more bodily aware, not less, as she moves her attention from the surface to the interior of her embodied experience. And this deepening embodied awareness is simultaneously a deepening philosophical awareness: the inner qualities of vital energy that the refined interoceptive attention perceives are the same qualities of Prana, Spanda, and Chit-Shakti that Shankaracharya’s philosophical vocabulary describes.
