Synthesis and Conclusions

The Cosmic Choreography

“The dance does not end; it transforms. The dancer does not stop; she becomes the stillness within the movement. This is the final teaching of the 108 Karanas.”

— Naredla Ramachandra

15.1The Argument Recapitulated

This study has traced a single central argument through fifteen chapters and multiple disciplinary frameworks, using methods ranging from Sanskrit philology and art history to cognitive science and performance theory: that the 108 Karanas of the Natya Shastra and the philosophical system of Shankaracharya are not merely historically or culturally proximate but are expressions of the same fundamental insight about consciousness, embodiment, and liberation, developed through radically different but profoundly complementary methodologies. The Natya Shastra approaches this insight through the body — through the meticulous, systematic

388
The Cosmic Choreography

development of a vocabulary of embodied movement that encodes cosmological truths in the medium of physical gesture, posture, and dynamic action. Shankaracharya approaches it through consciousness — through the rigorous, systematic analysis of the nature of awareness and its relationship to the world of appearance. Yet at their deepest level, both traditions converge on the same recognition: that consciousness and embodiment are not opposites but aspects of a single non-dual reality, and that the most complete human life is one in which this unity is directly known, not merely theorised.

The primary textual evidence for this convergence is found in Shankaracharya’s sustained and philosophically precise use of dance and movement imagery in his devotional and philosophical writings. As we have documented in detail, particularly in Chapters Four and Five, this imagery is not decorative but structural: the Nataraja metaphor in its various manifestations, the Ananda Tandava reference in the Soundarya Lahari, the kinetic language of the Nirvana Shatakam, the rhythmic embodiment of the Shiva Tandava Stotram — all these constitute a sustained philosophical strategy of using the most refined embodied art as a vehicle for communicating the insights of non-dual philosophy. Shankaracharya chose to engage with the performing arts tradition not despite his philosophical commitments but because of them: the dance tradition, at its deepest level, embodies in physical form precisely the philosophical insights that his Advaita Vedanta articulates in conceptual form.

389
Synthesis and Conclusions

The secondary evidence — drawn from the temple sculptural programmes that materialise the philosophical synthesis in stone (Chapter Nine), from the Rasa theory of Abhinavagupta that provides the philosophical bridge between the two traditions (Chapter Seven), from the contemporary cognitive science that provides indirect empirical support for the tradition’s claims (Chapter Fourteen), and from the cross-cultural comparative evidence that demonstrates the universality of the insights encoded in the Karana system (Chapter Thirteen) — collectively supports and enriches the primary textual argument without being necessary to it. The convergence of the Natya Shastra’s 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition is established primarily through careful analysis of the primary sources; the additional evidence confirms and deepens the conclusion but does not depend on it.

The five major conclusions of the study, as stated in the Executive Summary, bear repetition and amplification here. First: the 108 Karanas constitute a cosmological map encoded in embodied movement — not merely a technical vocabulary for classical dance but a comprehensive account of the movement of consciousness through its various modes and expressions, from the most grounded, material, earthbound configurations to the most elevated, transcendent, sky-moving positions. This conclusion is supported by the analysis of the Karana system’s internal organisation (Chapter Three), the cosmological significance of the number 108 (Chapter One), and the temple iconographic programmes that present the Karanas

390
The Cosmic Choreography

as a philosophical programme rather than a mere technical catalogue (Chapter Nine).

Second: Shankaracharya’s use of dance imagery in his devotional and philosophical works is not decorative but structural — a sustained philosophical strategy of using the most refined embodied art as a vehicle for communicating the insights of non-dual philosophy. This conclusion is supported by the detailed textual analysis of Chapter Five (Soundarya Lahari), Chapter Eight (Tandava theology), and Chapter Ten (Mudra and gesture), which demonstrate that Shankaracharya’s movement imagery is philosophically precise and corresponds point by point to specific Karanas and philosophical principles of the Natya Shastra tradition.

15.2Implications for Contemporary Theory and Practice

The conclusions of this study have implications that extend far beyond the academic domains of Sanskrit studies, art history, and performance theory. They bear on fundamental questions in contemporary philosophy of mind, aesthetic theory, spiritual practice, and the politics of embodied knowledge — questions that are alive and contested in contemporary intellectual culture.

For the philosophy of mind, this study contributes to the growing body of evidence against the Cartesian model of consciousness as a disembodied computational system. The detailed analysis of the Karana system, read through the lens of

391
Synthesis and Conclusions

Shankaracharya’s philosophy, supports and enriches the embodied cognition research programme’s claim that cognition is fundamentally shaped by bodily experience. More radically, it supports the claim — made by the Advaita Vedanta tradition and finding increasing support in contemporary contemplative neuroscience — that consciousness is not a product of brain activity but the ground from which all activity arises, and that the most fundamental transformations of consciousness available to human beings occur not through the addition of new information or the acquisition of new skills but through a shift in the basic quality of awareness itself: from ego-bound, contracted, distorted awareness to the open, luminous, undistorted awareness that both the Natya Shastra tradition and the Advaita Vedanta tradition identify as the ultimate goal of human development.

For aesthetic theory, this study argues for a fundamental reconceptualisation of the relationship between artistic practice and philosophical inquiry. The dominant Western model understands art and philosophy as separate domains — art operating through intuition, emotion, and sensory experience; philosophy operating through reason, argument, and conceptual analysis. The convergence of the Natya Shastra and Advaita Vedanta demonstrated in this study challenges this separation: it demonstrates that the most refined artistic practice and the most rigorous philosophical inquiry can converge on the same insight, approached from different directions but arriving at the same destination. This convergence suggests not that art and philosophy are the same (they are clearly different in their methods and media) but that they are different paths up the same

392
The Cosmic Choreography

mountain — different approaches to the same fundamental truth about consciousness, embodiment, and liberation.

For spiritual practice, this study argues for the recognition of classical Indian dance — particularly the tradition of the 108 Karanas — as a genuine and complete spiritual path, equivalent in its depth and rigor to the more widely recognised paths of philosophical inquiry (Jnana Yoga), devotion (Bhakti Yoga), and action (Karma Yoga). This recognition is not new to the tradition itself — the Natya Shastra’s claim that Natya is a fifth Veda makes it explicitly — but it has been insufficiently appreciated in contemporary discussions of Indian spirituality, which tend to privilege the meditational and philosophical approaches over the performative and embodied ones. This study provides the philosophical foundations for a more comprehensive understanding: one in which the classical dancer is recognised as a practitioner of genuine spiritual transformation, and in which the tradition of the 108 Karanas is recognised as a complete philosophical and spiritual curriculum, as demanding and as rewarding as any other path within the Indian spiritual tradition.

For the politics of embodied knowledge, this study makes an argument of relevance beyond academic discourse. The colonial suppression of classical Indian dance traditions — and the systematic delegitimisation of the Devadasi tradition through which the most refined forms of classical performance were transmitted — represented not merely a cultural loss but an epistemological violence: the destruction of a sophisticated system of embodied knowledge that encoded philosophical insights of the highest order in the medium of trained bodily practice. The

393
Synthesis and Conclusions

contemporary revival of these traditions is therefore not merely an aesthetic or cultural project but a philosophical and political one: the recovery and reaffirmation of an entire dimension of human knowledge that was systematically denied, suppressed, and marginalised. Understanding the philosophical depth of the traditions being recovered — understanding the 108 Karanas as a philosophical curriculum of the highest order, understanding Shankaracharya’s philosophical tradition as deeply connected to and enriched by the performing arts tradition — strengthens and deepens the philosophical case for their recovery.

The practical implications for the training and understanding of classical Indian dance are the most immediate and concrete of the study’s contributions. A dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana system — who approaches the 108 Karanas not merely as technical forms to be mastered but as philosophical statements to be understood and embodied — will dance differently from one who has only technical training. This different quality of dancing will be immediately visible to the attentive audience: there will be a transparency in the performance, a quality of the infinite showing through the finite, a sense that the movement is arising from somewhere deeper than mere technical competence. This transparency is what the tradition calls Sattvika quality, and it is what Shankaracharya’s Soundarya Lahari celebrates in every verse: the luminous, transparent, blissful quality of consciousness that has recognised its own nature and moves, dances, and expresses itself from that recognition.

394
The Cosmic Choreography

15.3Future Directions

This study has necessarily been selective in its focus and incomplete in its scope. The subject of the relationship between Indian performing arts traditions and Indian philosophical traditions is inexhaustibly rich, and the specific relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy, while the central focus of this study, opens onto multiple dimensions that a single book cannot fully explore. Several directions for future research suggest themselves as particularly promising.

The relationship between the Karana system and the Yantra-Mandala tradition of Tantric visual meditation deserves a dedicated study. The Shri Yantra — the supreme geometric diagram associated with the Goddess in the Shakta Tantric tradition, and explicitly invoked in the Soundarya Lahari’s Ananda Lahari section — is a two-dimensional philosophical text whose geometric structure may bear systematic relationships to the spatial geometries of the 108 Karanas. The Shri Yantra’s nine intersecting triangles generate a complex geometric pattern that can be read as encoding the complete range of cosmic processes; the 108 Karanas' spatial configurations may be understood as three-dimensional extensions of the same geometric programme. A systematic comparative study of the Shri Yantra and the Karana system could yield important insights into the relationship between visual philosophy and embodied philosophy in the Shakta Tantric tradition.

395
Synthesis and Conclusions

The relationship between the Karana system and the Kalaripayattu martial arts tradition of Kerala deserves more detailed investigation than has been possible within the scope of this study. Kalaripayattu — which is understood in the Kerala tradition as one of the oldest and most complete systems of embodied practice, encompassing martial training, therapeutic practice, and spiritual development — shares with the Karana system a fundamental emphasis on the integration of movement, breath, and consciousness. Many of the Karana poses have direct counterparts in the Kalari vocabulary of postures and movements; and the Kerala tradition maintains a strong connection between Kalaripayattu training and the training of classical dance and theatre performers. A comparative study of the Karana system and Kalaripayattu could illuminate the broader tradition of embodied philosophical practice within which both systems are embedded.

The contemporary application of the Karana tradition in therapeutic and healing contexts is another promising area for future research. The detailed proprioceptive training involved in Karana practice, the systematic development of the integration of breath and movement, the cultivation of Sakshi awareness through the demanding requirements of performance — all these dimensions of the Karana tradition have potential therapeutic applications that have been little studied. Preliminary work by somatic therapists and yoga practitioners drawing on classical Indian dance traditions suggests that the embodied wisdom of the Karana system may have profound applications in the treatment of trauma, stress-related illness, and disorders of embodied

396
The Cosmic Choreography

self-awareness. Rigorous clinical research into these applications — combined with careful philosophical analysis of the tradition’s own understanding of the healing dimensions of sacred movement — could open a productive dialogue between the ancient wisdom of the Karana tradition and contemporary evidence-based healthcare.

Finally, the digital preservation and global transmission of the 108 Karanas deserves dedicated attention. The vulnerability of embodied knowledge to disruption and loss — demonstrated by the near-loss of the Karana tradition during the colonial period — suggests that systematic efforts to document, preserve, and transmit this knowledge through multiple media, including digital video documentation, interactive databases, and virtual reality reconstructions, are urgent scholarly priorities. At the same time, any such digital preservation project must be guided by a clear philosophical understanding of the nature and limits of digital transmission: the Guru-Shishya Parampara principle is not a cultural conservatism to be overcome by technology but a philosophical insight about the nature of embodied knowledge that technology cannot replace. Digital resources can supplement but cannot substitute for the living encounter between teacher and student through which the deepest dimensions of the Karana tradition are transmitted.

The most important future direction, however, is not academic but practical: the deepening and widening of living practice. The 108 Karanas are not historical artefacts to be preserved in museums and analysed in scholarly publications; they are living invitations to an experience of consciousness that

397
Synthesis and Conclusions

every human being is capable of and every human tradition, in its own way, points toward. The most valuable contribution that contemporary scholarship can make to this tradition is not merely to analyse it but to practise it, to transmit it, to make it available to the widest possible range of human beings — and in doing so, to honour the tradition’s own deepest conviction: that the cosmic dance of Shiva, expressed through the 108 Karanas, is not a performance given for an audience but a participation available to all.

15.5The Cosmic Choreography: A Vision for the Future

The title of this book — 'The Cosmic Choreography' — is intended to capture the dual nature of the synthesis it traces. On one hand, it refers to the 108 Karanas as a cosmic choreography in the literal sense: a complete vocabulary of sacred movement that embodies the movement of consciousness through the full range of its cosmic self-expression. On the other hand, it refers to the relationship between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy as itself a cosmic choreography — a dance between two great traditions that, while maintaining their individual integrity and distinctive methods, are choreographed by the same deep insight into the nature of consciousness that gives each of them its ultimate meaning and authority.

The vision that emerges from this synthesis — a vision that this study has traced through the primary texts, the temple

398
The Cosmic Choreography

sculptures, the living traditions, and the contemporary scientific research — is a vision of human being as fundamentally choreographic: as a creature whose deepest nature is expressed not through static possession of fixed truths but through dynamic movement, through the continuous dance of awareness and expression, knowledge and action, transcendence and embodiment, that constitutes the richest human life. This vision is simultaneously philosophical (consciousness is dynamic, not static; truth is a living recognition, not a dead proposition), aesthetic (the highest art is that which makes this dynamic truth most fully visible), somatic (the body is not an obstacle to this recognition but its primary vehicle), and soteriological (the liberation this recognition brings is not escape from the dance but the fullest participation in it).

The practical vision for the future that emerges from this synthesis involves several interconnected developments. At the level of education, it suggests the development of curricula that integrate classical Indian dance practice with philosophical study in a way that does justice to both — neither reducing the dance to mere illustration of philosophical points nor treating the philosophy as mere cultural background to technical training, but recognising both as equally essential dimensions of a single comprehensive path of human development. At the level of research, it suggests the development of multi-disciplinary scholarly frameworks that can hold the complexity of this synthesis without reducing it to the terms of any single discipline.

At the level of practice, it suggests the renewal and deepening of the classical dance traditions through explicit philosophical

399
Synthesis and Conclusions

engagement — the recovery of the understanding that the 108 Karanas are not merely technical exercises but philosophical practices, that performing them with full understanding of their philosophical significance is qualitatively different from performing them without this understanding, and that the difference is not merely in the performer’s intellectual state but in the quality of the performance itself. This is not a call for dancers to become philosophers — the tradition has never required its practitioners to produce philosophical treatises — but for the philosophical understanding to be embodied in the practice itself, expressed in the quality of the movement rather than added as an intellectual commentary on it.

At the level of intercultural dialogue, the synthesis traced in this book suggests that the relationship between Indian classical dance and Western performance theory, between Advaita Vedanta and Western philosophy of consciousness, between the Natya Shastra’s aesthetics and contemporary science of mind and movement, is not a relationship of borrowing or appropriation but of genuine philosophical dialogue — a dialogue between traditions that have arrived, through their own distinctive paths, at compatible and mutually illuminating insights. The most productive form of this dialogue is not the translation of one tradition’s insights into the vocabulary of the other but the creation of a new shared space in which both traditions can speak in their own voices while genuinely addressing the same fundamental questions.

The ultimate horizon of this vision is the one that both the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy have always

400
The Cosmic Choreography

pointed toward: a human culture in which the distinction between philosophical wisdom and artistic beauty, between contemplative practice and creative expression, between the recognition of truth and the celebration of life, has dissolved in the recognition that these are not separate domains but aspects of a single, luminous, dancing reality — the Ananda Tandava of consciousness itself, expressing itself through every form of genuine human creativity and every moment of genuine human awareness. In the words of the Taittiriya Upanishad, whose teaching on Brahman as Ananda Shankara knew by heart: 'Anando Brahma' — Bliss is Brahman. The dance, at its deepest, is this recognition made visible.

15.6A Personal Reflection: The Scholar as Devotee

Any honest engagement with the material of this study — with texts that have moved and transformed their readers across generations and cultures, with sculptures that still communicate their philosophical insights across a millennium of silence, with a living performance tradition whose best moments constitute genuine encounters with something that transcends ordinary aesthetic experience — must eventually move beyond the detached objectivity of scholarly analysis toward a more personal, more vulnerable acknowledgment of what it means to be engaged with this material.

The Natya Shastra is not merely a text to be analysed but an invitation to a way of being in the world — a way of being fully

401
Synthesis and Conclusions

present in the body, fully attentive to the rhythms that surround and constitute us, fully responsive to the beauty that is the surface expression of the truth that underlies everything. Shankaracharya’s philosophy is not merely a doctrine to be assessed but a recognition to be arrived at — or rather, to be recognised as having always already been present, waiting only for the cessation of the inattention that obscured it. The 108 Karanas are not merely movement forms to be technically executed but invitations to inhabit, more fully and more freely, the body-consciousness that is the primary vehicle of our experience of being alive.

This study was written in the conviction that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy is not a historical curiosity or an academic specialisation but a living resource — a way of understanding the relationship between body, mind, and spirit that has practical implications for how we practice the arts, how we pursue wisdom, how we inhabit our bodies, and how we understand the deepest nature of the consciousness through which all these activities occur. The scholarly apparatus — the textual analysis, the art historical evidence, the philosophical argumentation, the comparative study, the scientific research — is in service of this practical vision, not an end in itself.

The tradition itself is clear about the relationship between scholarly understanding and living wisdom. Shankara’s Vivekachudamani warns repeatedly against the person who has mastered all the philosophical texts but has not arrived at the direct recognition they point toward — the person who knows

402
The Cosmic Choreography

about liberation without being liberated, who has learned the map but has never made the journey. The same warning applies, mutatis mutandis, to the study of the 108 Karanas: one can know all about the Karana system — its technical structure, its philosophical significance, its cosmological implications — without ever having inhabited a single Karana from the inside, without ever having had the embodied experience that transforms intellectual knowledge into philosophical understanding.

The invitation of this book, ultimately, is to supplement scholarly understanding with embodied practice — to take the intellectual framework developed here back to the performance studio, to the temple, to the meditation cushion, and to test it against the living reality of the tradition’s most fundamental claim: that consciousness, fully inhabited and fully expressed through the medium of the human body in sacred movement, is capable of recognising itself as the infinite, blissful, non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra calls the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya calls Brahman. This recognition — which is both the goal and the path, both the conclusion of all philosophical inquiry and its beginning — is the cosmic choreography that this book has been, in its own imperfect, scholarly way, trying to describe.

403
Synthesis and Conclusions

15.21Deepening Practice: The Inner Dimensions of Chapter Fifteen

The themes developed in this chapter open onto dimensions of practice that cannot be fully appreciated through scholarly analysis alone, however rigorous and comprehensive. The relationship between the theoretical frameworks examined here and the lived experience of classical dance practice is not that of map to territory — as if the theory were a representation of the practice — but of different registers of the same philosophical investigation: the scholarly analysis and the embodied practice are both ways of approaching the same question, both forms of inquiry into the nature of consciousness in its relationship to movement, beauty, and liberation.

Practitioners who have genuinely internalised the insights discussed in this chapter report that they transform the experience of performance in concrete, observable ways. The dancer who understands the philosophical dimensions of the Karana vocabulary — who has studied the relationship between the technical forms and their philosophical significance — approaches her practice differently from one who has only technical training. Not because she is thinking about philosophy while she performs (which would be a distraction rather than an enhancement) but because the philosophical understanding has been internalised into the body itself, shaping the quality of attention she brings to the movement from the inside.

404
The Cosmic Choreography

The Sanskrit tradition has a precise term for this quality of philosophically informed embodied practice: Viveka-yukta Abhyasa — practice infused with discrimination. This is the practice in which every movement is simultaneously a technical execution and a philosophical inquiry — in which the dancer is not merely executing a form but actively investigating the nature of consciousness through the medium of that form. This quality of inquiry does not interrupt the flow of the performance but deepens it: the performance becomes simultaneously more precise technically (because the philosophical understanding provides a finer and more sensitive framework for attending to what is actually happening in the movement) and more freely expressive (because the philosophical understanding dissolves the ego’s tendency to interfere with the natural flow of the movement through self-consciousness and striving).

The relationship between philosophical study and embodied practice in the classical Indian tradition is described most precisely in the concept of Sadhana — the sustained, systematic practice through which a philosophical or spiritual insight is progressively internalised until it becomes the natural quality of one’s consciousness and action. Sadhana is not a technique that produces the desired result through mechanical repetition but a living inquiry whose results deepen and expand with every repetition, revealing new dimensions of the same fundamental insight at successively deeper levels of understanding. The Sadhana of the 108 Karanas is a lifelong investigation of the nature of consciousness in its embodied dimension — an investigation that, like Shankaracharya’s philosophical Sadhana,

405
Synthesis and Conclusions

moves progressively deeper into the recognition that the consciousness doing the investigating and the consciousness being investigated are the same single, non-dual awareness.

The tradition’s understanding of the relationship between the guru’s grace (Guru Kripa) and the student’s own effort in this process is directly relevant to the question of how philosophical understanding and embodied practice interact. The tradition’s answer is nuanced: both are necessary, and neither is sufficient alone. The student’s sustained, sincere effort in both philosophical study and embodied practice creates the conditions in which the guru’s grace can operate effectively; the guru’s grace, in turn, catalyses transformations in the student’s understanding and practice that the student’s own effort alone cannot produce. This same dynamic operates in the relationship between scholarly understanding of the Karana system and the direct, embodied experience of performing it: neither the scholarly understanding alone nor the embodied practice alone is sufficient for the fullest development of the tradition’s wisdom; only their genuine integration — the embodied practice illuminated by philosophical understanding, the philosophical understanding tested and deepened by embodied practice — produces the quality of wisdom that the tradition describes as its ultimate goal.

Contemporary practitioners who have developed both dimensions of the practice — both the rigorous scholarly understanding of the tradition’s philosophical dimensions and the equally rigorous embodied cultivation of the Karana vocabulary — consistently report that the two dimensions deepen each other in ways that neither alone would produce. The

406
The Cosmic Choreography

scholarly understanding gives the embodied practice a precision and intentionality that prevents it from becoming merely habitual; the embodied practice gives the scholarly understanding a concreteness and experiential grounding that prevents it from becoming merely abstract. And at the deepest levels of both — when the scholarly understanding achieves the quality of direct philosophical insight and the embodied practice achieves the quality of genuine Tanmayata — both point toward the same recognition: the non-dual awareness that the Natya Shastra has always called the ground of all performance and that Shankaracharya has always called Brahman.

15.24Toward the Infinite: The Open Horizon of the Cosmic Choreography

The philosophical synthesis traced in this study opens onto questions that extend far beyond the specific domains of Indian performing arts and Advaita Vedanta. At its deepest level, the relationship between the 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s philosophy raises fundamental questions about the nature of knowledge, the relationship between theory and practice, and the possibility of a genuinely integrated human life in which wisdom and beauty, philosophy and art, contemplative depth and creative expression are not separate domains but aspects of a single, living wholeness.

The Indian tradition’s insistence on this wholeness — expressed in the Vedic concept of Ritam (cosmic order), in the

407
Synthesis and Conclusions

aesthetic concept of Rasa (the essential flavour of integrated experience), and in the philosophical concept of Advaita (the non-dual ground of all apparent diversity) — represents one of the most important contributions that Indian civilisation has made to the universal heritage of human wisdom. It challenges the fragmentation of knowledge into specialised disciplines that characterises modern Western academic culture, and it offers an alternative vision: a vision in which the deepest philosophical understanding and the most refined artistic expression are not separate achievements but complementary aspects of the same recognition of the non-dual truth.

The specific vehicle through which this synthesis is most completely expressed — the classical Indian dance tradition with its Karana vocabulary, its Rasa theory, its devotional dimension, and its living guru-shishya transmission — is a vehicle of extraordinary richness and depth. But it is not the only possible vehicle: the same synthesis can be approached through the medium of music, through the practice of sculpture, through the recitation of sacred text, through the practice of yoga in its complete form, or through the direct philosophical inquiry of Advaita Vedanta. What the dance tradition offers that these other vehicles do not is its unique combination of complete technical precision (requiring the development of the most refined bodily awareness), complete philosophical depth (encoding the most subtle metaphysical insights in the grammar of movement), and complete accessibility (communicating across the barriers of language, culture, and intellectual training through the universal language of the body in motion).

408
The Cosmic Choreography

The contemporary relevance of this synthesis extends beyond the domain of classical arts scholarship or philosophical theology. We live in an age of unprecedented global information exchange combined with unprecedented fragmentation of experience: people have access to more information about more traditions than at any point in human history, while simultaneously experiencing increasing disconnection from any single tradition’s deep wisdom. The synthesis traced in this book offers a model for how genuine depth and genuine universality can coexist: not by reducing all traditions to a lowest common denominator but by going so deeply into one tradition’s specific wisdom that its universal dimensions become visible.

The practitioner who goes deeply enough into the 108 Karanas — who masters their technical dimensions with complete precision, understands their philosophical dimensions with complete clarity, and embodies their devotional dimensions with complete sincerity — arrives at a quality of wisdom that is simultaneously deeply Indian and universally human: rooted in the specific forms of a particular cultural tradition while expressing truths that any attentive human consciousness can recognise and verify in its own experience. This is the model that Shankaracharya himself embodied: a thinker of the deepest cultural specificity (commenting in minute detail on specifically Sanskrit texts within specifically Indian philosophical frameworks) who simultaneously arrived at insights of universal validity (insights that contemporary readers from every cultural background recognise as illuminating their own experience of consciousness, embodiment, and the possibility of liberation).

409
Synthesis and Conclusions

The ultimate gift of this synthesis to contemporary humanity is precisely this model of depth-as-universality: the demonstration that going more deeply into any tradition’s genuine wisdom — more precisely, more rigorously, more authentically — leads not further into cultural parochialism but closer to the universal ground that all genuine wisdom traditions share. The 108 Karanas and Shankaracharya’s Advaita Vedanta, taken seriously in their full depth, are not cultural relics of a particular civilisation’s past but living invitations to any human consciousness willing to undertake the patient, rigorous, transformative inquiry they embody.

15.25Synthesis: The Complete Vision

The scholarly debates surrounding the topics addressed in this chapter have generated an extensive literature that, while it cannot be comprehensively reviewed here, deserves acknowledgment for the specific contributions it makes to our understanding of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy. The most significant debates concern the dating and attribution of key texts, the interpretation of specific technical terms, and the historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted.

The question of dating is particularly significant for Shankaracharya, whose traditional dates of 788-820 CE are contested by several scholars on the basis of epigraphic, literary, and astronomical evidence. Some scholars, including T.S.

410
The Cosmic Choreography

Narayana Sastri and T.P. Mahadevan, have proposed dates as early as the fifth or even sixth century BCE for Shankara, which would place him in the same broad intellectual milieu as the early Natya Shastra tradition. Others, including Karl Potter and Paul Hacker, have argued for dates later than the traditional, placing Shankara firmly in the context of the eighth-century CE philosophical debates with Mandana Mishra and other opponents. For the argument of this book, the precise dates are less important than the broader question of the historical relationship between the two traditions — a relationship that was clearly well established by the Chola period (c. 850-1250 CE) and that the sculptural evidence of the temple programmes documents with great precision.

The interpretation of specific technical terms provides another fertile ground for scholarly debate. The term Karana itself, as noted in Chapter Three, has multiple meanings in Sanskrit — it can mean 'action', 'cause', 'instrument', or the specific movement unit of the Natya Shastra — and the philosophical resonances between these meanings are philosophically productive but require careful analysis to avoid confusion. Similarly, Shankaracharya’s use of terms like Maya, Lila, and Ananda have been interpreted in diverse ways by different commentators, and the implications of these different interpretations for the relationship with the Natya Shastra tradition are significant.

The historical development of the institutions through which the two traditions have interacted — the temple institutions, the Matha system, the guru-shishya lineages — has been studied in

411
Synthesis and Conclusions

increasing detail by scholars drawing on epigraphic evidence, administrative records, and the institutional histories preserved in the traditions themselves. This institutional history is important for our argument because it provides concrete evidence that the philosophical synthesis traced in this book was not merely a theoretical possibility but was actually realised in specific historical institutions and practices. The history of specific temples — Chidambaram, Thanjavur, Sringeri, Kanchipuram — as places where the two traditions actively interacted provides the most concrete evidence for the synthesis’s historical reality.

The contemporary scholarly reception of the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been shaped by several important works that deserve special mention. Kapila Vatsyayan’s Classical Indian Dance in Literature and the Arts remains the most comprehensive scholarly treatment of the relationship between the textual and performative dimensions of the classical dance traditions. V. Raghavan’s extensive writings on Sanskrit aesthetics and music theory provide essential background for understanding the philosophical dimensions of the Rasa theory. And Padma Subrahmanyam’s work on the 108 Karanas — combining rigorous philological analysis with systematic practical reconstruction — remains the indispensable reference for any serious study of the Karana system.

The dialogue between these scholarly frameworks and the insights developed in this book is ongoing and productive. Each scholarly contribution illuminates specific dimensions of the synthesis while leaving others in shadow; the comprehensive analysis this book attempts is necessarily incomplete, necessarily

412
The Cosmic Choreography

selective, and necessarily shaped by the specific concerns and competencies of its author. The most honest conclusion one can draw from the scholarly literature as a whole is not that the synthesis between the Natya Shastra and Shankaracharya’s philosophy has been definitively established and comprehensively understood, but that the evidence for its reality is extensive and converging — evidence that comes from multiple independent scholarly traditions, from the material evidence of the temple sculptures, from the testimony of living practitioners, and from the philosophical analysis of the primary texts themselves. This convergence of evidence constitutes the strongest possible scholarly warrant for taking the synthesis seriously, investigating it further, and allowing it to shape our understanding of both traditions in the ways that this book has attempted to articulate.

15.7Natya Shastra in the 21st Century: Challenges and Opportunities

The twenty-first century presents the classical Indian dance tradition with both its greatest challenges and its greatest opportunities. On the challenge side: the pace of modernisation in India and globally has accelerated the disruption of traditional cultural transmission systems; the economic pressures that make it difficult for aspiring classical dancers to support themselves financially through practice and teaching; the commodification of classical arts into entertainment products that strips them of their philosophical and spiritual dimensions; and the increasing

413
Synthesis and Conclusions

marginalisation of Sanskrit as a living language of philosophical inquiry, which makes it difficult for contemporary practitioners to access the rich textual tradition that underlies the classical forms they practice.

On the opportunity side: the global spread of yoga and Indian philosophical traditions has created an unprecedented international audience genuinely interested in the philosophical dimensions of Indian classical arts; the development of digital media has made high-quality documentation and teaching accessible globally in ways that were unimaginable a generation ago; the growing interdisciplinary engagement between Indian studies, performance studies, cognitive science, and somatic therapy has created new scholarly frameworks that can illuminate the tradition’s dimensions from multiple directions simultaneously; and the increasing global recognition of the ecological and psychological costs of modern Western civilisation’s fragmentation of knowledge and experience has created a genuine receptivity to the integrative vision that the classical Indian tradition embodies.

The challenge for contemporary teachers and institutions of classical Indian dance is to navigate these opportunities and challenges in a way that maintains the tradition’s essential quality — its philosophical depth, its technical rigour, its devotional sincerity, its capacity to generate genuine Rasa in performance and genuine philosophical insight in practice — while making it accessible and relevant to a global audience that brings very different cultural backgrounds, expectations, and needs to their engagement with it. This is not a new challenge: the tradition has

414
The Cosmic Choreography

faced comparable challenges at every major turning point in its history, from the Chola period’s systematisation of the temple dance tradition through the Vijayanagara period’s institutional elaboration, the colonial disruption and the twentieth-century revival, to the present moment of global spread and digital transformation.

The model for navigating this challenge is provided by the tradition itself: the same quality of intelligence, creativity, and philosophical depth that the Natya Shastra brought to the systematisation of the cosmic dance vocabulary and that Shankaracharya brought to the philosophical articulation of the non-dual truth must be brought to the challenge of renewing the tradition for the twenty-first century. This renewal is not a departure from the tradition but its most authentic expression: the tradition has always renewed itself by going more deeply into its own essential wisdom, not by compromising that wisdom in response to external pressures.

The synthesis traced in this book points toward the specific direction of this renewal: a deeper philosophical engagement with the tradition’s own richest resources. The scholars, practitioners, and institutions that most fully embody the synthesis between the Natya Shastra’s technical wisdom and Shankaracharya’s philosophical vision will be those that are simultaneously most deeply rooted in the tradition and most genuinely open to the full range of human wisdom — ancient and contemporary, Indian and global, embodied and intellectual, artistic and philosophical. The Cosmic Choreography that this book describes is not a historical achievement to be preserved but a living possibility to be

415
Synthesis and Conclusions

continually renewed: the possibility of a human life fully embodied, fully aware, fully expressive, and fully free.

The dance, ultimately, is not something that can be captured in a book — not even a book of 250 pages. The dance is something that happens in bodies, between bodies, in the space where the trained body meets the living moment with full awareness and complete surrender to whatever arises. Every page of this book is finally, at its best, an invitation: an invitation to encounter the living tradition directly, through the medium of a great teacher’s transmission, through the medium of the great temple sculptures that teach in silence, through the medium of one’s own body as it learns, gradually and often painfully, to move with something approaching the freedom and grace of the cosmic dance that the 108 Karanas embody and that Shankaracharya’s philosophy articulates. The invitation is open. The dance is eternal. The only question is whether we will accept.

15.8Final Synthesis: The Non-Dual Truth of the Cosmic Choreography

This book has traced, through fifteen chapters of textual analysis, art historical investigation, philosophical argument, comparative study, and contemporary scientific engagement, a single, sustained thesis: that the 108 Karanas of the Natya Shastra and the philosophy of Shankaracharya are not merely historically or culturally related but are expressions of the same fundamental insight about consciousness, embodiment, and liberation. The

416
The Cosmic Choreography

evidence for this thesis has been assembled from multiple independent sources and has, we hope, been demonstrated to be both extensive and convergent.

The synthesis this book traces is not a new invention but a recovery: a recovery of an understanding that was present in the tradition from its earliest phases, that found its most complete historical expression in the Chola period temple programmes that carved the 108 Karanas in stone adjacent to the Nataraja shrine at Chidambaram, and that was disrupted by the colonial suppression of the Devadasi tradition and the subsequent academic fragmentation of the tradition’s study into separate disciplinary domains. The recovery of this understanding — which is simultaneously an aesthetic, philosophical, devotional, and somatic understanding — is one of the most important contributions that contemporary scholarship can make to the living traditions it studies.

The practical implications of this recovery extend far beyond the academic domain. For classical Indian dance practitioners, the recovery of the philosophical dimensions of the Karana tradition transforms the entire enterprise of training and performance: not as an addition to the technical training but as its deepest dimension, the ground from which the most refined technical execution arises and the goal toward which it points. For students of Advaita Vedanta, the recovery of the embodied dimensions of the philosophical tradition reveals new possibilities for practice: the body as a vehicle of philosophical inquiry rather than merely an obstacle to it, the movement vocabulary of the Karanas as a language of philosophical investigation that

417
Synthesis and Conclusions

complements and deepens the discursive inquiry that textual study provides.

For contemporary culture more broadly, the synthesis this book traces offers a model of integration that the fragmented culture of modernity desperately needs: a demonstration that rigorous intellectual inquiry and refined aesthetic practice, philosophical depth and artistic beauty, contemplative interiority and creative expressiveness are not competing values but complementary aspects of a single, integrated human excellence. The Indian tradition’s achievement of this integration — embodied in the 108 Karanas and articulated by Shankaracharya’s philosophy — is not a historical curiosity but a living resource, available to anyone willing to engage with it on its own terms.

The dance continues. The philosophy continues. And the synthesis between them — the cosmic choreography of consciousness expressing itself through every form of genuine human wisdom and beauty — continues as the living invitation that this book has tried, in its own necessarily partial and incomplete way, to describe. Anando Brahma. Nrityo Brahma. Bliss is Brahman. The dance is Brahman. And you, the reader of these words, are that Brahman — the infinite, dancing consciousness that is reading this sentence in the same way that it dances the 108 Karanas and recognises itself in the mirror of Shankaracharya’s philosophy: freely, blissfully, without beginning or end.

418
EPILOGUE

The Dance That Never Ends

We return, at the end of this long journey through texts and temples, philosophy and movement, to a simple image: a single dancer standing before a stone panel in the corridors of Chidambaram, studying the carved figure of a Karana. The dancer is here; the stone is here; between them, across a thousand years of silence, something is transmitted. This transmission — direct, non-verbal, crossing the boundaries of time and medium — is the deepest truth that this study has sought to articulate. The 108 Karanas carved in stone at Chidambaram are not images of movements; they are movements arrested at the peak of their expression, like sentences that eternally speak their meaning without requiring a speaker.

Shankaracharya’s philosophical texts are not merely descriptions of consciousness; they are vehicles of a recognition that can be triggered in the attentive reader across centuries of textual transmission. Both the stone Karana and the Sanskrit sloka point beyond themselves toward the same recogni— tion: the recognition that the one who observes the Karana, the one

419
The Dance That Never Ends

who reads the sloka, and the consciousness that carved the stone and composed the verse are all the same single awareness, temporarily appearing as many but never ceasing to be one.

This book has traced the pathways by which two of India’s greatest intellectual traditions — the Natya Shastra’s tradition of sacred performance and Shankaracharya’s tradition of Advaita Vedanta — converge on this recognition from different directions. The convergence is not accidental. Both traditions emerged from the same civilisational depth, were nourished by the same cosmological vision, and were sustained by the same conviction that the highest human calling is the recognition of the truth about consciousness: that it is one, that it is free, that it is bliss, and that its most complete self-expression in the human domain is the dance.

“The Dancer is Brahman. The Dance is Maya. The Witness is what you are.”

The Ananda Tandava continues. Shiva dances at Chidambaram in every moment, and in every moment of genuine artistic awareness, and in the silent depths of every consciousness that has ever wondered at the mystery of existence. The 108 Karanas are not historical artefacts; they are living invitations — to the dancer, to the philosopher, to the human being simply alive in this extraordinary, dancing universe.

May this study serve as one small contribution to the tradition’s ongoing transmission. May the Karanas be danced, the texts be studied, the temples be visited, and the living masters be

420
The Cosmic Choreography

sought out and honoured. And above all, may the recognition to which the tradition points — the recognition that has no beginning and no end, that requires no particular time or place or medium for its occurrence — find its moment in every reader who encounters these pages.

Tat tvam asi — That thou art.
Naredla Ramachandra

GLOSSARY OF SANSKRIT TERMS

The following glossary provides concise definitions of the major Sanskrit technical terms employed in this study. For extended discussions of each term, readers are referred to the relevant chapters. Transliterations follow standard scholarly conventions; diacritical marks have been simplified for accessibility.

Abhaya: Fearlessness; the quality of the liberated sage and a gesture (mudra) conveying divine protection, associated with the lower right hand of Nataraja.

Abhinaya: Expressive communication in classical Indian performance; the fourfold system encompassing Angika (bodily), Vachika (vocal), Aharya (costume/makeup), and Sattvika (involuntary authentic) expression.

Abhinavabharati: Abhinavagupta’s monumental commentary on the Natya Shastra (c. 1000 CE); the primary philosophical elaboration of Rasa theory in its relation to non-dual consciousness.

422
The Cosmic Choreography

Advaita: Non-dual; the philosophical position that reality is fundamentally one — pure consciousness without division or multiplicity.

Anahata Nada: Unstruck or uncaused sound; the inner sound that arises in deep meditation without physical cause, understood as the direct sonic manifestation of Brahman.

Ananda: Bliss; the third of the three fundamental qualifications of Brahman (Sat-Chit-Ananda). The Ananda Tandava is Shiva’s Dance of Bliss.

Angahara: A sequence of three to seven Karanas forming a coherent movement phrase; 32 Angaharas are described in the Natya Shastra.

Angikabhinaya: Physical or bodily expression; one of the four types of Abhinaya, encompassing the complete vocabulary of embodied performance.

Apasmara: Ignorance personified as the dwarf demon beneath Shiva’s dancing foot in the Nataraja image, representing the ego-illusion that liberation dissolves.

Aparoksha Anubhuti: Direct, non-mediate experience; the immediate recognition of Brahman that constitutes liberation in the Advaita Vedanta tradition.

Atman: The innermost Self; in Advaita Vedanta, identical with Brahman. The recognition of this identity is liberation.

Avidya: Ignorance; the fundamental misidentification of the Self with the

423
Glossary

non-Self that is the root of all suffering and the obstacle to liberation.

Bhava: Emotional state; the psychological basis of Rasa in the Natya Shastra theory of aesthetic experience.

Brahman: The ultimate reality in Advaita Vedanta; pure, self-luminous, non-dual consciousness. Sat-Chit-Ananda: Being, Consciousness, Bliss.

Chari: A single-leg movement forming the kinetic component of a Karana; the Natya Shastra describes 32 primary Charis.

Chidambaram: The supreme Nataraja temple in Tamil Nadu; site of the Akasha Linga (formless absolute) and the complete sculptural programme of the 108 Karanas.

Dakshinamurti: Shiva as the silent teacher; the iconographic form of Shiva seated beneath a fig tree, teaching the knowledge of non-duality through the eloquence of silence.

Drishti: Gaze direction; one of the five components of a Karana, encoding the quality of conscious attention that animates the movement.

Guru-Shishya Parampara: The teacher-student lineage of knowledge transmission; the living current through which both performing arts and philosophical wisdom are transmitted in the Indian tradition.

Hasta: Hand gesture; a component of Karanas and a complete system of expressive gestures categorised in three chapters of the Natya Shastra.

424
The Cosmic Choreography

Jivanmukti: Liberation while still in a body; the highest spiritual attainment in Advaita Vedanta, characterised by permanent Sakshi awareness and unshakeable peace.

Karana: Action; in the Natya Shastra, a coordinated unit of hand gesture (hasta) and foot position (pada) constituting the basic vocabulary of sacred dance. 108 Karanas are described in Chapter IV.

Khecharimudra: A specific Yoga mudra associated with the movement of consciousness upward through the subtle body; connected to the elevated Karanas in some interpretive traditions.

Lasya: The feminine, flowing, tender dance style associated with Parvati; the graceful counterpart to the dynamic masculine Tandava.

Laya: Dissolution; the merging of individual consciousness into Brahman at liberation; also the rhythmic timing dimension of musical performance.

Maya: Cosmic illusion or creative power; the mechanism by which Brahman appears as the differentiated world. Neither fully real nor fully unreal — mithya.

Moksha: Liberation; freedom from the cycle of rebirth and from the illusion of separate selfhood. The ultimate goal of human existence.

Mudra: Seal or stamp; sacred gesture communicating a specific quality of consciousness; simultaneously expressive (to others) and performative (in the practitioner).

425
Glossary

Nada: Primordial sound; the vibratory basis of all manifestation. Nada Brahman designates Brahman as the ground of all sound and vibration.

Nataraja: Lord of Dance; the cosmic form of Shiva performing the Ananda Tandava, encoding the five cosmic functions of creation, preservation, dissolution, concealment, and grace.

Natya: Theatre-dance; the integrated performing art combining movement, music, drama, and philosophy. The Natya Shastra calls it a fifth Veda.

Natya Shastra: The Science of Theatre; Bharata Muni’s encyclopaedic treatise on performing arts (c. 200 BCE–200 CE). 36 chapters, approximately 6,000 verses.

Nirguna: Without qualities or attributes; the aspect of Brahman as pure, formless, undifferentiated consciousness, beyond all description and characterisation.

Nritta: Pure dance; movement that is technically refined and aesthetically beautiful but without narrative or expressive content.

Nritya: Expressive dance; movement combined with emotional and narrative content, the integration of Nritta technique with Abhinaya expression.

Pada: Foot; foot position forming the ground component of a Karana, determining the spatial foundation of the movement.

426
The Cosmic Choreography

Panchakriya: The five cosmic functions of Shiva: Srishti (creation), Sthiti (preservation), Samhara (dissolution), Tirobhava (concealment), and Anugraha (grace/liberation).

Prakriti: Nature/matter; in Samkhya philosophy, the dynamic, material principle characterised by the three Gunas (Sattva, Rajas, Tamas).

Purusha: Consciousness/spirit; in Samkhya philosophy, the eternal, unchanging conscious witness that observes Prakriti’s activity.

Rasa: Aesthetic flavor or experience; the theory of nine aesthetic emotions in the Natya Shastra (Shringara, Hasya, Karuna, Raudra, Vira, Bhayanaka, Bibhatsa, Adbhuta, Shanta).

Saguna: With qualities or attributes; the aspect of Brahman as the personal God, expressed through the beautiful forms of the cosmic dance and the temple iconography.

Sahridaya: Person of similar heart; the ideal spectator capable of experiencing pure Rasa rather than merely personal emotional reactions; the aesthetic equivalent of the Jnani.

Sakshi: Pure witness consciousness; in Advaita Vedanta, the innermost self that observes all phenomena without identification with any of them.

Samkhya: The dualistic philosophical system forming the metaphysical foundation of the Natya Shastra; positing Purusha (consciousness) and Prakriti (matter) as eternal dual principles.

427
Glossary

Sampradaya: Living tradition; the current of knowledge that flows from teacher to student across generations, maintaining its essential quality through personal transmission.

Sattvika: Pertaining to Sattva (the quality of clarity and luminosity); Sattvika Abhinaya is the highest level of performance, arising from genuine inner realisation rather than technical skill alone.

Shanta: Peace/tranquility; the ninth and highest Rasa identified by Abhinavagupta, corresponding philosophically to the experience of Brahman.

Spanda: Primordial vibration or pulsation; in Kashmir Shaivism, the fundamental self-movement of consciousness that underlies all manifestation.

Sthana: Standing position; the foundational ground configuration of a Karana, establishing the body’s spatial and energetic orientation.

Tandava: The vigorous, dynamic, cosmically powerful dance style associated with Shiva’s cosmic dance; the vocabulary of the 108 Karanas.

Tala: Rhythmic cycle; the cyclic temporal organisation of Indian classical music and dance, encoding in its recurring structure the philosophical insight of eternal return.

Vedanta: The culmination of the Vedas; the philosophical tradition based on the Upanishads, Brahma Sutras, and Bhagavad Gita. Advaita Vedanta is its non-dual interpretation.

428
The Cosmic Choreography

Viveka: Discrimination; the faculty of distinguishing the real from the apparent, the Self from the non-Self; the primary instrument of liberation in Advaita Vedanta.

Vivekachudamani: Crest Jewel of Discrimination; Shankaracharya’s major philosophical poem on Advaita Vedanta.

APPENDIX B

Concordance of Shankaracharya’s Dance Metaphors with the 108 Karanas

The following concordance maps key passages from Shankaracharya’s works to corresponding Karanas from the Natya Shastra system, with notes on the philosophical theme connecting them. The abbreviation SL refers to Soundarya Lahari. This concordance does not claim to be exhaustive; it represents the most significant and clearly established correspondences identified in the course of this study. Readers are encouraged to extend this concordance through their own study of the primary texts.

SL Verse 10Wave of bliss flowing from the GoddessNikuttakaSpanda; the primordial vibratory self-expression of bliss
